works.title: PANGEA: an integrated cell atlas across diverse biological contexts enables systematic profiling of multicellular responses in human diseases
Decomposition of the S. aureus pangenome reveals evolving genetic repertoire associated with adaptation and virulence
works.abstract: Bacterial pangenomes are mosaics of vertically inherited chromosomal backgrounds and horizontally acquired mobile elements, yet existing analysis methods either assign each genome to a single phylogenetic group or treat genes independently, failing to resolve this composite architecture. Here, we show that non-negative matrix factorization decomposes the accessory pangenome of 1,398 curated Staphylococcus aureus genomes into 24 additive gene modules (“phylons”) that cleanly separate lineage-defining components from mobile genetic element repertoires, achieving 90% reconstruction accuracy with 96% precision. The additive representation, where each genome equals a primary lineage phylon plus one or more mobilome phylons, recovers known biology (clonal complex structure, immune evasion cluster types) and reveals previously uncharacterized structure, including multiple horizontal transfer events linking the CC30 and hybrid ST239 pandemic lineages. Annotation-independent validation with geNomad confirmed that 75–96% of mobilome phylon gene instances physically reside within prophage regions across all 1,398 genomes, while coordinate-level analysis of the remainder revealed prophage boundary effects, chromosomally integrated elements, and composite mobilome architecture rather than false assignments. External validation on 966 independent draft genome assemblies yielded zero false-positive lineage assignments (mean AUC = 0.996) with no dependence on assembly quality, and mobilome phylons discriminated human from livestock hosts and methicillin-resistant from methicillin-susceptible isolates without retraining. A lightweight projection tool, phylon_assign, enables rapid classification of new genomes. The generalization of this framework from Escherichia coli and Enterobacter to Staphylococcus aureus – species with fundamentally different pangenome structures – establishes non-negative matrix factorization as a scalable, organism-agnostic approach for resolving the modular architecture of bacterial pangenomes.

works.title: SWANS: a highly configurable analysis pipeline for single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-sequencing data
works.abstract: Abstract Background Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is a powerful technique that enables the analysis of gene expression at the individual cell level. Bioinformatic tools for scRNA-seq data analysis have many different options throughout the typical scRNA-seq workflow (normalization, integration, annotation, clustering, and visualization), and the choice of method(s) and parameter(s) at each stage can impact results. Results Here, we introduce SWANS (v2.0), a configurable analysis pipeline that, in a single run, can employ multiple analysis methods, resolutions, and modifiable parameters. The resulting clustering arrangements, differential gene expression results, and other quantitative measurements can be dynamically visualized and compared in a Shiny interactive report to assist in choosing a single analysis schema for annotation and downstream analysis. Once a final approach is chosen, SWANS will perform differential gene expression (DGE) analysis based on experimental conditions and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA) in addition to creating reports that display figures and interactive tables, quality control metrics, and benchmarking information. SWANS uses Snakemake as a workflow manager, Cell Ranger for alignment and gene expression quantification, Seurat for single cell data analysis, and additional single cell R packages for quality control and downstream single cell analysis. Conclusion SWANS is a tailorable pipeline that provides options for quality control, dimensionality reduction, clustering, differential gene expression analysis, gene set enrichment analysis, and trajectory analysis. Additionally, SWANS generates a series of reports that facilitate sharing large volumes of complex data in a clear and concise manner with other investigators.

works.title: Robust model calibration in large-scale systems biology via an adaptive hybrid algorithm
works.abstract: Abstract Parameter estimation is a central challenge in systems biology, particularly for large dynamic models described by nonlinear ordinary differential equations (ODEs). These global optimization problems exhibit landscapes which are topologically heterogeneous, often exhibiting a pathological mixture of stiff, smooth valleys and rugged, noisy plateaus, making single-strategy hybrids ineffective. While methods like enhanced Scatter Search ( eSS ) represent the current state-of-the-art, their rigid intensification strategies can limit performance in large-scale or ill-conditioned scenarios. In this work, we introduce eLSHADE+ , a novel metaheuristic architecture designed to adapt to these topological challenges. The proposed algorithm augments a recent Differential Evolution variant ( LSHADE ) with a probabilistic multistrategy hybridization. Unlike standard memetic algorithms, eLSHADE+ uses three distinct operational modes: (i) gradient-based intensification for precision in differentiable regions, (ii) derivative-free search for robustness against numerical noise, and (iii) pure global exploration to conserve computational resources in complicated basins. Additionally, a logarithmic parameter space transformation is incorporated to facilitate search across multi-scale biological constants. We rigorously evaluated eLSHADE+ using the BioPreDyn benchmark suite, comprising challenging real-world problems. Comparative analysis demonstrates that this adaptive multi-strategy approach yields statistically superior convergence speed and solution accuracy compared to eSS and other competitive metaheuristics, establishing a new baseline for robust model calibration in computational biology. Code and data are available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.18379327 .

works.title: Open foundation models for clinical AI
Peptide-binding motifs define the functional architecture of human leukocyte antigens
works.abstract: Abstract Background Peptide presentation by polymorphic human leukocyte antigens (HLA) is central to adaptive and innate immunity. HLA polymorphism gives rise to allele-specific peptide-binding motifs (PBM) that shape the immunopeptidomes presented across individuals. However, the global functional architecture imposed by this diversity remains poorly understood. Methods Here, we leveraged large-scale immunopeptidomics datasets to perform a comprehensive analysis of PBM across HLA class I (HLA-A, -B, -C) and class II (HLA-DR, -DQ, -DP) molecules. PBM were derived from public resources and de novo motif deconvolution of 334,089 class II peptides, followed by hierarchical clustering to define functional groups. We systematically evaluated the association of these groups with immunopeptidome overlap and their relation to established models of HLA functional diversity. Results We identified 40 discrete PBM-defined functional groups across 155 class I and 93 class II allotypes. Molecules within the same PBM group showed significantly higher immunopeptidome similarity compared to those across groups. In class II, PBM grouping was further shaped by HLA-DRB3/4/5 paralogues and by α-chain polymorphism in HLA-DQ and -DP, which modulated group assignment of specific β-chains. PBM classification showed only partial concordance with serological antigen groups and evolutionary divergence metrics, but captured differences in peptide repertoires with higher resolution than existing sequence- or epitope-based models. Overall, PBM-based grouping provided a more direct representation of immunopeptidome diversity. Conclusions This pan-HLA PBM framework comprehensively maps the functional architecture of antigen presentation and provides a unified platform to functionally classify HLA diversity. By capturing immunopeptidome divergence, PBM groups offer a foundation for improving the interpretation of HLA variation in immunogenetics, transplantation, and immune-mediated diseases.

works.title: Novel enzymes for amino acid biosynthesis in diverse bacteria and archaea: GapMind 2026
works.abstract: We previously described GapMind, an automated web-based tool for annotating amino acid biosynthesis pathways in bacterial and archaeal genomes. We used GapMind to identify gaps in biosynthetic pathways and systematically used comparative genomics and high-throughput genetics to identify candidate genes to fill these gaps. We confirmed the activity of ten of the proposed enzymes by using cross-species complementation assays. Highlights include a route to glycine via glyoxylate, two families that can replace phosphoserine phosphatase, an alternative N-succinyl-L,L-diaminopimelate desuccinylase, an alternative N-acetylornithine deacetylase, and a putative bifunctional MetB/MetC. We updated GapMind to include these additional enzymes. Across 208 prokaryotes that have high-quality genomes and can grow in minimal media, the average number of unexplained missing steps or gaps in amino acid biosynthesis dropped from 1.4 per genome to 0.7 per genome. The majority of remaining gaps involve the gain or loss of phosphate groups.

works.title: MetaHQ: Harmonized, high-quality metadata annotations of public omics samples and studies
works.abstract: SUMMARY: Public omics databases like the Gene Expression Omnibus and the Sequence Read Archive offer substantial opportunities for data reuse to address novel biomedical questions. However, it is still difficult to find samples and studies of interest since they are described by free-text metadata and lack standardized annotations. To address this issue, multiple research groups have undertaken curation efforts to add standardized annotations to large collections of these data, but these annotations are fragmented across online resources and are stored in different formats subject to varying standardization criteria, hindering the integration of annotations across sources. We developed MetaHQ to harmonize and distribute standardized metadata for public omics samples. MetaHQ comprises a database with annotations for >567k samples and >27k studies in GEO from 13 sources and a user-friendly command-line interface (CLI) to query the database and retrieve annotations. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: The MetaHQ CLI is deployed as a Python Package on PyPI at https://pypi.org/project/metahq-cli that accesses the MetaHQ database available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17663086. Project source code and documentation are available at https://github.com/krishnanlab/meta-hq. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

works.title: Advancing multimodal tools to decode organoid complexity
Spatial transcriptomics defines segmental and temporal dynamics of pig intestinal epithelium
works.abstract: The pig ( Sus scrofa ) is widely studied as a large-animal model for human gastrointestinal biology, including gut physiology, pathology and disease. However, the spatial and developmental organisation of the pig intestine is not yet fully understood. Here, we generate a comprehensive spatiotemporal atlas of pig intestinal development by applying spatial transcriptomics to three intestinal segments across five developmental stages and an additional four intestinal segments at the adult stage. We identify spatial separation among enterocytes, plasma cells and stem cells, observing more pronounced separation in the small intestine compared to the large intestine. Pseudotime analysis of enterocyte-enriched regions reveals a gradient along the crypt-villus/crypt axis as early as post-conception day 70 in the jejunum, becoming fully evident across all intestinal segments by birth in the large intestine, with all three intestinal segments reaching a mature state by postnatal day 33. Our analysis indicates that the maturation of enterocytes during migration along the crypt-villus axis involves transcriptional programs similar to those governing enterocyte maturation across developmental stages, suggesting conserved molecular mechanisms governing both spatial and temporal differentiation. In the large intestine, nutrient transport-related gene expression declines progressively during development, transitioning from jejunum-like levels at early stages to markedly reduced levels in adulthood, consistent with functional specialization of distinct intestinal segments. Our study provides a high-resolution spatiotemporal framework of pig intestinal development and establishes a valuable resource for comparative biology and translational research.

works.title: FDTest: Fluctuation-dissipation theorem as a test for memory effects in brain dynamics
works.abstract: A central challenge in neuroscience is to understand how the brain flexibly balances local and distributed information processing to support diverse cognitive and conscious states. We hypothesize that a key signature of this balance is the presence of memory effects, which arise when a brain region's future activity depends not only on its current state, but also on past information fed back from the wider network. Here we introduce the FDTest, a method for assessing local memory effects in multidimensional systems by measuring violations of a generalized Fluctuation-dissipation theorem (FDT). We first apply this framework to whole-brain models fitted to human neuroimaging data, demonstrating that the brain's memory structure reflects its underlying connectivity. We then extend the analysis to individualized models of subjects during wakefulness and deep sleep. Memory effects are consistently stronger in wakefulness, indicating richer inter-regional dependencies and more integrated dynamics. These findings establish local memory as a dynamical marker of brain state and position the FDTest as a principled tool for probing the hidden structure of neural dynamics.

works.title: PhysInfer: A physics-constrained neural network for adaptive inference of transcriptional bursting from single-cell RNA-seq
works.abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has established that gene expression is driven by stochastic transcriptional bursting. However, inferring burst dynamics from static scRNA-seq snapshots is fundamentally constrained by parameter unidentifiability and model topology mismatch. Here, we propose PhysInfer, an unsupervised framework that integrates a physics-constrained neural network with adaptive model selection and parameter decoupling. A physics-informed loss function, combining stationary-distribution likelihood with zero-count anchoring, reparameterizes the optimization from unidentifiable microscopic rates to an interpretable macroscopic burst-quantity representation of burst size and burst frequency, thereby providing an interpretable parameterization for assessing practical recoverability in static data. Validation on synthetic data with known ground-truth parameters confirms high inference accuracy in low-to-medium activation regimes and shows that recovery of BS and productive BF becomes increasingly condition-dependent as the ON-state probability approaches saturation; under different recovery criteria, the condition-specific upper Pon limit for simultaneously recovering BS and productive BF varies with cell number and capture efficiency. Applied to a mouse embryonic fibroblast (MEF) dataset, PhysInfer reconstructs a transcriptional dynamic manifold across the 2,137-gene secondary BIC analysis set, showing cross-gene variation in fitted burst frequency and burst size. A model-specific stationary likelihood combined with zero-count anchoring improves robustness to zero-heavy observations. The adaptive topology module further identifies a distinct subset of genes with stable support for an effective sequential 3-state representation, revealing distributional structure beyond that captured by standard 2-state fitting. PhysInfer thus provides a robust, topology-adaptive, and interpretable solution for characterizing transcriptional kinetic patterns from static single-cell transcriptomic snapshots.

works.title: Sphinx: An R package for adaptive spatial neighborhood modeling and functional analysis in spatial omics
works.abstract: Spatial omics enables analysis of tissue microenvironmental heterogeneity, but most spatial tools are optimized for transcriptomics and poorly suited to proteomics data. We developed Sphinx, an R package providing a comprehensive workflow for spatial proteomics, including preprocessing, cell annotation, adaptive spatial neighborhood modeling, and functional characterization. Importantly, it introduces an adaptive parameter selection framework guided by spatial statistical metrics and incorporates computational optimizations for large-scale datasets, enabling robust neighborhood modeling. Notably, Sphinx offers improved computational efficiency and scalability. Across lung adenocarcinoma, colorectal cancer, and mouse spleen datasets, Sphinx robustly identifies cell types and spatial functional units, including tertiary lymphoid structures. We also explored the application of Sphinx to paired high-resolution spatial transcriptomics datasets, illustrating its potential applicability. Sphinx provides a flexible and efficient framework for spatial proteomics, enabling robust characterization of spatial organization and tissue microenvironments.

works.title: An antigen-specific protein language model guides CDR optimization for antibody design
works.abstract: The capacity of an antibody to recognize and bind an antigen with high specificity and strength (i.e., its binding affinity) is a key determinant in the design and optimization of neutralizing antibodies against pathogenic targets. Here we introduce Ab-Affinity, a fine-tuned protein language model (PLM) that predicts the binding affinity of an antibody against a target peptide within the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. Cross-validation results shows that that Ab-Affinity outperforms other PLM-based affinity predictors when evaluated on a held-out validation and independent test sets. When integrated with a genetic algorithm and simulated annealing for sequence diversification and fitness optimization, Ab-Affinity enables the generation of candidate antibodies exhibiting over 100-fold improvement in predicted binding affinity relative to its parental (natural) antibody. More broadly, antibodies designed with Ab-Affinity attain higher predicted binding affinities than those produced by alternative mutational strategies, yielding synthetic antibodies with favorable predicted biophysical characteristics. Molecular docking and molecular dynamics simulations for the strongest synthetic candidates indicate enhanced interactions and increased stability with the target peptide epitope within the spike protein. Experimental validation in vitro for a top-ranked candidate reveals an apparent increase in binding relative to its parental antibody. All model weights, source code, and analysis pipelines are publicly released to allow full reproducibility.

works.title: Burst-to-burst information resetting in sequential rhythmic neural activity
works.abstract: In multiple neural systems, networks of bursting neurons generate and coordinate robust sequential rhythms, such as those observed in central pattern generators (CPGs) that control motor activity. In this paper, we combine electrophysiological experiments and biophysical models of the pyloric CPG to investigate cycle-by-cycle coordination resetting in sequential rhythms. In particular, we focus our analysis on the variability constraints of sequence intervals defined by the burst onset and offset time references, which structure the timing of the rhythmic CPG sequence cycle-by-cycle. We identified the conditions under which sequential dynamical invariants emerge as robust relationships between specific intervals within the same cycle, and when such relations reset at each cycle or extend between intervals of consecutive cycles. Our results help understand the mechanisms underlying the autonomous cycle-by-cycle sequential coordination and the relationships between intervals from consecutive cycles when a slow modulatory action establishes a common trend across the rhythm.

works.title: Pepti-DrugPhAI: Multimodal AI-evaluator for functional pharmacokinetics and toxicity of peptides
works.abstract: Peptide drugs exhibit exceptional selectivity for biological targets and high functional activity making them among the most promising therapeutic agents. However, unsatisfactory pharmacokinetic characteristics remain a critical barrier to their implementation. They often become the primary reason for the failure of promising candidates in preclinical and clinical trials. To address this issue, we present Pepti-DrugPhAI - a comprehensive algorithm for the precise prediction of the pharmacokinetics and toxicity of a wide range of peptide compounds. Unlike many existing solutions, the proposed algorithm is multimodal and can simultaneously process both SMILES representations of chemical structures and amino acid sequences. This ensures efficient processing not only of canonical peptides but also of non-canonical modifications, cyclic structures, and peptide-like small molecules. We also created an original dataset for model training integrating data from public databases and relevant scientific publications. The algorithm simultaneously predicts key parameters including membrane permeability (Caco-2 and PAMPA penetration), distribution and excretion (half-life, clearance, volume of distribution), as well as general and specific toxicity profiles (neurotoxicity, hemolytic activity). A key innovation of the study is the integration of functional pharmacokinetic scoring. The model not only predicts ADMET values but also calculates an adaptive suitability rating for a compound in the context of its specific biological activity. We have conducted a comparative analysis of various data encoding strategies implementing a stack of models ranging from classical machine learning methods to modern transformers and language models in classification modes. Results from testing on independent test sets demonstrate high prediction accuracy and interpretability of features making Pepti-DrugPhAI a powerful tool for more robust selection of promising peptide drug candidates. All data and the code are available in the GitHub repository at https://github.com/EABogdanova/Pepti-DrugPhAI.

works.title: Check my sample sheet: a web application for validating illumina sample sheets before demultiplexing
works.abstract: Proper configuration of an Illumina sequencing run is crucial for ensuring successful outcomes, with the sample sheet serving as a vital component by summarizing sample metadata. Accurate demultiplexing and downstream analysis depend heavily on the correctness of this sample sheet. To address this need, validation of the sample sheet becomes essential to prevent errors during sequencing processes. We present a browser-based web application built using Streamlit, which incorporates the IEM Python module from the Sequana Python library to perform comprehensive sanity checks on Illumina sample sheets. This application allows users to upload or paste sample sheet files through a simple interface that requires no installation, where automated validation checks are performed. These checks assess key parameters such as sample duplication, consistency, and adherence to Illumina formatting standards. HierHGT-DTI provides an effective multiscale relation-aware framework for cold-start DTI predictiConclusions. The “Check My Sample Sheet" web application enables users to preemptively detect and resolve potential issues in their sample sheets, reducing errors and improving sequencing outcomes. The application supports both the legacy bcl2fastq (v1) and the newer bclconvert (v2, BCL Convert) sample sheet formats, detecting the version automatically. Additionally, the application’s open-source nature supports extensibility, making it adaptable to specific workflow requirements.

works.title: LoRA-BERT: a natural language processing model for robust and accurate prediction of long non-coding RNAs
works.abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are key regulators in many biological processes. While they share some sequence features with messenger RNAs (mRNAs), lncRNAs have distinct functions, opening new research opportunities. Recent advances in next-generation sequencing have made it easier to detect lncRNAs, and deep learning methods are increasingly used to classify these transcripts. Although these methods have significantly improved the efficiency of identifying lncRNAs, they often lack robustness, and the prediction accuracy tends to vary significantly depending on the quality of the transcript. To tackle this issue, we introduce LoRA-BERT, a novel lncRNA prediction algorithm built on the bidirectional encoder representation from transformers (BERT). LoRA-BERT is designed to effectively capture information at the nucleotide level that is important for lncRNA classification, leading to more robust and accurate prediction outcomes that are not significantly affected by the quality of the input transcript. Through performance evaluations on comprehensive benchmarks, we demonstrate that LoRA-BERT outperforms existing schemes in terms of accuracy, efficiency, and robustness. Especially, unlike other methods, LoRA-BERT retains good predictive capability for partial transcripts, a critical feature that makes it applicable for reliable lncRNA prediction even when the sequencing depth is relatively low. Availability and implementation: The code repository is available at https://github.com/Nick-Jeon/LoRA_BERT .

works.title: PHI: a Galaxy-based workflow for reproducible prophage-host interaction analysis and standardized viral-genomics reporting
works.abstract: Abstract Background Viruses that infect bacteria, known as bacteriophages or phages, are widespread in nature and play important roles in shaping microbial communities and ecosystem functions. Some phages can integrate into bacterial genomes as “prophages”, where they may influence the biology of their host by carrying genes that affect metabolism, virulence, or environmental adaptation. Despite their importance, studying prophages and their interactions with bacterial hosts remains challenging because it typically requires combining many complex computational tools and can be resource-intensive. Results In this study, we introduce the Prophage-Host Interaction Toolkit (PHI), a user-friendly and automated workflow available through the Galaxy platform. PHI brings together multiple established tools into a single, reproducible pipeline that identifies candidate prophages, evaluates their quality, predicts host relationships, and characterizes key functional genes. Importantly, all results are summarized in an interactive report that simplifies interpretation. Applied to the MBARC22 mock community of 22 bacterial reference genomes as a workflow demonstration, PHI identified 41 candidate prophages across 14 hosts, including high- and medium-quality viral genomes. Most host genomes exhibited > 99% completeness and < 1% contamination, while DefenseFinder identified between 3 and 24 antiviral defense systems per genome. To further evaluate applicability to metagenome-derived assemblies, PHI was also applied to three MAGs and their matched reference genomes. Differences in candidate prophage counts and sequence-level correspondence between MAGs and references demonstrated that prophage recovery can be strongly influenced by genome fragmentation and assembly continuity, even in otherwise high-quality MAGs. Conclusions By removing installation barriers and consolidating the outputs of multiple established tools, PHI lowers the barrier to advanced phage analysis, enabling both specialists and non-experts to explore phage-host interactions and their implications in areas such as microbiome research, biotechnology, and environmental science.

works.title: Benchmarking precision matrix estimation methods for differential co-expression network analysis
works.abstract: Abstract Background Gene expression profiling is widely used to investigate disease mechanisms, but classical approaches such as differential expression or pairwise correlation analyses provide limited interpretability. Network-based differential co-expression methods that model conditional dependencies through partial correlations offer richer insights, yet their application in high-dimensional settings requires estimation of precision matrices. Numerous precision matrix estimation methods (PMEMs) have been proposed, but these are typically validated in a narrow range of simulation settings and benchmarked against only a small number of competing methods, so their relative performance under diverse conditions remains unclear. Results Simulated gene expression datasets with known ground truth correlation structures were used to benchmark a broad set of PMEMs for their suitability in differential co-expression network analysis of transcriptomic data. Performance was strongly affected by data characteristics, including covariance structure, matrix density, covariance values, sample size-to-dimension ratio, and sampling distribution. Among the evaluated methods, GLassoElnetFast generally achieved high accuracy in recovering differential edges across the simulated scenarios, although high signal-to-noise ratios and sufficient sample sizes remain essential for reliable inference. Applying a subset of these methods to a real transcriptomic dataset reproduced this estimator-dependent variability, with limited overlap between the differential edges recovered by different methods. Conclusions Evaluation across diverse simulation conditions demonstrated that no single metric or condition was sufficient to assess PMEM performance. Therefore, less extensive evaluations may only capture part of this variability and limit the generalizability of their conclusions. Our simulation and benchmarking framework supports future method development and ensures reproducible evaluation of newly developed approaches.

works.title: Track display jockey (trackDJ): a user-friendly R package for visualization of epigenomic data
works.abstract: Abstract Background Visualization of epigenomic data such as coverage tracks, peak calls, and chromatin interactions is a critical task in genomic data analysis. Although genome browsers such as the Integrative Genomics Viewer (IGV) and the UCSC Genome Browser permit user-friendly exploration of genomic tracks, they are not optimized for fully programmatic and reproducible generation of publication-quality figures. In contrast, existing programmatic tools lack a user-friendly interface and require extensive configuration. Results We present trackDJ (Track Display Jockey), an R package for visualization of epigenomic data. trackDJ prioritizes usability by favoring convention over configuration; it provides high-level plotting functions with sensible defaults, aiming to allow users with minimal programming experience to generate clear, publication-quality figures with relatively little coding. Within a unified plotting framework, users can stack and align multiple data types, including coverage tracks, peak annotations, chromatin loops, and gene annotations. trackDJ allows users to select plotted genomic regions by coordinates or by gene name, enabling rapid visualization without knowledge of precise locus boundaries. Conclusions trackDJ complements existing epigenomics toolkits by providing a user-friendly, reproducible alternative to interactive genome browsers for epigenomic visualization. By enabling scripted generation of clean, customizable genomic illustrations, trackDJ readily integrates into R-based analysis workflows to streamline the creation of publication-quality figures.

works.title: TADDM-WMHHGCN: a weighted multi-head hypergraph convolutional network for predicting triple associations among drugs, diseases, and miRNAs
works.abstract: Associations among drugs, diseases, and microRNAs (miRNAs) are important for elucidating disease mechanisms and supporting drug repositioning. Several computational models predict pairwise drug-disease, drug-miRNA, or miRNA-disease associations. However, few models have addressed associations involving all three entity types, and no model has specifically focused on triple associations among drugs, diseases, and miRNAs (TADDMs). We developed TADDM-WMHHGCN, a weighted multi-head hypergraph convolutional network for predicting TADDMs. Candidate TADDMs were constructed by integrating validated drug-disease, drug-miRNA, and miRNA-disease pairwise associations and were represented using a three-dimensional (3D) adjacency matrix. Raw drug, disease, and miRNA features were derived from this matrix as 3D Gaussian interaction profile (GIP) kernel matrices. We then constructed a weighted heterogeneous hypergraph from the adjacency and GIP kernel matrices. After linear transformation, the raw features were passed through a multi-head hypergraph convolutional network to obtain high-level representations, and a multilayer perceptron decoder generated the predictions. In internal cross-validation on four datasets containing different categories of unlabeled triples of drugs, diseases, and miRNAs, the model achieved AUROC and AUPR values above 0.94 for every dataset. TADDM-WMHHGCN outperformed several existing triple-association prediction models across most evaluation metrics, demonstrating its potential as a tool in the research on the associations among drugs, diseases, and miRNAs.

works.title: BactFlow: a graphical workflow for bacterial genome assembly and annotation
works.abstract: Bacterial genome reconstruction increasingly uses short-read, long-read, and hybrid sequencing strategies. However, coordinating read processing, genome assembly, quality assessment, and downstream characterization across these data types can require substantial bioinformatics expertise. We developed BactFlow ( https://github.com/farhadm1990/bactflow ), an open-source interactive app for bacterial single isolate genome assembly and downstream analysis. It supports Nanopore and PacBio long reads, Illumina short reads, and Nanopore-Illumina data for hybrid assembly. A single local browser interface integrates read processing and quality assessment, genome assembly, and post-assembly analysis, with run-status monitoring. BactFlow combines genome-quality assessment, taxonomic classification, gene annotation, plasmid prediction, and interactive genome visualization. We demonstrated four assembly routes using publicly available Nanopore, Illumina, and PacBio datasets, as well as Nanopore-Illumina hybrid assembly. After initial setup on Linux, BactFlow can be launched with a single command line using Docker, Apptainer/Singularity, or Conda. Users can then configure and run analyses through the user interface (UI) without manually invoking each bioinformatics tool. The integrated interface supports bacterial isolate genome analysis across multiple sequencing strategies.

works.title: Distance, Survival and Sex: Addressing a Three-Way Trade-Off in Healthspan Trial Recruitment
Collective Mechanical Modes in a Minimal Model of Ion Channel Gate Dynamics
Editorial Summary for Mechanistic Insights into Membrane Protein Dynamics and Allostery: Implications in Drug Discovery
Saturation genome editing of BRCA1 across cell types improves interpretation of variant pathogenicity
works.abstract: Abstract Germline pathogenic BRCA1 variants predispose women to breast and ovarian cancer. Despite accumulation of functional evidence, over half of reported single-nucleotide variants in BRCA1 lack a definitive clinical interpretation. Furthermore, the consistency of variant effects across cell types remains largely unexplored. Here we performed saturation genome editing (SGE) of BRCA1 in HAP1 cells to score 4,113 previously unassayed variants. Additionally, we developed an SGE assay in human mammary epithelial cells (HMECs), allowing comparison of effects across cell lines, drug treatments and genetic backgrounds. We identified 538 variants impacting gene function through distinct mechanisms. HAP1 function scores discriminate between known pathogenic and benign variants with near-perfect accuracy. Intriguingly, however, nearly half of HAP1 loss-of-function variants scored neutrally in HMECs. We show that discordantly scored variants are hypomorphic and confer intermediate cancer risk. Overall, this work demonstrates how performing SGE across cell models improves the functional interpretation of rare variants.

works.title: Identification of (ultra-)rare candidate functional promoter mutations in cancer using sequence-based deep learning models
works.abstract: Abstract Background The identification of non-coding somatic cancer-driver mutations remains challenging due to difficulties in interpreting rare and ultra-rare variants. We hypothesized that sequence-based models can be used to systematically prioritize such mutations for their functional relevance. Methods Here, we developed a computational framework that leverages two sequence-based models to assess the functional impact of (ultra-)rare somatic single nucleotide variants (SNVs) in promoter regions. We first tested the validity of our approach by analysing SNVs derived from 3,825 whole-tumour genomes from patients for whom we also had matching RNA-seq data available. Results This very strict validation strategy yielded 57 genes that contain promoter mutations that our model consistently predicts to preferentially activate or repress gene expression in three cohorts of different patients. For nine genes we could confirm a nominally significant change using actual gene expression level measurements as well (6.32× higher than expected by chance, p -value = 1.16 × 10 − 5 ). These genes include well known cancer genes such as TERT and PMS2 , but also several new candidates for which no coding mutations have previously been implicated in cancer, including AIMP2 , SASS6 , ALKBH4 , FICD , TTK , YAE1 and ETF1 . We subsequently conducted a meta-analysis across 24,529 samples that revealed 619 genes, whose promoters are significantly enriched for candidate functional SNVs. These genes are significantly enriched for cancer-driver genes ( p -value = 5.94 × 10 − 3 ), cell cycle genes ( p -values ranging from 1.24 × 10 − 3 to 2.82 × 10 − 2 ) and are more evolutionary conserved than expected by chance ( p -value = 0.022). Conclusions These findings demonstrate the utility of sequence-based models for identifying candidate functional non-coding mutations and suggest that many non-coding somatic mutations contribute to cancer development.

works.title: A genome-wide association study and genetic risk score for age at diabetes diagnosis support beta-cell dysfunction in young-onset diabetes in Chinese
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: We investigated genetic variations driving young age-at-diabetes-diagnosis (ADD) and developed a genetic risk score (GRS) to identify Chinese individuals at risk of young-onset diabetes (YOD with ADD<40). METHODS: We performed genome-wide association studies (GWAS) for ADD with internal and external replication in 22,611 individuals with type 2 diabetes (T2D, 20% with YOD) and identified Chinese-prioritized loci by conditioning on the polygenic risk score (PRS) of ADD constructed from publicly available datasets. We constructed ADD-GRS using genome-wide independent variants (p<5E-08) and examined its associations with glycemic traits in diabetes and non-diabetes cohorts. RESULTS: We identified three independent signals at genome-wide significance (P < 5×10-8) mapping to CDKAL1 (rs2206734, β=-0.75 (SE:0.13) per copy of T allele, effect allele frequency (EAF)=0.38, p=2.12E-09), PAX4 (rs61160304, β=-1.01 (SE:0.17) per copy of T allele, EAF=0.19, p=2.51E-09), and KCNQ1 (rs2299620, β=-0.77 (SE:0.14) per copy of G allele, EAF=0.70, p=2.80E-08). The variants at PAX4 and KCNQ1 were independent of the genetic liability estimated by ADD-PRS from Europeans and South Indians. In the diabetes cohort, the ADD-GRS was associated with younger ADD, lower C-peptide, higher HbA1c and pathway-specific T2D-PRS for beta-cell+proinsulin and residual glycemia. Using YOD versus later-onset diabetes as a secondary outcome, LINC02783/PADI1 (rs72895704, OR:1.52 per copy of A allele, EAF=0.02, p=1.93E-06) and TARS2P1 (rs145218437, OR: 1.73 per copy of C allele, EAF=0.02, p=7.57E-08) showed suggestive significance. CONCLUSIONS: Both known and novel T2D loci contribute to ADD in Chinese people and may be used to detect high risk individuals for early intervention to prevent or delay onset of YOD.

works.title: Tachykinin-like NLP-58 signaling through TKR-1 modulates thermotaxis behavior in Caenorhabditis elegans
works.abstract: Neurokinin B (NKB) signaling plays a central role in mammalian thermoregulatory dysfunction associated with menopause, yet the underlying neural mechanisms remain incompletely understood. Here, we establish Caenorhabditis elegans thermotaxis as a genetically tractable system for investigating conserved tachykinin signaling. We demonstrate that overexpression of nlp-58, the C. elegans ortholog of mammalian NKB, induces abnormal thermotaxis behavior without impairing the temperature response of the thermosensory neurons. NLP-58 is expressed in multiple neurons, including the AIY interneurons, a central integrative node of the thermosensory circuit. AIY-specific overexpression of nlp-58 is sufficient to reproduce the thermotaxis defect, identifying AIY as an important site of NLP-58-dependent behavioral modulation. Genetic analyses further demonstrated that the thermotaxis behavior is mediated primarily through the tachykinin receptor TKR-1, the homolog of mammalian tachykinin 3 receptor (NK3R), acting in ASG and/or ASJ sensory neurons. We also identified a genetic interaction between dhs-4, a lipid metabolic enzyme gene, and nlp-58, suggesting that lipid metabolic pathway modulate tachykinin-dependent thermotaxis behavior. Furthermore, endogenous NLP-58/TKR-1 signaling contributed to the age-dependent decline in thermotaxis behavior. Finally, treatment with fezolinetant, a selective NK3R antagonist used clinically for menopausal vasomotor symptoms, partially improved the thermotaxis defect caused by nlp-58 overexpression. Together, our findings identify the NLP-58/TKR-1 signaling pathway as a modulatory component of thermotaxis behavior and provide a framework for investigating conserved principles of tachykinin-dependent circuit modulation.

works.title: RSMViewer: A PyMOL plugin for RNA structural motif visualization
works.abstract: SUMMARY: RNA structural motifs (RSMs) are recurrent three-dimensional RNA structural elements characterized by conserved three-dimensional geometries and often associated with specific molecular functions. Their identification, validation, and functional characterization frequently require labor-intensive manual inspection. However, existing molecular visualization tools provide limited support for motif-centric exploration, making large-scale visualization and comparative analysis of RNA motifs inefficient and time-consuming. To address this limitation, we present RSMViewer, an open-source PyMOL plug-in that integrates heterogeneous motif annotations and supports batch visualization and efficient structural superimposition of RNA motif instances. RSMViewer streamlines the exploration and comparative analysis of RNA structural motifs, substantially reducing manual effort and facilitating downstream structural and functional interpretation. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: RSMViewer is implemented in Python and is freely available at https://github.com/Rakib-Hasan-Rahad/RSMViewer.git. It is compatible with PyMOL 2.x and later, on all major operating systems. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

works.title: In situ profiling of plasma cell clonality with image-based single-cell transcriptomics
works.abstract: Image-based single-cell transcriptomics can identify diverse cell types in intact tissues. However, in adaptive immunity, V(D)J recombination generates unique immune receptors in cells of the same type, leading to important functional variation that is not yet defined by these methods. Here we introduce B cell receptor multiplexed error-robust fluorescence in situ hybridization (BCR-MERFISH), which measures plasma cell clonality based on V gene usage in combination with transcriptome profiling. We demonstrate that BCR-MERFISH accurately identifies V gene usage in cell culture and in mice with restricted or native plasma cell diversity. We then use BCR-MERFISH to elucidate the microbiota-dependent changes in plasma cell abundance, clonal diversity, and public clonotype usage in the mouse gut and the non-uniform distribution of plasma cell clones along the mouse ileum. Given that tissue context is an essential modulator of plasma cell dynamics, we anticipate that BCR-MERFISH may offer new insights into a wide range of immunological questions.

works.title: Short-read sequencing benchmarking with donor-specific assemblies
works.abstract: High-throughput short-read sequencing has become a core technology for genomics, but the rapid expansion of available platforms has made it increasingly important to benchmark them under standardized conditions. A major challenge is that conventional reference-based comparisons confound true sequencing errors with inherited variation and reference bias, making it difficult to isolate platform-intrinsic performance. We benchmark nine short-read chemistries across seven DNA sequencers using two highly characterized benchmark samples, HG002 and COLO829BL, together with donor-specific assemblies to measure sequencing errors against sample-matched genomic references. This strategy separates authentic platform errors from biological divergence and reveals substantial differences in substitution, indel, read-position, and sequence-context error profiles. Element AVITI UltraQ and Roche SBX-D show the lowest substitution error rates, whereas Ultima and Roche chemistries exhibit the strongest indel-associated biases. We find pronounced platform-specific effects in low-complexity regions and trinucleotide contexts, including homopolymer-associated errors and context-dependent substitution skews that are directly relevant to rare-variant detection. In addition, we show that donor-specific references are essential for unbiased base-quality recalibration because they minimize reference bias and more faithfully support cross-platform comparison and low-frequency variant-calling thresholds. Donor-specific assembly-based benchmarking provides a robust framework for measuring true short-read sequencing errors and comparing platforms on a common, sample-matched basis. Our results establish a comprehensive reference for the community and show that authentic error profiles can guide platform selection, quality filtering, and improved detection of rare somatic variation.

works.title: Ultrafast alignment-free detection of viral genome variation with bronko
works.abstract: As viral sequencing datasets continue to grow, traditional alignment-based variant calling pipelines are becoming computationally prohibitive. To address these challenges, we developed bronko, an ultrafast alignment-free framework for detecting viral variation directly from sequencing data. The novel computational approach implemented in bronko allows scaling to massive viral sequencing datasets and has four key components: i) a locality-sensitive bucketing function to rapidly identify single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) relative to reference(s), ii) a direct k -mer count pseudo-mapping approach that approximates a pileup without alignment, iii) a greedy de novo assembly algorithm to reconstruct mutation-dense regions and indels and iv) a streaming-based sliding window outlier test to estimate baseline noise across the genome and precisely differentiate real minor variants from noise. Together, these components yield near-linear computational complexity with respect to sequencing depth, enabling bronko to process thousands of viral samples rapidly on modest hardware. Our results are threefold: 1) On simulated amplicon sequencing, bronko recovers variants with higher precision and comparable recall to existing tools while running up to one to three orders of magnitude faster; 2) bronko generates sequence alignments directly from sequencing data, with SNP content nearly identical to that of whole-genome alignment while also running in a fraction of the time, and 3) applying bronko to longitudinal sequencing data from chronically infected SARS-CoV-2 patients revealed consistent patterns of intrahost diversification and adaptive mutations over time. Altogether, these results demonstrate bronko's potential as a scalable tool for large-scale viral genomic analyses, overcoming longstanding computational barriers for intrahost and interhost characterization of viral variation.

works.title: Derivation of doxorubicin mutational signatures in cancer
works.abstract: Doxorubicin is a chemotherapeutic agent used for the treatment of solid and hematopoietic malignancies. Doxorubicin acts as a DNA intercalator and inhibits the topoisomerase II enzyme, leading to double-stranded breaks. We hypothesize that doxorubicin mutagenesis leads to a nonrandom pattern of somatic mutations on the genome, termed a mutational signature. We expose cells to doxorubicin using two different methodologies: (1) continuous exposure of a constant dose of doxorubicin and whole-genome sequencing of single-cell clones (previously published methodology) and (2) pulsed exposure of escalating doses of doxorubicin and whole-genome sequencing of a bulk population. We first confirm that the methodologies do not yield differing results through previously published cisplatin-exposed single-cell clone genome data compared with the dose escalation and bulk genome data. We then derive two doxorubicin signatures. The first, SBS-doxorubicin-1, is defined by an abundance of C > A mutations. The second, SBS-doxorubicin-2, is defined by a higher occurrence of T > C mutations. We then assess for the presence of our signatures within the genomes of patients treated with a doxorubicin-containing regimen. Across 10 bulk immune sorted samples from three patients with follicular lymphoma/diffuse large B cell lymphoma, as well as two metastatic samples from one patient with renal medullary carcinoma, we are able to detect both signatures in 83% of samples, with remaining samples harboring either signature. In summary, we experimentally derive two doxorubicin mutational signatures and demonstrate their presence in patient samples.

works.title: Microfluidic concatemer sequencing unveils cooperative and competitive enhancer clusters in gene regulation
works.abstract: Chromatin looping plays a pivotal role in eukaryotic gene regulation; however, technical limitations have hindered the comprehensive characterization of higher-order interactions among genomic loci. As a result, key questions, such as whether enhancers function cooperatively or competitively at the single-molecule and ensemble levels, remain largely unresolved. Here, we present Drop-t, a novel microfluidics-based method that enables systematic profiling of higher-order chromatin architecture at both the single-molecule and population scales. We demonstrate that Drop-t is not only resistant to common ligation-induced DNA entanglements, which frequently cause nanopore clogging, but also provides greater relevance for elucidating regulatory mechanisms compared to existing ligation-free approaches. Using Drop-t, we uncovered extensive, previously underappreciated non-specific enhancer-promoter interactions (EPIs) and showed that these may influence transcriptional variability by competing with specific EPIs. Notably, we identified two major gene classes, dictator genes and leader genes, based on whether their promoters are predominantly regulated by competitive or cooperative specific EPIs, respectively. Together, our findings established Drop-t as a powerful tool for decoding the higher-order organizational principles of chromatin architecture and their impact on transcriptional regulation and variability.

works.title: Bipartite DNA-binding domain of transcription factor BCL11B binds clustered short DNA sequence motifs
works.abstract: B-cell leukemia/lymphoma 11B (BCL11B), despite its name, is a key regulator of T-cell development, lineage specification, and T-cell malignancies. BCL11B contains a bipartite DNA-binding domain composed of two C2H2 zinc finger arrays: low-affinity ZF2-3 and high-affinity ZF4-6. These arrays recognize similar six-nucleotide motifs, TG(n)CC(n), as seven of the eight DNA base-contacting residues are conserved between them. The most conserved interactions involve the central GG dinucleotides, recognized by arginine and lysine residues at the key base-interacting positions of ZF3 and ZF5. We determined eight crystal structures of ZF2-3 bound to 12- or 20-base pair DNA duplexes containing either one or two binding motifs. The structures reveal that ZF2-3 recognizes DNA with remarkable configurational flexibility, binding motifs on either the same or opposite DNA strands with variable spacing in three relative orientations: head-to-tail (or tail-to-head), head-to-head, and tail-to-tail. Analysis of BCL11B ChIP-seq peaks revealed a strong enrichment of 1-bp-spaced, same-orientation TGACC(c/t) motif pairs. We also examined six neurodevelopmental disorder-associated missense variants affecting DNA base-contacting residues. Substitutions that replace bulky, positively charged arginine or lysine with smaller or hydrophobic amino acids weaken DNA-binding affinity and specificity, whereas substitutions between asparagine and lysine alter base recognition preferences.

works.title: Correction to ‘Different modes of engagement with the nucleosome acidic patch yield distinct functional outcomes’
Estimating rates of SARS-CoV-2 lineage spread using graph spectra from genetic sequence data
works.abstract: The modern enormous scale of viral genomic data, as exemplified by SARS-CoV-2, presents unique opportunities for epidemic inference and real-time monitoring. A key challenge is to wade through the extremely large stream of sequence data in order to identify small subsets of sequences that may represent rapid population growth of newly emerged lineages. To address this challenge, we developed a new approach that combines techniques in graph theory and machine learning. We represent distances between small subsets of sequences as graph Laplacians and identify from them features of rapid population growth. From early sequence data collected in the US and the UK between 2021 and mid-2022, we identified two features—genetic diversity and graph connectivity—that allow us to reliably estimate growth rates of newly emerged lineages. To test our model, we used data collected from mid-2022 to end-2024 and accurately inferred the growth rates of lineages that appeared during this period. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for data collected in 2023 when the sequencing efforts were relatively high (thousands of sequences per day) in the US and the UK, our model correctly identified the most rapidly expanding lineages when they were still at low frequencies. Overall, our work provides a scalable and adaptable tool to estimate the growth rate of newly emerged SARS-CoV-2 lineages.

works.title: Beyond unseen entities: Auditable cold-start evaluation for drug interaction prediction
works.abstract: Reliable generalization is essential for deploying drug-drug interaction (DDI) and drug-target interaction (DTI) models in drug discovery, pharmacovigilance, and clinical decision support. However, strong performance on random splits or weakly constrained evaluations may not reflect how well a model generalizes to new drugs, targets, or deployment conditions. In pairwise prediction, test instances may still resemble training examples in molecular structure, sequence, or network context. Such overlap can inflate performance estimates and make interpolation appear to be extrapolation. In this Perspective, we argue that cold-start evaluation should be treated as an auditable deployment claim. We organize common evaluation settings by their source and scope of novelty, ranging from random splits and entity-disjoint protocols to structure-level, temporal, domain-disjoint, and many-domain evaluations. The L0-L5 framework clarifies which deployment claim each setting is designed to test. Coverage, overlap, and distance quantify the resulting train-test discrepancy. We further provide a practical checklist for leakage control, validation alignment, candidate-pair construction, and domain-level risk reporting. This Perspective clarifies the boundaries and evidential scope of cold-start evaluation, providing a common basis for interpreting and comparing results across DDI and DTI studies.

works.title: Auditing correlational gene regulatory networks through perturbation-grounded causal analysis for drug target prioritization
works.abstract: Abstract Gene regulatory network (GRN) inference for drug-target prioritization relies overwhelmingly on undirected co-expression, with highly connected “hub” genes routinely advanced as candidate regulators without independent causal verification. Although perturbation-based technologies now make direct causal validation feasible at genome scale, no study has directly tested whether correlational hub status reliably predicts causal regulatory importance or real-world druggability against an independent outcome rather than another network. This study evaluates that question and tests whether a simple, perturbation-free correction can recover any resulting predictive gap. Using the K562 essential-gene Perturb-seq dataset (2,285 pseudobulk CRISPR-interference profiles; 8,563 genes), an undirected correlational network and an independently constructed, perturbation-anchored causal network were built from identical data and compared across 1,868 shared genes via Spearman rank correlation and top-K overlap across three thresholds; both rankings were cross-referenced against Open Targets for documented drug mechanisms, and a logistic regression classifier quantified predictive value for known-drug status, with two specificity-adjustment refinements tested symmetrically on both networks. Rank agreement was weak and threshold-invariant (ρ = 0.091–0.158; zero top-20 overlap), yielding 77 correlational “false hubs” and 92 causal “hidden drivers.” Hidden drivers showed no category-level druggability enrichment (7.6% vs. 10.9% background) but included compelling, independently corroborated exceptions, CDK7 and AURKB, both invisible or near-invisible to correlation alone. Causal position outperformed correlational position for predicting known-drug status (AUC 0.655 vs. 0.625; combined 0.704), and specificity correction applied to the correlational network matched causal performance without perturbation data (AUC 0.655), reaching AUC 0.736 combined. These findings indicate correlational hub centrality is an unreliable proxy for causal importance and druggability, but a simple correction can recover much of the causal network’s advantage when tested empirically in both directions.

works.title: CREMA: recovery of high clonal fraction mosaic chromosomal alterations missed by phase-based detection
works.abstract: Abstract Background Mosaic chromosomal alterations (mCAs), a type of clonal hematopoiesis, are large somatic gains, losses, and copy-neutral events associated with age-related genomic instability and cancer susceptibility. Phase-based mCA detection methods such as MoChA are highly sensitive for low clonal fraction events, including events present in approximately 1% of blood cells, because they leverage long-range haplotype imbalance. However, when clonal fraction is very high, heterozygous genotypes can be misclassified as homozygous because allelic imbalance becomes extreme. This misclassification of phase-informative heterozygous sites can reduce sensitivity, particularly for high clonal fraction copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity (CN-LOH), which retains near-normal log R ratio (LRR) and can resemble constitutional autozygosity. Sensitive detection approaches for high clonal fraction mCAs are needed as these events are more likely to manifest in phenotypic consequences and confer elevated risk of hematologic malignancies. Results We developed CREMA (Clonal Recovery using Expectation-Maximization Algorithms), a standalone post-processing framework that identifies and classifies high clonal fraction mCA candidates within runs of homozygosity (RoH) or other segmentation outputs. CREMA recenters LRR, models central B-allele frequency (BAF) distributions using expectation-maximization, selects one- or two-band models using Akaike information criterion, and applies a geometric classifier in BAF-derived clonal fraction and LRR space. Across test analyses, RoH nomination followed by CREMA post-processing identified high clonal fraction mCA candidates, predominately CN-LOH events, that were not present in the MoChA call set. The largest contribution was observed in a myelofibrosis cohort enriched for high clonal fraction 9p CN-LOH involving the JAK2 region, where RoH plus CREMA recovered 232 additional CN-LOH events, corresponding to 11.1% of autosomal mCAs of at least 2 Mb. In two population-based PLCO datasets, CREMA recovered smaller targeted sets of additional high clonal fraction CN-LOH events, adding 0.5% and 0.4% to the autosomal mCA call sets. Conclusions CREMA complements phase-based mCA detection by using RoH or other segmentation methods for candidate generation and BAF/LRR modeling for candidate-level classification. This workflow improves detection of high clonal fraction events, particularly CN-LOH, while remaining applicable to high clonal fraction gains and losses.

works.title: SNPWay: streamlined SNP-to-function and pathway over-representation analysis
works.abstract: Translating variant lists such as lead SNPs, curated panels, or credible sets into pathway-level hypotheses typically requires stitching together tools for annotation, identifier handling, and statistical testing, and the resulting pipelines inherit the known disagreements among variant annotators and gene models.We present SNPWay, a free, login-free web server and R package that performs end-to-end SNP-to-function and pathway over-representation analysis.SNPWay accepts rsIDs or VCF input (GRCh37, with native hg38 support in development), intended for LD-pruned or otherwise independent variant sets, retrieves annotations from ANNOVAR, SnpEff, and VEP under both Ensembl and RefSeq gene models together with PEREGRINE enhancer-gene links through the AnnoQ API, normalizes gene names against the HGNC nomenclature, and submits the combined gene list, or any user-selected source, to the PANTHER API for over-representation testing against a whole-genome or user-supplied background, reporting per-gene source provenance throughout.Applied to 204 colorectal cancer GWAS variants, SNPWay reproduced the four pathways of the published analysis with identical supporting genes.Beyond describing the tool, we characterize its statistical behavior: across 300 matched null variant sets per annotation configuration, the full pipeline reported at least one significant pathway for 10.7% of random inputs under the default union (range 3.3 to 15.0% across configurations), while the observed results exceeded the null distribution (empirical p = 0.010) and the top pathway never arose by chance in 2,700 null tests.Together with locus-level sensitivity analyses, this calibration yields concrete guidance for interpreting pathway results from variant lists.SNPWay is available at https://snpway.annoq.org/.

works.title: Efficient count-based models improve power and robustness for large-scale single-cell eQTL mapping
works.abstract: This study presents jaxQTL, an efficient count-based pseudobulk single-cell eQTL mapping framework. When applied to OneK1K data, jaxQTL discovers more eGenes than existing methods while running faster.

works.title: Enhanced prediction and risk stratification of atrial fibrillation with polygenic risk score in Chinese patients with type 2 diabetes
authors: The Hong Kong Diabetes Biobank Study Group
works.abstract: Abstract Background Atrial fibrillation (AF) is a common adverse outcome in patients with type 2 diabetes (T2D); however, the role of genetics in identifying those at risk of AF within this high-risk group have not been comprehensively studied. Methods A total of 20,009 individuals from two prospective cohorts of Chinese patients with T2D were analyzed. We calculated a polygenic risk score (PRS AF ) comprising 97 variants previously associated with AF risk. Associations of PRS AF with incident AF and other cardiovascular endpoints were assessed using Cox regression, adjusted for baseline covariates. We also determined whether adding PRS AF improved prediction compared to the CHARGE-AF score using C-index, net reclassification improvement index, and integrated discrimination improvement index. Results Incident AF occurred in 986 patients (5.1%) across the two cohorts. A higher PRS AF , adjusted for sex, age, duration of diabetes, and principal components, was associated with increased risks of incident AF (HR [95% CI] per SD = 1.42 [1.33–1.51]), stroke (1.07 [1.01–1.12]), and congestive heart failure (1.10 [1.04–1.17]). These associations remained significant in the fully adjusted model. Patients in the top PRS AF quintile were over 2.5-fold (95% CI = 2.08–3.17) as likely to develop AF than those in the bottom quintile. A novel risk score that integrates the PRS AF into the CHARGE-AF score significantly improved both discrimination and reclassification compared to the CHARGE-AF score alone. Conclusions In patients with T2D, PRS AF is an independent risk factor for AF, providing incremental value in prediction and risk stratification, beyond that achieved with a validated clinical risk score.

works.title: Paralogous guanine deaminases acquired from bacteria by horizontal gene transfer promote purine homeostasis in Caenorhabditis elegans
works.abstract: Disruptions in purine metabolism contribute to a range of human diseases, from rare genetic disorders such as Lesch-Nyhan syndrome and xanthinuria to common conditions including gout and cancer. To better understand the metabolic networks that regulate purine homeostasis, we developed a Caenorhabditis elegans model of xanthine dehydrogenase (xdh-1) deficiency. Remarkably, xdh-1 mutant animals form rare xanthine stones, recapitulating a hallmark of human xanthinuria. To uncover genetic regulators of purine homeostasis, we performed a forward genetic screen for mutations that exacerbate xanthine stone formation in xdh-1 mutants. This approach identified multiple loss-of-function alleles in a previously uncharacterized gene, which we named gda-1. We show that gda-1 encodes an intestinal guanine deaminase that mediates a key enzymatic step in purine catabolism. The C. elegans genome also encodes a paralog, gda-2, which shares guanine deaminase activity but is expressed in distinct tissues. While gda-2 can compensate for gda-1 loss in guanine metabolism, the two genes exhibit non-redundant roles in regulating xanthine accumulation and stone formation. Interestingly, our evolutionary analyses suggest that gda-2 was acquired by nematodes via horizontal gene transfer from bacteria. These findings reveal a spatially regulated purine catabolism pathway in C. elegans and suggest that acquisition of bacterial genes has shaped a core nematode metabolic network.

works.title: DTBNet: Multimodal 3D Geometric Perception with Hierarchical Attention for Robust Drug–Target Interaction and Binding Affinity Prediction
works.abstract: MOTIVATION: Accurate prediction of drug-target interactions (DTIs) and binding affinity (DTA) constitutes a core challenge in accelerating drug discovery. While existing computational methods have made progress, most models struggle to capture critical physicochemical interactions in 3D space due to reliance on 1D sequences or 2D graph structures, and exhibit limited generalization in cold-start scenarios. This study proposes DTBNet, a unified prediction framework integrating multimodal geometric perception and hierarchical attention. The framework constructs heterogeneous embeddings combining local chemical details with global biological information by incorporating protein 3D geometric features and multilevel drug representations. During cross-modal interaction, atom-residue cross-attention first captures pair-specific local associations, followed by group-level multi-head self-attention that integrates complementary chemical-semantic, global structural, and local geometric interaction representations. RESULTS: Experiments on benchmark datasets (Davis, KIBA, PDBBind) demonstrate that compared with the optimal baseline models, DTBNet achieves up to 19.8% reduction in mean squared error and 8.0% improvement in Pearson correlation coefficient, maintaining optimal performance in drug cold-start, target cold-start, and completely novel pairing scenarios, showcasing robust cross-domain adaptability. Independent validation on GPCR targets achieves RMSE 0.783, confirming real-world applicability. Visualization analyses reveal DTBNet precisely identifies interaction sites between key transmembrane helical domain residues and drug aromatic rings, with attention distribution highly consistent with experimentally resolved binding conformations. These results establish DTBNet as a new performance benchmark through 3D geometric perception and dynamic attention mechanisms, providing interpretable molecular insights for structure-based rational drug design and demonstrating broad potential in virtual screening and target discovery. AVAILABILITY: The source code and data are available at https://github.com/wyx2012/DTB_Net. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

works.title: Deciphering the gene-centric spatial dynamics across tissue and time with GeneSPOT
High school science ambitions
Looking back on the adolescence of GFP research
Community benchmarking of generative models for privacy-preserving synthetic bulk RNA-seq data generation
works.abstract: Abstract Background The synthesis of anonymized data derived from real-world cohorts offers a promising strategy for regulatory-compliant and privacy-preserving biological data sharing, potentially facilitating model development that can improve predictive performance. However, the extent to which generative models can preserve biological signals while remaining resilient to adversarial privacy attacks in high-dimensional omics contexts remains underexplored. To address this gap, the CAMDA 2025 Health Privacy Challenge launched a community-driven effort to evaluate synthetic and privacy-preserving data generation for bulk RNA-seq cohorts. Results Building on this initiative, we systematically benchmark 11 generative methods across two cancer cohorts (~ 1,000 and ~ 5,000 patients) over 978 landmark genes. Methods are evaluated across distributional fidelity, downstream utility, biological plausibility and empirical privacy risk, with emphasis on trade-offs between vulnerability to membership inference attacks and other evaluation dimensions. Expressive deep generative models achieve strong predictive utility and differential expression recovery, but are often more vulnerable to membership inference risk under the evaluated threat model. Differentially private methods improve resistance to attacks at the cost of reduced utility, while simpler statistical approaches offer competitive utility with moderate privacy risk and fast training. Conclusions Synthetic bulk RNA-seq quality is inherently multi-dimensional and shaped by trade-offs between utility, biological preservation and privacy. Our results indicate that model architecture drives distinct trade-offs across these axes, suggesting that model choice should align with dataset characteristics, intended downstream use and privacy requirements. Privacy risk should also be assessed using multiple complementary attack methods and, where possible, mitigated through formal differential privacy protection.

works.title: CAPOS: A Context-Aware Gated Fusion Network for Protein Homo-Oligomeric State Prediction
Incremental Predictive Value of Stochastic Ensemble Dispersion Beyond Sequence Length in an RNAbpFlow Evaluation Cohort
Interpretable Blood Transcriptomic Classification of Ebola Survivors: A Machine Learning Framework for Post-Recovery Immune Profiling
StructGRPO: Structure-Feedback Reinforcement Learning for Fixed-Backbone Protein Sequence Design
A multi-tissue atlas of genetic regulatory effects in sheep
Computational repurposing and cellular evaluation of enalaprilat as a PD-1/PD-L1 interaction modulator
NPCAtlas: a multi-omics data resource and bioinformatics platform for nasopharyngeal carcinoma
works.abstract: Nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) is a prevalent head and neck malignancy in Southeast Asia and Southern China.The generation of large and complex multi-omics data provides a foundation for elucidating the biological mechanisms of NPC.However, these data are scattered across various databases and lack unified, standardized processing.Here, we developed the NPCAtlas (http://210.37.77.200:8080/NPCAtlas/), a comprehensive and systematic multidimensional omics resource platform for NPC patients.NPCAtlas aggregates, harmonizes, and visualizes 50 multi-omics datasets.Using the standardized NPC multi-omics datasets, the platform provides interactive tools that enable deep feature mining, supporting differential expression, genomic variation, non-coding RNA networks, proteomics, epigenetic methylation, clinical survival, and single-cell-level analysis of heterogeneity and cell communication.Users can search for and visualize results for genes of interest to explore their multi-omics characteristics.In summary, NPCAtlas provides a freely accessible multi-omics resource focused on NPC that supports hypothesis generation and candidate biomarker prioritization.

works.title: PFM: perturbed flow matching for structure-based drug design
works.abstract: MOTIVATION: Target-specific 3D molecular generation is a promising approach for structure-based drug design. However, existing diffusion-based methods are generally restricted to marginal distributions with closed-form solutions, limiting the flexibility of generative process design, especially for the forward noising process. As a result, these methods may be less effective in modeling the complex distributions underlying pocket-conditioned molecular generation. RESULTS: We develop Perturbed Flow Matching (PFM), a flow-matching-based framework for protein pocket-conditioned 3D molecular generation. PFM employs a perturbed conditional probability path that incorporates both pocket binding-site information and coupled atom type-coordinate information, enabling more effective generation of molecules in protein binding environments. On CrossDocked2020, PFM achieves competitive structural quality and the best average Vina score among the evaluated unguided methods (-7.12); PFM-G further improves the score to -8.70 with tailored classifier-free guidance. Experiments on additional molecular datasets further confirm the effectiveness and generalizability of the proposed framework. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: https://github.com/kurisu92725/PFM.

works.title: MIRAGE-DTA: conflict-aware multimodal evidence arbitration for drug–target affinity prediction
works.abstract: MOTIVATION: Multimodal drug-target affinity (DTA) models can incorporate molecular, protein, assay and textual evidence whose availability and reliability vary under missing modalities, cold-start entities and assay distribution shift. RESULTS: We present MIRAGE-DTA, a reliability-oriented evidence-arbitration layer that complements DTA encoders by keeping current-sample and training-set retrieval evidence as two explicit chains, carrying modality masks into fusion, retrieving training-only neighbors, and resolving disagreement with an interaction gate and validation-selected anchor. Across BindingDB_Kd, DAVIS, KIBA and a 2010-2024 CHEMBL_ASSAY benchmark with 35,238 interactions, experiments tested cold-start, missing-modality and assay/temporal shift settings. Under 35% sequence/text missingness on CHEMBL_ASSAY, 10-seed paired evaluation showed that MIRAGE-DTA reduced expected calibration error relative to late fusion by 0.0524, 0.0923 and 0.1018 on assay-cold, target-cold and temporal splits. Risk at 80% coverage was significantly lower on target-cold and temporal splits and numerically lower on assay-cold. A complementary complete-evidence direct-pChEMBL regression analysis also showed lower RMSE for the two-branch model than for current-only and retrieval-only regressors across assay-cold, target-cold and temporal splits. Ranking remained broadly competitive, with a modest trade-off on the temporal split, indicating that the principal benefit lies in calibrated and selective prediction under incomplete or shifted evidence. Shortcut audits quantified neighbor-overlap effects and showed that temporal retrieval was not driven by repeated compounds or near-duplicate scaffolds. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Source code is available at https://github.com/wushen1103-collab/mirage_drug_miniprototype and archived on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22695984; data come from public sources.

works.title: CADE: a reference-free workflow for coefficient-sensitivity analysis in bulk transcriptomic differential expression
works.abstract: Bulk differential-expression (DE) coefficients can change when disease alters cell-type abundance, but matched single-cell references are often unavailable in small or rare-disease studies. Existing marker-covariate adjustments can produce an adjusted DE table, yet they do not directly report which gene-level coefficients are stable, attenuated, amplified or representation-sensitive after composition adjustment. Coefficient-sensitivity analysis deliberately asks a narrower question than deconvolution: for each gene, how much does the reported group effect change once marker-derived composition weights are added to the model, in which direction does it change, and is that change stable to marker choice and to the coordinate representation of the weights? The output is a per-gene ranking of coefficient stability, not an estimate of cell-type fractions. We developed CADE (Composition-Aware Differential Expression), an R workflow that estimates marker-derived relative composition weights, fits paired unadjusted and composition-adjusted limma models, and computes a per-gene Composition Confounding Index (CCI).
