CADE reports signed coefficient-change labels, marker-dropout bootstrap rank stability (repeatedly omitting markers and re-ranking genes, to show which rankings persist), label-permutation calibration, denominator-threshold diagnostics, stabilised-denominator output and isometric log-ratio coordinate-sensitivity analysis. Genes whose classification depends on the coordinate representation of the composition weights are explicitly identified. In the controlled synthetic composition-bias benchmark, CADE preserved recovery of cell-intrinsic DE genes under composition bias, including AUROC 0.996 at 100% synthetic bias versus 0.902 for unadjusted limma. Marker-derived weights recovered PBMC ground-truth relative composition with mean r = 0.993, and a macrophage activation syndrome pseudobulk evaluation against scRNA-seq-derived composition showed mean r = 0.779, with all seven mappings that had a usable scRNA-seq reference showing p < 0.001 (of eight preset categories; Neutrophils had no reference in this ground truth). In familial hemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis PBMCs (GSE26050; n = 11 versus 33 controls), CADE illustrated the separation of low-CCI from model-sensitive coefficients within a targeted immune, iron and ferroptosis panel. CADE provides a reference-free, reproducible workflow for characterising how sensitive bulk transcriptomic DE coefficients are to marker-derived composition adjustment. It reports coefficient stability and does not estimate absolute cell fractions. The FHL analysis is used as a small-cohort worked example, and disease-specific findings remain hypothesis-generating.

works.title: CellSavior: an open-source framework for improved cell calling in targeted single-cell DNA sequencing
works.abstract: MOTIVATION: Single-cell DNA sequencing (scDNA-seq) has emerged as a key approach for studying complex genomic variation, including tumor heterogeneity. Despite its increasing commercial availability, exemplified by the Tapestri platform, analytical reproducibility remains limited due to reliance on proprietary and non-transparent pipelines. Among preprocessing steps, cell calling is particularly critical, as it determines which barcodes correspond to true cells rather than background noise and directly shapes all downstream analyses. However, existing methods typically rely on empirical thresholding and exhibit inconsistent performance across datasets. These limitations underscore the need for a robust and generalizable cell calling framework for reliable scDNA-seq analysis. RESULTS: We developed CellSavior, an open-source cell calling algorithm with an integrated downstream pipeline that produces standardized outputs. CellSavior employs an ensemble clustering strategy across multiple distance metrics, combined with confidence-weighted merging, to generate a consensus classification that reduces bias and improves robustness. Across 33 public and in-house single-cell DNA sequencing datasets, CellSavior recapitulated cell annotations generated by commercial software (CellFinder) in 31 cases (93.9%). In the remaining discordant cases, CellSavior yielded more biologically interpretable annotations, rescuing previously undetected clusters enriched for key hotspot genomic alterations. AVAILABILITY: The source code for CellSavior is freely available at https://github.com/dauer-tgilab/CellSavior; DOI: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22744146. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

works.title: Bacterial protein function prediction via multimodal deep learning
works.abstract: Abstract Bacterial proteins are specialized with extensive functional diversity for survival in diverse and stressful environments. A significant portion of these proteins remains functionally uncharacterized, limiting our understanding of bacterial survival mechanisms. Hence, we developed Deep Expression STructure (DeepEST), a multimodal deep learning framework designed to accurately predict protein function in bacteria by assigning Gene Ontology (GO) terms. DeepEST comprises two modules: a multi-layer perceptron that takes gene expression and gene location as input features, and a protein structure-based predictor. Within DeepEST, we integrated these modules through a learnable weighted linear combination and introduced a novel masked loss function to fine-tune the structure-based predictor for bacterial species. These modeling choices are particularly well suited for bacteria due to the spatial organization of their circular genomes. Functionally related genes frequently co-localize and are co-transcribed within operons, allowing transcription dynamics to serve as crucial, condition-dependent regulatory signals. We show that DeepEST outperforms existing protein function prediction methods on a 25-species benchmark, relying solely on amino acid sequence or protein structure. Moreover, DeepEST predicts GO terms for unclassified hypothetical proteins across 25 human bacterial pathogens, facilitating the design of experimental setups for characterization studies. By combining expression, localization, and structure information in a unified deep learning framework, DeepEST bridges organism-specific data integration and structure-based transfer learning, providing a method tailored for bacterial protein function prediction in settings with structural and multi-condition expression data. Availability Accompanying code and data can be found under https://github.com/BorgwardtLab/DeepEST .

works.title: PmiREN3.0: a multi-omics integrated and AI-assisted encyclopedia for plant microRNA research
works.abstract: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are key post-transcriptional regulators in gene regulatory networks (GRNs). Comprehensive research on miRNAs increasingly requires the integration of large and heterogeneous datasets, together with more efficient approaches to knowledge exploration. Here, we present PmiREN3.0, a major update of the Plant MicroRNA Encyclopedia. Compared with PmiREN2.0, species/subspecies coverage increased from 179 to 340, adding 22 orders, 51 families, and 108 genera. Using the same standardized workflow and annotation criteria as previous releases, high-confidence miRNAs were identified from 5319 small RNA sequencing (sRNA-seq) datasets, with miRNA loci increasing from 39 751 to 87 667 and miRNA families from 7838 to 18 389. Resources and tools from previous releases were extensively updated, while six new modules were added for primary transcripts, DNA methylation, RNA modifications, stress-responsive expression, metabolic pathways, and core GRNs. PmiREN3.0 also introduces miRai+, a knowledge service powered by artificial intelligence (AI) that combines a language model fine-tuned on miRNA knowledge with retrieval augmented generation. Evaluation yielded scores of 0.910 for answer relevance, 0.965 for faithfulness, and 0.906 for factual correctness. Together, PmiREN3.0 provides an expanded plant miRNA dataset and an integrated platform combining multi-omics data and AI-assisted knowledge services for plant miRNA research. PmiREN3.0 is available at https://pmiren.com/.

works.title: Sequence-based coevolutionary prediction of species-specific interactomes
works.abstract: Evolutionarily conserved protein-protein interactions (PPIs) reveal fundamental biological processes. However, predicting protein function solely from these interactions provides an incomplete picture of biological systems. Computational methods for predicting PPIs often struggle due to limited functional annotations in databases, making it difficult to fully understand unique biological systems. This study introduces ContextMirror2.0 (CM2.0), a coevolution-based method designed to address these limitations. Coevolutionary approaches, unlike supervised machine learning methods, do not rely on labelled datasets, proving valuable in addressing the scarcity of data for species-specific PPIs. Around 40% of CM2.0's top-1000 predicted PPIs for E. coli, S. enterica, and S. aureus are supported by experimental PPI databases. However, comparative analysis of the resulting functional communities further revealed both highly conserved interaction patterns and species-specific interactions. CM2.0 leverages coevolutionary information at the phylogenetic level to explore protein interaction dynamics and understand the functional consequences of species-specific variations. This information can inform further studies on the emergence of novel functions, adaptation to specific environments, and the development of targeted therapies.

works.title: SwimmingIndividuals: A high-performance agent-based model for marine ecosystems
works.abstract: Because they are based on established theory, mechanistic models are essential for projecting ecological responses to novel conditions. Yet mechanistic agent-based model (ABM) applications have often been limited by computational constraints. This paper introduces SwimmingIndividuals , an open-source ABM framework that advances our ability to simulate physiological processes, animal movement, higher trophic level marine ecosystem dynamics, and fisheries removals at large ecological scales. The software's key contributions are a suite of mechanistic sub-models governing the full life cycle of each agent, including visual prey detection, adaptive behaviors such as diel vertical migration (DVM), a flexible bioenergetics engine with three taxon-specific metabolic architectures, and a spatial pathfinding algorithm for habitat-seeking movement. These processes are made computationally tractable through a hybrid CPU/GPU architecture written in Julia. Unlike prior ABMs that use fixed perception radii or single-equation bioenergetics, SwimmingIndividuals enables emergent ecological dynamics across populations of superindividual agents. We demonstrate the framework through three Gulf of America simulations. The model reproduced DVM, cetacean diving patterns, size-based trophic shifts, and von Bertalanffy growth curves consistent with published King Mackerel stock assessments. Long-term simulations generated realistic population dynamics and quantified impacts of fishery harvest control rules across five fleets. SwimmingIndividuals provides a powerful, flexible, open-source platform for mechanistic marine ecosystem research and ecosystem-based fisheries management.

works.title: kinGEMs: A robust and scalable framework for resource-constraint models through stochastic tuning of deep learning-predicted kinetic parameters
works.abstract: The construction of accurate enzyme-constrained genome-scale models (ecGEMs) remains a critical challenge in systems biology, limited by sparse kinetic data and the need for biologically meaningful representations. This work presents an integrated framework combining CPI-Pred, a deep learning model to predict kinetic parameters ( k c a t ) from sequence and compound embeddings, with kinGEMs, a pipeline to incorporate these uncertainty-aware parameters into ecGEMs for metabolic optimization. By leveraging representations at multiple scales, the approach captures sequence, structure, and kinetic data to enhance model generalizability and accuracy. Rigorous benchmarking demonstrates the framework’s capability to predict growth rates and fluxes that are consistent with experimental observations and measured proteome fractions, reduce median flux variability by several folds, and yield better-constrained metabolic models by explicitly accounting for the uncertainty inherent in ML-predicted kinetic parameters. kinGEMs successfully generated ecGEMs for 93 models spanning a phylogenetically diverse set of organisms including Gram-negative and Gram-positive bacteria, mycobacteria, parasitic protists, fungi, and mammalian cell lines. These innovations breakdown the barrier to application of ecGEMs to non-model organisms and open new avenues for metabolic engineering and synthetic biology in more industrially relevant hosts.

works.title: PINN-based functional inference in size-structured population models: Application to fish oogenesis
works.abstract: Early oogenesis in juvenile fish establishes the ovarian reserve, which conditions lifelong reproductive capacity. This process is regulated by local hormonal feedback mechanisms, mainly involving Anti-Müllerian Hormone (AMH). In this work, we develop a mechanistic size-structured population model describing an unstructured germ-cell compartment and a population of growing oocytes, with AMH feedback on the renewal of the precursor cells compartment. Using repeated cross-sectional observations of oocyte size distributions in fish ovaries, we formulate and solve a nonlinear inverse problem with Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to infer three demographic functions: the size-dependent oocyte growth rate, the AMH-regulated net renewal rate of the precursor cells compartment, and the recruitment rate of new oocytes. We introduce an auxiliary PINN formulation to handle the nonlocal interaction term and jointly infer unobserved state variables and demographic functions. Our inference strategy combines non-parametric PINNs with a data-guided model-selection step: demographic functions are first inferred without prescribing their functional forms, and the learned profiles are then used to select parsimonious parametric laws, whose parameters are subsequently estimated within a parametric PINN. We investigate identifiability at both the functional and parametric levels, combining structural identifiability analysis with synthetic-data experiments assessing the practical recovery of functions and parameters. The inference procedure is embedded within an individual-level bootstrap framework to assess sensitivity to repeated-cross-sectional sampling and stochastic training. Applied to juvenile fish oogenesis, the framework recovers interpretable growth and renewal dynamics, provides access to unobserved quantities, and enables conditional in silico investigation. More broadly, this work provides a framework for functional and parametric inference in size-structured population models with nonlocal interactions from sparse cross-sectional data.

works.title: Ten simple rules for a department chair
works.abstract: Department chairs occupy a pivotal position in the university. Teaching, research, graduate education, and much of the academic community's professional and administrative activity are organized at the departmental level. Yet, despite the importance of the position and the considerable challenges it entails, many scientists assume the role with little or no formal preparation for academic leadership. This paper is intended as a practical primer rather than a comprehensive guide to academic leadership. The proposed rules provide a framework that prospective and current department chairs can adapt to their own institutional circumstances, experience, and leadership style.

works.title: BICEP: an extension to indels and copy number variants for rare variant prioritisation in pedigree analysis
works.abstract: BICEP is a Bayesian inference model that evaluates how likely a rare variant is to be causal for a genomic trait in pedigree-based analyses. The original prior model in BICEP was designed for single nucleotide variants only. This is a limitation as other types of rare variants are known to influence Mendelian and complex traits. Here, we have developed an extension of the prior models for more comprehensive genomic analysis to include indels and copy number variants. We benchmark the performance of these new priors and show comparable performance accuracy with the existing single nucleotide variant prior model. For copy number variants we evaluate four different input predictors to the models and recommend the best performing ones as the default. We have described an extension of the original BICEP model to other classes of variants important for genomic traits. The updated prior models have been implemented in the current version of BICEP available from the project GitHub: https://github.com/cathaloruaidh/BICEP .

works.title: GraphPepTox: a structure-aware pre-trained framework for peptide toxicity prediction using geometric graph transformer and LoRA-based fine-tuning
works.abstract: Peptides are widely used as potential therapeutic agents in drug development, vaccines, and antimicrobial treatments for their specificity, effectiveness, and relatively low production cost. Nevertheless, peptide toxicity remains a major concern due to its toxic consequences, such as membrane rupture, haemolysis, tissue damage, and adverse immunological responses. Early detection of toxic peptide candidates is vital for the development of safe and effective therapies. Current computational methods for predicting peptide toxicity are largely based on hand-crafted sequence descriptors or sequence-only deep learning architectures that may not fully account for the underlying three-dimensional structural determinants of peptide toxicity. We introduce GraphPepTox, a structure-aware geometric deep learning framework, which combines pre-trained geometric graph representation learning with hierarchical structural modelling to accurately predict peptide toxicity. Our framework learns geometry-aware embeddings from peptide structural graphs via self-supervised masked residue reconstruction, which is based on a Masked Graph Autoencoder (MGAE) built on a Geometric Graph Transformer (GGT) encoder. The pretrained structural representations are cross-fused via a multi-scale U-Net architecture to capture both local residue-level interactions and global conformational patterns associated with peptide toxicity. GraphPepTox explicitly models spatial relationships between residues, thereby efficiently capturing structural aspects that are generally neglected by sequence-based predictors, such as residue clustering, hydrophobic interactions, and electrostatic organization. On benchmark datasets, our framework shows decent performance improvement and interpretability over the existing state-of-the-art methods. Improved peptide toxicity prediction accuracy of GraphPepTox will expedite the construction of safer peptides in therapies.

works.title: Database for ancestry-specific cross-tissue gene expression models: AGEMdb
works.abstract: Abstract Background Transcriptome-wide association studies (TWAS) integrate genetically regulated gene expression with genome-wide association study (GWAS) data to identify gene–trait associations. These analyses rely on accurate gene expression prediction models trained using genotype and transcriptomic data from the same set of individuals. However, most publicly available TWAS models are based on resources that predominantly consist of participants of European ancestry. This European ancestry bias limits the transferability and generalizability of gene expression models across diverse populations. Description Using genotype and gene expression data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) Project, we curated datasets comprising 689 European ancestry individuals and 111 African American individuals after quality control and confounder adjustment. We then developed ancestry-specific cross-tissue gene expression imputation models using the UTMOST framework. These models are accessible through AGEMdb, a web-based database that allows users to browse, search, and download gene expression imputation models with flexible filtered options (e.g. by tissue and gene). By incorporating African American-specific models, AGEMdb addresses the European ancestry bias present in existing TWAS resources and supports more equitable gene–trait association analyses. Conclusion AGEMdb provides a valuable resource for ancestry-specific TWAS, which promotes more inclusive studies that support the advancement of equitable genomic research.

works.title: KlaDB: a multi‑species database of protein Lysine Lactylation with benchmarking of prediction models
works.abstract: Abstract Lysine lactylation (Kla), a lactate-derived lysine post-translational modification (PTM), has emerged as an important mechanistic interface between cellular metabolism and gene regulation. Kla has been implicated in diverse biological processes, including tumorigenesis, immune regulation, inflammation, and plant growth and development. Advances in high-resolution mass spectrometry (MS)-based proteomics have led to the identification of a rapidly expanding number of Kla sites. However, a dedicated and comprehensive resource for lysine lactylation remains lacking. Here, we present KlaDB, a manually curated Lysine Lactylation Database comprising 64,072 experimentally identified Kla sites from nine species. KlaDB provides a user-friendly and interactive web interface that enables intuitive browsing, searching, and retrieval of site-level information for each Kla event. Based on the curated dataset, we further performed cross-species motif and background-corrected enrichment analyses, showing lysine-rich flanking regions and differences in local sequence patterns among the analysed datasets. In addition, we performed a systematic multi-species comparative evaluation of four published Kla-site prediction models under a standardized benchmarking framework. By consolidating experimentally identified Kla sites with standardized model benchmarking, KlaDB provides a valuable resource for the lactylation research community and will facilitate future studies on the biological functions and regulatory mechanisms of Kla. The database is publicly accessible at https://kladb.wuxl-group.com .

works.title: SigBridgeR: An R Toolkit for Standardized Identification and Benchmarking of Phenotype-Associated Cell Subpopulations in Single-Cell Transcriptomics
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has revolutionized our understanding of cellular heterogeneity, yet linking specific cell subpopulations to clinically relevant phenotypes remains a major challenge. Although multiple computational methods have been developed to integrate bulk transcriptomic and single-cell data for phenotype-associated cell identification, differences in algorithmic strategies, parameter configurations, software implementations, and output formats make it difficult to compare methods fairly, reproduce analyses, and determine which approach is most suitable for a given biological question. RESULTS: Here, we present SigBridgeR, an extensible R framework that integrates eight representative phenotype-associated cell subpopulation identification algorithms within a unified workflow. Using paired bulk RNA-seq and scRNA-seq datasets from four cancer types under both binary and survival phenotypes, we performed a comprehensive benchmark combining positive and negative control experiments, accuracy evaluation, Hallmark pathway enrichment analysis, parameter sensitivity analysis, and computational performance profiling. The benchmark revealed substantial differences in algorithm robustness, biological consistency, computational efficiency, and parameter sensitivity. Across multiple evaluation criteria, Scissor and scAB consistently achieved the most balanced overall performance, whereas several methods exhibited important limitations, including poor scalability, high parameter sensitivity, or unstable phenotype detection. CONCLUSIONS: SigBridgeR provides standardized preprocessing, unified algorithm interfaces, and an extensible registry-based architecture for phenotype-associated cell subpopulation analysis. By integrating systematic benchmarking and optimized implementations into a single platform, SigBridgeR facilitates reliable evaluation of existing methods, simplifies multi-algorithm analyses, and supports the development of improved phenotype-guided single-cell analysis methods for precision medicine.

works.title: Prevalence of anti-HCV and incidence rate of HCV seroconversion in a large multiregional health check-up population in China: a cross-sectional and longitudinal study of 1.6 million adults
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: China carries one of the heaviest burdens of hepatitis C virus (HCV) infection worldwide. This study aimed to estimate the prevalence of anti-HCV and incidence rate of HCV seroconversion in a large health check-up population in China. METHODS: This cross-sectional, and longitudinal study used data from the Meinian health check-up database, covering participants from all 31 provinces of mainland China between 2017 and 2023. Serological samples were tested for anti-HCV using ELISA. The weighted prevalence of anti-HCV and the incidence rate of HCV seroconversion were calculated. Poisson regression was used to identify risk factors for HCV seroconversion. RESULTS: A total of 1,610,735 participants were included in the analysis of anti-HCV prevalence. The prevalence of anti-HCV in the study population was 0.89% (95% CI, 0.77%-1.01%), with significantly higher prevalence found in females and elderly individuals. Geographically, the prevalence was significantly higher in Central and West China compared to East China. Individuals with abnormal liver function or liver fibrosis, abnormal thyroid function or antibodies, diabetes, and impaired kidney function had significantly higher prevalence. The analysis of HCV seroconversion included 179,447 participants, showing an incidence rate of 0.72 per 1,000 person-years during a median follow-up of 1.5 years. Risk factors for HCV seroconversion included older age, as well as living in Central or West China, border regions, areas with low GDP per capita, and areas with high anti-HCV prevalence. CONCLUSIONS: Our study reveals significant anti-HCV seroprevalence burden and ongoing risk of HCV transmission in a large health check-up population in China, highlighting the urgent need for systematic screening and enhanced prevention efforts to control HCV transmission.

works.title: Codon Usage and Sequence-composition Characteristics Associated with the Malignant Ductal Transcriptional State in Pancreatic Cancer
OmicsBridge: A Shiny-based Interface for Bridging Omics Datasets and Exploring Clinical Relevance
works.abstract: Abstract Motivation Comprehensive omics datasets are now routinely generated across diverse biological conditions, including in laboratories without dedicated bioinformatics support. When integrated and analyzed collectively, these datasets can uncover biologically meaningful relationships and molecular targets with potential clinical relevance. However, efficient integration and exploration of these datasets often require advanced computational workflows. Many existing tools are optimized for single-omics analysis or require users to re-upload datasets for each session, which becomes increasingly time-consuming and inefficient as dataset accumulate. Results We developed OmicsBridge, an intuitive and user-friendly platform for integrating and visualizing diverse omics datasets. OmicsBridge supports over 50 visualization and analysis modules, that help researchers identify genes with functional and clinical relevance and generate hypotheses. It also serves as a centralized database for efficient data storage and retrieval, reducing repetitive data uploads and improving data accessibility and workflow efficiency. As a case study, we used OmicsBridge to identify pathophysiologically relevant molecular determinants of T-cell chemoattractant CXCL10 expression, explore the underlying mechanisms, and assess their association with cancer patient outcomes through multi-omics integration. Availability and implementation OmicsBridge is freely available and platform-independent. A demo web interface is accessible at https://omicsbridge.dkfz.de, and the R/Shiny source code for local deployment is available at https://github.com/htsmto/OmicsBridge.

works.title: SpatialROI: An Interactive R Shiny Platform for Customized Region-Aware Spatial Transcriptomics Analysis
works.abstract: Abstract Motivation Spatial transcriptomics captures high-throughput molecular information across tissue sections, but histological context remains essential for accurate biological insight. Clustering-derived spatial domains are sensitive to technical noise and may not align with morphologically defined structures that pathologists rely on for disease interpretation. Expert-guided region definition directly on H&E images enables precise identification of molecular signals within tissue architecture. However, existing tools require substantial programming expertise or lack seamless integration between image-based region selection and downstream transcriptomic analysis, limiting accessibility for non-computational users. Results We present SpatialROI, an interactive platform that enables users to define regions of interest (ROIs) directly on H&E images and perform targeted analyses without programming. SpatialROI supports standard 10x Visium data as both raw Space Ranger outputs and preprocessed Seurat objects. The platform incorporates eight analytical modules: ROI drawing, gene set and pathway visualization, ligand–receptor colocalization, cell-type deconvolution, spot clustering, differential expression, within-sample group comparison, and multi-sample ROI comparison. ROIs are exportable as Seurat objects or reusable spot-index files. Collectively, SpatialROI facilitates expert-guided, region-aware exploration of spatial transcriptomic data for biologically meaningful insights into tissue architecture. Availability and implementation SpatialROI is freely accessible at https://shiny.crc.pitt.edu/spatial_api/. Source code and example datasets are available at https://github.com/myaol/SpatialROI.

works.title: Efficient and accurate mixed model association tool for single-cell eQTL analysis
works.abstract: Genetic effects on gene expression often vary across cell types, motivating expression quantitative trait loci (eQTL) mapping in single-cell RNA sequencing data. Existing approaches generally aggregate expression across cells, use Gaussian models poorly suited to read counts or do not scale. Here we show that SAIGE-QTL, a Poisson mixed model that directly models single-cell read counts, enables calibrated and computationally scalable eQTL mapping while accounting for donor-level and cell-level covariates and unequal numbers of cells per donor. In simulations and three single-cell datasets, SAIGE-QTL improved statistical efficiency and discovery of genes with significant eQTLs (eGenes) relative to pseudobulk methods and produced results consistent with existing single-cell models at substantially lower computational cost. In 1.2 million immune cells, SAIGE-QTL identified 48.8% more eGenes than pseudobulk analysis. SAIGE-QTL further enabled genome-wide trans-eQTL mapping and rare variant set-based testing, identifying rare variant associations independent of common eQTL signals. SAIGE-QTL therefore expands single-cell eQTL discovery across common, rare and trans-acting genetic variation.

works.title: Robust fine-mapping in the presence of linkage disequilibrium mismatch
Quantitative lineage tracing in mouse embryogenesis
MMEJ repair safeguards cancer ecDNA
Mapping somatic mutations in every corner of the genome
New neuronal microexons linked to autism
Transcriptome- and methylome-wide association studies prioritized lung cancer genes in East Asian populations
works.abstract: The relationship between gene expression, DNA methylation, and lung cancer remains elusive in East Asian (EAS) populations. Transcriptome- and methylome-wide association studies (TWAS/MWAS) help uncover gene-trait associations by integrating multi-omics data, yet models trained mainly on European references limit cross-population generalizability. To address this, we developed EAS-specific gene expression and DNA methylation prediction models using whole-blood data from over 800 and 4,300 individuals, respectively. Applying these to lung cancer GWAS from Nanjing Medical University (13,327 cases; 13,328 controls) and Biobank Japan (4,444 cases; 489,012 controls), we identified 25 genes and 42 CpGs associated with lung cancer risk in the discovery stage, with seven genes and 32 CpGs replicated. Three novel genes outside known GWAS loci-RP11-57K17.1 (6q22.31), RP11-313J2.1 (10q11.21), and BMS1P2 (10q11.22)-were identified. In addition, Mendelian randomization analyses suggested that methylation-mediated downregulation of RP11-147L13.11 can reduce lung cancer risk. Our study reveals new susceptibility genes and offers insights into genetic-epigenetic regulatory mechanisms in lung cancer among EAS populations.

works.title: DeSCENT: Deconvolutional Single-Cell RNA-seq Enhances Transcriptome-based Cancer Survival Analysis
works.abstract: MOTIVATION: Single-cell RNA-seq captures tumor heterogeneity, but it is rarely available together with patient survival outcomes. Bulk RNA-seq cohorts provide survival data but lack direct measurements of cellular expression. RESULTS: DeSCENT generates reference-informed cellular profiles from bulk RNA-seq and combines both representations for survival prediction. We evaluated DeSCENT with three survival models on eight TCGA cancer cohorts. Compared with Bulk, DeSCENT improved average C-index and generally improved time-dependent AUC, while integrated Brier score results were mixed. External validation showed higher average C-index than all three baselines, although performance was lower than in internal evaluation. These findings support the use of cellular representations in the evaluated transcriptome-only setting. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Code: https://github.com/YonghaoZhao722/DeSCENT. Archival snapshot: doi:10.5281/zenodo.22073099. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

works.title: scPhyloGRN: gene regulatory network inference guided by lineage topology in single-cell developmental data
works.abstract: MOTIVATION: Gene regulatory network (GRN) inference from single-cell transcriptomes is complicated by expression patterns associated with both cell state and shared ancestry. Cellular phylogenies provide developmental context, but incorporating relationships among individual cells into gene-level regulatory inference remains challenging. RESULTS: We present scPhyloGRN, a supervised framework that integrates single-cell gene expression with cellular phylogeny to prioritize directed transcription factor (TF)-target candidates within the observed gene set. The framework maps cell ancestry to gene associations that guide graph construction, attention in a dual-stream encoder, and lineage-consistency regularization. We evaluated scPhyloGRN against ten methods across 17 dataset-reference settings spanning four mouse embryos and one Caenorhabditis elegans dataset. scPhyloGRN showed an overall advantage in regulatory edge prioritization, supported by additional evaluations using shared candidate spaces. Removing lineage information reduced AUPRC in the ablation analyses, while branch-level and regulator-level analyses showed improved ranking and recovery of reference-supported regulatory candidates. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Source code and analysis workflows are available at https://github.com/Maria0852/scPhyloGRN, with a versioned archive at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22793831.

works.title: Automated identification of individual birds by song enables multi-year recapture from passive acoustic monitoring data
abcFISH enables multiplexed, single-molecule visualization of circular RNA spatial heterogeneity
Integration and annotation of spatial multi-omic data with DIRAC
works.abstract: Spatial multi-omic technologies measure multiple molecular layers within intact tissues. Two central challenges are vertical integration, which combines different molecular modalities, and horizontal integration, which aligns cell types across studies. Here we show domain invariant representation through adaptive calibration (DIRAC), a geometric deep learning model that unifies these tasks in a generalized domain adaptation framework. DIRAC learns task-discriminative features that are insensitive to domain shifts caused by batch effects, omic modalities or study sites, enabling a shared embedding space and automated cell-type annotation through label transfer from reference datasets. Across sequencing-based and imaging-based datasets, DIRAC identified a new microvascular proliferation domain in glioblastoma, corrected cortical-layer annotations in severe Alzheimer's disease, resolved subtle structures in mouse embryos and remained robust to missing data and unseen cell types. We generated mouse spleen and thymus Stereo-CITE-seq data and used DIRAC to reveal thymic T cell migration and splenic immune cell interactions. DIRAC is fast and scales to millions of cells.

works.title: Unlocking spatial diversity of circular RNAs with abcFISH
DIRAC makes complex spatial multi-omic data simpler to analyze
Genome-wide scan for transmission ratio distortion in trios from the Norwegian MoBa cohort rules out moderate distortion at common variants
works.abstract: Abstract Transmission ratio distortion has been demonstrated in model organisms but is understudied in humans. We conduct single- and multi-locus transmission disequilibrium tests to detect transmission ratio distortion in up to 43,829 parent–offspring trios from the Norwegian Mother, Father and Child Cohort Study. We find little evidence for moderate to high levels of transmission ratio distortion at common variants. However, our multi-locus analyses implicate genes involved in meiosis, fertility, and prenatal development.

works.title: Ribocentre-FoldBridge: a comprehensive database bridging RNA chemical probing data and 3D structures
works.abstract: RNA chemical probing generates nucleotide-resolved profiles in vitro and in cells, while X-ray crystallographic or cryo-electron microscopy models provide high-resolution structural models but remain comparatively low throughput. Aligning these experiments from different modalities may provide insights into RNA structure formation and molecular functions. Here, we present Ribocentre-FoldBridge (https://foldbridge.ribocentre.org/), an AI-assisted, curator-reviewed database linking curated chemical-probing profiles with experimentally determined 3D structures. This database catalogues 12 types of RNAs, linking 256 929 probing profiles across five experimental categories to 5321 structure-linked cases. It interactively visualizes the probing profiles that align with RNA secondary and tertiary structures at nucleotide resolution. We demonstrate probe-specific reactivity patterns across paired, unpaired, and solvent-accessible structural contexts. The database aims to provide a reproducible evidence layer for examining RNA structure-function relationships across heterogeneous experiments, and thus facilitate the development of new RNA structure or function prediction programs.

works.title: R-loopBase v2.0: species- and cell type-resolved quantitative R-loop maps and R-loop regulatory resources
works.abstract: R-loops are non-canonical nucleic acid structures implicated in diverse cellular processes and diseases. We previously developed R-loopBase to address the pressing challenges of inaccurate R-loop maps and the limited understanding of the R-loop regulatory network. However, R-loopBase provided only human R-loop maps with categorical confidence and did not account for cell type specificity. These limitations, coupled with the emerging R-loop profiling technologies and advances in R-loop regulatory mechanisms, have motivated the development of R-loopBase v2.0 (https://rloopbase.nju.edu.cn). After uniformly re-analysing 358 R-loop mapping datasets generated by 16 technologies, we introduce a quantitative R-loop scoring framework that assesses genome-wide R-loop confidence in human, demonstrating strong concordance with known R-loop biology. We further extend the framework to specific cell types and mouse, fruit fly, and yeast. In parallel, we substantially expand the collection of R-loop regulators across species, enabling the inference of changes in R-loop homeostasis. Building on these expanded datasets, we implement several new interactive features and analytical tools, including an expanded multi-species genome browser, deep learning-based R-loop prediction, R-loop homeostasis analysis, and a streamlined data download portal. We anticipate that R-loopBase v2.0 will serve as an enhanced, up-to-date one-stop resource for the R-loop research community.

works.title: BioImage Archive: bringing bioimaging data together
works.abstract: The BioImage Archive (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/bioimage-archive) is EMBL-EBI's flagship resource for life sciences image data. It serves as a deposition database for biological images across scales from near-atomic through to whole organisms, and across imaging modalities. The Archive's mission is to support the reproducibility of quantitative results based on imaging, support methods development including modern deep-learning-based approaches, and allow large-scale reanalysis of image data. Across the Archive's ecosystem, we provide access to over 11 PB of image data. Recent developments in underpinning infrastructure now allow interactive exploration, visualization, and streaming access to a subset of the Archive's data using the new OME-Zarr file format, and will ultimately provide access to all of EMBL-EBI's archived image data, including data from the Electron Microscopy Public Image Archive. Migration of all holdings and a unified submission system are in progress.

works.title: The UCSC Genome Browser database: 2027 update
works.abstract: Since 2000, the UCSC Genome Browser (https://genome.ucsc.edu) has served as a standard tool for visualizing and comparing annotations across thousands of genome assemblies. Users can browse and visualize a wide range of data types from gene annotations to regulatory regions and comparative genome alignments. Once the data view is configured, the Genome Browser image can be exported for use in publications. Beyond visualization, users can use our tools to compare and export the annotations for further analysis. This year's feature updates include the full release of a tool to copy annotations between related assemblies, QuickLift; feature additions to our data-hosting service HubSpace to enable live editing of configuration files; two new display configurability options: "My Annotations" and custom item coloring; and several improvements to genome assembly discovery and track management. Beyond these new features, 28 new annotation tracks have been added across three broad categories: variant databases and interpretation, gene regulation, and transcriptome and gene expression. These include ENCODE4 cCREs and other ENCODE4 regulatory annotations, variant frequencies and phased variants from national sequencing projects, and two massively parallel reporter assay tracks.

works.title: OrganiZymeDB: a comprehensive database of enzyme stability and function in the presence of organic solvents
works.abstract: Low enzymatic tolerance to organic solvents is a major bottleneck for the development of industrial biocatalysis, since many substrates have limited water solubility, thus requiring the use of organic solvents for substrate solubilization and process economic viability. Yet, despite decades of experimental research in this field, no public resource currently exists that systematically collects and curates these data, limiting their accessibility and reuse for large-scale analyses and for the development and validation of computational methods. To address this gap, we present OrganiZymeDB (https://organizymedb.org/), a comprehensive, manually curated database of 28,121 experimental measurements of enzyme stability and function in the presence of organic solvents, compiled from 646 publications and covering 704 distinct proteins. Each entry is extensively annotated with the experimental conditions, including assay type, solvent identity and volume fraction, assay solution composition, pH, temperature, substrate(s), product(s), and enzyme production method, as well as the protein 3D structure and cross-links to other databases. OrganiZymeDB will assist both experimentalists, by providing straightforward access to solvent-compatibility data for enzymes of interest, and computational scientists, by providing a well-curated dataset to develop and evaluate methods for predicting enzyme solvent tolerance, ultimately enabling the design of robust industrial biocatalysts.

works.title: LncRNAfunc 2.0: an evidence-integrated knowledgebase for regulatory and functional interpretation of lncRNAs in cancer
works.abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) play diverse regulatory roles in cancer, yet their functional interpretation remains largely based on molecular associations and computational predictions, while experimentally derived evidence is fragmented across heterogeneous resources. Here, we present lncRNAfunc 2.0, an updated knowledgebase for systematic functional interpretation of cancer lncRNAs through multi-source evidence integration. Compared with the previous version, lncRNAfunc 2.0 reprocesses pan-cancer data from The Cancer Genome Atlas, incorporates normal-tissue and cancer-cell-line contexts from GTEx and CCLE, substantially expands binding and interaction evidence, and introduces perturbation evidence for lncRNAs and their regulators. These resources are integrated with association-based analyses and computational predictions as complementary evidence for interpreting lncRNA-associated regulatory relationships. lncRNAfunc 2.0 organizes functional knowledge into six biological dimensions: dysregulation, upstream regulation, lncRNA-mediated mRNA regulation, transcript remodeling, protein regulation, and tumor phenotypes. This framework connects regulatory determinants of lncRNAs with their downstream molecular relationships and phenotypic associations, including mRNA regulation, alternative splicing, protein regulation, survival, molecular and immune phenotypes, and drug response. Overall, lncRNAfunc 2.0 provides an evidence-integrated framework for exploring context-dependent lncRNA functions and regulatory mechanisms across cancers. lncRNAfunc 2.0 is freely available at https://lncrnafunc.xu-bioinfo.com/.

works.title: GlyTouCan v4: a redesigned interface and expanded functionality for the international glycan structure repository
works.abstract: GlyTouCan (https://glytoucan.org) is the international, species-neutral glycan structure repository that assigns stable, globally unique accession numbers to glycan structures independently of the experimental method used to determine them. Here, we describe GlyTouCan version 4, released on June 22, 2026, which introduces a completely redesigned user interface with substantially faster browsing and searching, including a new "archetype" view that groups registrations that differ only in the anomeric or ring form of the reducing-end residue together for clearer filtering of the >256,000 glycans now registered. Version 4 provides an improved graphical structure input, via the updated browser-embedded GlycanBuilder application, for both searching and registering structures. Users may now sign in with an ORCID ID in addition to a Google account, and all previously released v3 REST API endpoints remain fully backward compatible. Version 4 also introduces a framework for industry affiliates, providing a structured pathway for commercial organizations that work with or synthesize glycans, while all existing academic database-partner relationships are maintained. GlyTouCan remains freely available to all users without charge, login, or registration for browsing and searching. We also summarize the repository's data content, which spans >600 monosaccharide types and, judging from these, includes many glycans of probable bacterial or plant origin.

works.title: iGPSC-DB: a comprehensive database for an inferred single-cell genetic perturbation atlas
works.abstract: Genetic perturbation-induced transcriptional reprogramming drastically remodels tumor cellular phenotypes and tumor microenvironment crosstalk. Unraveling the heterogeneous cellular responses to genetic perturbations is essential for the mechanistic dissection of tumors and the discovery of therapeutic targets. Here, we present iGPSC-DB (https://bio-bigdata.hrbmu.edu.cn/iGPSC-DB), a database designed to infer connections between tumor microenvironmental cells and diverse genetic perturbation events and to dissect the heterogeneous cellular responses to these perturbations. iGPSC-DB curates associations linking 178 114 perturbation events that target 7407 genes to 9 249 080 single cells from 1580 samples across 88 cancer types. iGPSC-DB also provides seven user-friendly tools for retrieving and analyzing: (i) inferred associations between genetic perturbation events and cells/cell types; (ii) the inferred perturbation-associated effects of perturbations on cellular functions, developmental trajectories, and cell-cell communication within the tissue microenvironment; (iii) the combined effects of different perturbations on cells, facilitating the design of combination therapeutic regimens; (iv) the impact of different perturbations on the differentiation trajectories and functional states of malignant cells; and (v) the association between perturbed target genes and clinical survival outcomes. iGPSC-DB will serve as a valuable resource to advance single-cell-resolution research on gene functions, regulatory mechanisms, and the discovery of tumor therapeutic targets.

works.title: Social manipulations trigger shifts in group-level dominance patterns
works.abstract: Within dominance hierarchies, individuals often direct aggression based on their own rank and the rank of others. When many group members make the same rank-informed aggression decisions, a broader group-level "dominance pattern" can emerge which further structures aggression within the framework of the dominance hierarchy. However, whether groups can change their group-level dominance patterns over time, and what factors might drive these changes, are not well understood. We investigated aggression dynamics by experimentally manipulating captive groups of monk parakeets (Myiopsitta monachus) using targeted rank-based removals and reintroductions of group members to induce social instability. Dominance patterns often shifted after experimental perturbations but remained stable in their absence. The rank of the perturbed individual affected both individual aggression decisions and the shifts in dominance patterns observed. In particular, reintroductions of top-ranked birds led to marked changes in aggression and shifts in dominance patterns. Understanding the factors that shape these dynamics can help explain how animal societies respond to social disturbance.

works.title: A computational framework to model cartilage degeneration induced by mechanoinflammation and cytokine-driven inflammation in post-traumatic osteoarthritis
works.abstract: Knee joint injury is a major risk factor for post-traumatic osteoarthritis (PTOA), often associated with early cartilage degeneration. Mechanical overloading and cytokine-driven inflammation are key drivers of this process, yet the underlying mechanisms and their distinct temporal and spatial contributions to cartilage degradation remain unclear. Here, we present a mechanobiological finite element framework that simulates cartilage degradation through cell-mediated proteolytic activity triggered by injurious loading-driven mechanoinflammation and cytokine-driven inflammation. The model reproduces experimentally observed depth-dependent loss of collagen and aggrecan, with mechanoinflammation inducing a transient response and cytokine-driven inflammation sustaining prolonged matrix degradation. Sensitivity analysis further shows that mechanoinflammation-driven degradation is governed mainly by protease production per cell, whereas cytokine-driven degradation is more sensitive to the rate of cellular stimulation. Together, this framework provides a mechanistic basis to study proteolytic cartilage degeneration and supports future in silico evaluation of therapeutic strategies aimed at mitigating cartilage degradation in PTOA.

works.title: TriTower-m6Am: A triple-tower heterogeneous deep learning architecture integrating semantic, sequential, and structural information for mRNA N6,2′-O-dimethyladenosine site prediction
works.abstract: Background N 6 ,2′-O-dimethyladenosine (m6Am) is a cap-proximal mRNA modification deposited by PCIF1 (phosphorylated C-terminal domain (CTD)-interacting factor 1) at the first transcribed nucleotide of eukaryotic mRNAs. Knowing where m6Am sites sit would help explain how cells tune mRNA stability and translation, but current predictors typically depend on a single representation and do not jointly model multiple views of the same RNA sequence. Results We present TriTower-m6Am, combining semantic (RNA-FM, a pretrained RNA foundation model, with BellPooling), sequential (One-Hot BiLSTM, bidirectional long short-term memory), and structural (RGCN, a relational graph convolutional network, over the 41-nt window) representations of each RNA window. On an independent test set of 640 sequences, TriTower-m6Am reaches an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.776 and a Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) of 0.425, against DTC-m6Am’s AUC = 0.765 and MCC = 0.411, using 4.4 times fewer trainable parameters; at every matched specificity between 0.40 and 0.70 it recovers 1–7 more true sites out of 320 than DTC-m6Am. The AUC-weighted voting keeps every tower’s contribution readable for any individual prediction. Analyses of the graph tower delimit its benefit to the relational aggregation of local backbone adjacency over sequence-derived node features: the edge-type ablation, the node-feature ablation, and a structure-permutation control agree that the specific RNAfold-predicted fold carries no attributable signal, and a probing analysis shows that per-base base-pairing status is largely recoverable from the sequence-derived RNA-FM embeddings (AUC = 0.72 vs. 0.65 from the raw sequence), so the fold annotation is substantially redundant with the semantic representation the ensemble already receives. Conclusions Combining semantic, sequential, and structural views of the same RNA sequence improves m6Am prediction beyond any single representation, and the ensemble’s voting weights make each prediction auditable without a post-hoc explainer. Whether the triple-tower pattern transfers to other RNA modification prediction tasks remains to be tested in future work.

works.title: Membrane tension and cell–nucleus mechanical coupling regulate confined cell migration
works.abstract: Cell migration is a fundamental physiological process essential from embryogenesis to cancer metastasis. It is primarily governed by the coupled mechanics of the plasma membrane (PM) and the nucleus, together with cytoskeletal dynamics. Being the largest and stiffest organelle, the nucleus is considered a rate-limiting factor in confined migration. However, nuclear positioning varies across cell types and migration modes, and the forces orchestrating its mechanical coupling with the PM are not completely understood. In recent decades, mathematical modelling has gained relevance to support cell migration research, yet models face the fundamental challenge of balancing mechanistic detail with computational efficiency. Here, we develop a dimensionless, biophysically grounded model based on geometric surface partial differential equations (GS-PDEs) for cell migration. This approach benefits from dimensional reduction-the PM and the nuclear envelope (NE) are modelled as energetic geometric membranes-and is solved using the evolving surface finite element method (ESFEM), balancing mechanistic detail with computational feasibility. The model reproduces experimentally observed migration patterns: exhaustion of lipid reservoirs and nuclear-lamina unfolding limit PM and NE surface area, blocking cell passage through constrictions; nuclear velocity peaks upon pore exit; and nuclear movement alternates between pulling and pushing regimes. Moreover, the modelling approach makes key predictions: the velocity peak upon nuclear pore exit is driven by the release of the curvature-elastic energy stored as membrane tension at the NE rear, and PM-NE mechanical coupling can hinder cell translocation, since part of the locomotion energy is invested in nuclear positioning. The model quantifies forces that are not easily experimentally accessible, including membrane tension, bending energy, osmotic pressure, PM-NE elasticity, and contact forces, offering an interpretable platform to test and propose mechanistic hypotheses on confined cell migration.

works.title: Ten simple rules for a successful global health roundtable
works.abstract: Qualitative approaches play a critical role in global health research by capturing the social, political, and contextual dimensions that shape health outcomes. While interviews and focus groups are widely used, these methods are often time‑limited and project‑specific. Global health roundtables offer a complementary approach, providing a flexible and long-term platform for engaging diverse stakeholders-including researchers, practitioners, policymakers, and community representatives-in collective dialogue, knowledge exchange, and collaboration. When designed well, roundtables can support co‑production of knowledge, address complex system‑level challenges, and generate insights with relevance beyond a single event. Despite their growing use, practical guidance on how to design and run roundtables specifically for global health remains limited. In this article, we present ten simple rules for organising successful global health roundtables, drawing on existing literature, practice‑based experience, and examples from different geopolitical and health‑system contexts. The rules address key stages of the roundtable lifecycle, including topic selection, objective setting, inclusive participation, management of power dynamics, optimisation of engagement and commitment, ethical recognition of contributions, and translation of dialogue into meaningful outputs and sustained collaboration. Together, these rules provide an accessible framework to support researchers, practitioners, and policy actors in using roundtables as ethical, inclusive, and impactful tools for global health research, policy development, and practice.

works.title: Short-Interval MRI Volume Change and 24-Month Recorded Alzheimer's Disease Diagnosis in Mild Cognitive Impairment: An Exploratory Landmark Analysis
Scalable physical deep learning using optical dynamics with state-skipping training and single-map architecture
works.abstract: Abstract The escalating energy demands for high-performance machine learning have sparked growing interest in unconventional computing paradigms rooted in physical systems. At the core of this emerging direction is the leveraging of physical properties to design computing frameworks that integrate strong learning capabilities, efficient training strategies, and practical implementability. Here, we present a simple, efficient, and scalable framework aimed at achieving this, and validate it on an optoelectronic platform. This framework features our proposed training mechanism—state-skipping direct feedback alignment—which eliminates access to intermediate states of the system and thereby significantly simplifies the error backpropagation process, enhancing both training efficiency and practical feasibility. Compared to conventional deep neural networks, our approach substantially reduces computational costs and training parameter count while achieving comparable performance. Furthermore, we integrate our scheme into modern architectures, attaining improved performance with an approximately 40% reduction in computational resources. Notably, our approach challenges the scaling laws of conventional counterparts, underscoring its strong scalability and practical promise.

works.title: Ridge Redundancy Analysis for High-Dimensional Omics Data
works.abstract: Abstract Motivation Redundancy Analysis (RDA) is a popular reduced rank regression approach for modeling the relationships between two sets of variables. In omics studies, RDA provides a flexible framework for investigating associations between high-dimensional molecular data. However, omics datasets often exhibit strong multicollinearity and suffer from the “large p, small n” problem, where the number of predictor variables p exceeds the number of samples n. Ridge RDA addresses multicollinearity by introducing a ridge penalty in addition to the rank restriction. Despite these advantages, its application to high-dimensional omics data remains challenging due to i) difficulties in manipulating the large coefficient matrix of dimensions p×q, where q represents the number of response variables, and ii) the need to jointly select the rank and the regularization parameter that both influence the performance of the method. Results We propose an efficient computational framework for ridge RDA that overcomes these challenges by leveraging the Singular Value Decomposition of the predictor matrix X. This approach eliminates the need for direct covariance matrix inversion, improving computational efficiency. Furthermore, we introduce a novel strategy that reduces the memory burden associated with the storage of the coefficient matrix from pq to (p+q)r, with r the chosen reduced-rank dimensionality. Our method enables an efficient grid search to jointly select the ridge penalty λ and r via cross-validation. The proposed framework is implemented in the R package rrda, providing a practical and scalable solution for the analysis of high-dimensional omics data. Availability The R package rrda is available on CRAN: https://CRAN.R-project.org/package=rrda. Scripts and data used for the analysis are available on GitHub: https://github.com/Yoska393/rrda.

works.title: GPCRVS in the detection of target-selective molecular scaffolds based on deep learning and gradient boosting
works.abstract: Abstract Motivation High drug selectivity minimizes unintended interactions that cause adverse effects, decreases drug potency, and are failure-prone factors in many clinical trials due to a poor balance between drug efficacy and toxicity. Sharing similar structural folds and modes of activation, G protein-coupled receptors may represent difficult drug targets in terms of optimization of pharmacodynamic profiles towards drug target selectivity. Here, we describe GPCRVS, a web service for GPCR virtual screening, designed to detect selective drug-like compounds. GPCRVS combines machine learning for ligand-based approaches using deep learning and gradient boosting, together with multi-target, structure-based virtual screening. Results GPCRVS performed well in binary classification (GPCR ligand vs non-GPCR ligand) with an F1 score of 0.875 and in multiclass classification for predicting drug target and drug target class with precision of 0.421 and 0.914, respectively, demonstrating its ability to detect active compounds with improved pharmacological characteristics. For receptors with sparse ChEMBL datasets such as active-state CCRL2, CXCR5, CCR6, CCR7, CCR8, CCR9, CCR10, and inactive-state CCR7, mixed training datasets based on receptor sequence homology were used for the ML model training with resulting accuracy of 85.5% obtained, e.g., for the CCR8-active ML model. In addition, GPCRVS detected target-selective, distinct molecular scaffolds with the LightGBM module such as fluorinated fragments in CCR6 inhibitors, or nitrogen-rich heterocyclic fragments in CXCR3 inhibitors. Availability and implementation GPCRVS is available on: https://gpcrvs.chem.uw.edu.pl.

works.title: scICER: clustering stability assessment for integrated single-cell analyses
works.abstract: Abstract Motivation Clustering is essential in single-cell and spatial omics for identifying cell types and states, but stochastic algorithms such as Leiden can reduce cluster stability and compromise annotation reliability. We present scICER, an R/Seurat implementation of single-cell Inconsistency Clustering Estimator (scICE)-style inconsistency analysis that evaluate clustering stability on user-provided graphs stored in Seurat objects from standard or integrated workflows. Results Compared with the original Julia implementation, the scICER adds ecosystem-native input/output, fixed-resolution evaluation, optional handling of very small clusters, and practical workflows for large objects. Across 48 benchmark datasets and integrated analyses, scICER reproduced reference scICE behavior while enabling stability assessment after Harmony or scVI correction. Availability and implementation scICER is implemented in R and is freely available at https://github.com/ATPs/scICER. A companion Python implementation with similar functionality, scICEpy, is available at https://github.com/ATPs/scICEpy.

works.title: Multiscale multimodal integration of spatial omics through a deep generative model with CORAL
AI-guided cancer survival prediction could spare some children high-dose brain radiation
An information-theoretic framework for inferring T cell dynamics from single-cell RNA and T cell receptor sequencing
works.abstract: Single-cell T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire sequencing enables simultaneous profiling of gene expression and TCR sequences, providing a coregistered measure of T cell phenotypic diversity and clonal dynamics. However, principled probabilistic frameworks for joint modeling of clonotype and phenotype have remained limited. Here we introduce TCRi, a hierarchical Bayesian information-theoretic framework that infers the joint probability distribution between genetic clonotype and transcriptional phenotype from paired single-cell transcriptomic and TCR sequencing data. TCRi treats phenotype assignment as a probabilistic inference problem: a variational autoencoder embeds single-cell expression into a structured latent space, and a hierarchical Bayesian model learns clonotype-specific phenotype distributions through principled information-sharing across clonotypes, patients and covariates. From these distributions, TCRi computes information-theoretic quantities: clonotypic entropy, phenotypic entropy, phenotypic flux and mutual information between clonotype and phenotype. When TCRi was applied to four real-world datasets comprising 167,118 CD8 T cells from patients with cancer treated with anti-PD-(L)1 immune checkpoint blockade, mutual information emerged as a robust discriminator of therapeutic response.

works.title: Decoding neuroendocrine tumors: a cross-site multiomic approach unveils clinically relevant molecular subtypes
works.abstract: Neuroendocrine tumors (NETs) comprise a heterogeneous family of malignancies of wide anatomic distribution but shared clinical and molecular features. Although tissue-specific biology has been well characterized for some common primary sites, comprehensive analyses capable of defining biologically meaningful, site-independent subtypes are lacking. This study aimed to identify and validate cross-site molecular subtypes of NETs and to evaluate their clinical relevance. Multi-omic factor analysis (MOFA) and unsupervised clustering were used to integrate tumor gene expression and DNA methylation data from 194 patients with lung, stomach, pancreas, small intestine, and colorectal NETs. Latent factors representing biologically meaningful sources of variation were leveraged to generate a robust consensus clustering derived from eight unsupervised algorithms. Each molecular subtype was comprehensively characterized by integrating clinical, pathological and molecular features with survival through multivariable Cox proportional hazards models. Validation was performed in independent external cohorts of lung, small intestine, and pancreatic NETs with publicly available multi-omic datasets. We identified three distinct molecular subtypes (NS1–3). NS1 exhibited a strong immune phenotype and was enriched in metabolic and nutrient-digestion pathways. NS2 showed pronounced neuroendocrine differentiation with enrichment of neuronal and secretory programs. NS3 was characterized by global DNA hypermethylation, enrichment in DNA-replication pathways, and significantly poorer prognosis (10-year OS: 51.9% vs. 83.2–83.9% for NS3 vs NS1/NS2; p = 3 × 10 −4 ). NSs were independent of primary tumor location and retained independent prognostic significance in multivariable models adjusting for age, sex, TNM stage and tumor site. Validation in an external cohort confirmed the robustness of these findings. This new cross-site classification of NETs reveals convergent biological traits and common potentially targetable vulnerabilities, providing a framework for biomarker development and the rational design of novel therapeutic strategies.

works.title: Genomic ascertainment refines the population prevalence and phenotype associations of germline TERT variants
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: Individuals with deleterious germline variants in telomerase (encoded by TERT) are at high risk of pulmonary fibrosis (PF), liver disease (LD), bone marrow failure, head/neck squamous cell carcinoma (HNSCC), and other complications. Clinically ascertained cohorts are subject to biased ascertainment of affected individuals and families with early onset, complex disease. This study used genomic ascertainment to determine prevalence of deleterious TERT variants and the associated risks of telomere biology disorder (TBD) phenotypes. METHODS: TERT variants were extracted from exome sequencing data in UK Biobank (UKB, 469,377 exomes) and Geisinger-Regeneron DiscovEHR collaboration (DiscovEHR, 170,503 exomes). Cases were individuals with heterozygous deleterious TERT variants classified per modified ACMG/AMP criteria. Controls excluded rare, exonic, and splice site TERT variants. Electronic health records were assessed for TBD-related ICD10 codes. Case-control comparisons were done separately for UKB and DiscovEHR, accounting for smoking, alcohol, BMI, sex, genetic ancestry, and birthyear. RESULTS: There were 64 deleterious TERT variants in 203 UKB participants and 32 in 138 DiscovEHR participants. Prevalence estimates were 1:2,312 in UKB and 1:1,235 in DiscovEHR. Risk of PF was significantly increased for TERT heterozygotes compared with controls (UKB: odds ratio [OR] 10.9 95% confidence interval [CI]: 6.11-19.45, p < 0.001; DiscovEHR: OR 6.64, 95% CI: 3.31-13.3, p < 0.001). Deleterious TERT variants were also associated with higher risk of LD (OR 2.4, 95% CI:1.25-4.59, p = 0.038) and HNSCC (OR 5.75, 95% CI: 2.36-14.02, p = 0.001) in UKB but not in DiscovEHR. CONCLUSIONS: Rare deleterious TERT variants were present in 0.04 to 0.08% of the populations studied. Genomic ascertainment shows a predominance of pulmonary phenotypes, with PF associated with deleterious TERT variants in both cohorts. Associations with LD and HNSCC were observed only in UKB, possibly reflecting cohort differences including healthy volunteer bias. These findings illustrate the clinical importance of genetic diagnosis, and need for TBD-specific clinical trials.

works.title: RobPicker: a meta-learning framework for robust identification of macromolecules in cryo-electron tomograms
More is more: why cell number matters in microscopy
Fast and accurate resolution of ecDNA sequence using Cycle-Extractor
works.abstract: Extrachromosomal DNA (ecDNA) plays a key role in cancer pathology. ecDNAs mediate high oncogene amplification and expression and are associated with worse patient outcomes. Accurately determining the structure of these circular molecules is essential for understanding their function, yet reconstructing ecDNA cycles from sequencing data remains challenging. We introduce Cycle-Extractor (CE) for this task. CE takes as input a breakpoint graph derived from either short or long read sequencing data and extracts cycles of maximum length-weighted copy number. CE utilizes a mixed-integer linear program (MILP) and a separate traversal procedure, enabling fast optimization and compatibility with open-source ILP solvers. We evaluated CE against CoRAL (long-read, mixed-integer quadratically constrained programming), Decoil (long-reads), and AmpliconArchitect (AA; short reads) on both simulated data and real cancer cell lines. On simulated ecDNA, CE achieves accuracy comparable to CoRAL across three metrics and consistently outperforms AA and Decoil. On cancer cell lines, CE produces longer and heavier cycles than AA, and performs comparably to CoRAL, while being on average 40× faster. These results demonstrate that CE accurately reconstructs ecDNA from both short and long-read sequencing data, and that long-read inputs allow CE to recover more complete, higher-confidence ecDNA structures. CE improved the prediction of many ecDNA structures. On PC3 ecDNA containing MYC, CE uses ONT data to reconstruct a substantially larger and higher-copy sequence (4.2 Mbp) compared to the short-read-derived reconstruction (690 kbp). CRISPR-CATCH experiments confirm the presence of a large ecDNA molecule, validating the long-read-based CE reconstruction.

works.title: ECOD in 2027: a modernized interface and an updated classification of protein domains
works.abstract: The Evolutionary Classification of Domains (ECOD) organizes protein domains into a hierarchy of evolutionary relationships, encompassing both experimentally determined and computationally predicted structures. ECOD now classifies 2.9M domains, of which ∼1.37M derived from the Protein Data Bank and 1.51M from predicted models in the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. The principal development we report here is a complete rebuild of the ECOD web resource. Search has been reconstructed around three modalities: (i) sequence, (ii) structure, and (iii) keyword. Foldseek now is the primary search method for the ECOD web page, searching a ∼457k representative domain database that is also distributed for local use. Results are presented through a Mol* interactive viewer, and a new API has been developed for programmatic access to the database. Alongside the interface, the pipeline for classifying new PDB entries has been rebuilt and returned to a regular cadence, family groups have been synchronized with Pfam v38.2, the bulk distributables have been reorganized and now include the search databases, the ligands in contact with each domain are recorded for experimental structures and annotated with drug cross-references from DrugDomain, and a registry has been introduced through which ECOD assigns stable identifiers to gene-called proteins and records the structures it predicts. ECOD is freely available at http://prodata.swmed.edu/ecod.

works.title: Correction to ‘Conformational reorganization and phase separation drive hyper-editing of ADR-2–ADBP-1 complex’
Bayesian efficient coding
works.abstract: The efficient coding hypothesis, which proposes that neurons are optimized to maximize information about the environment, has provided a guiding theoretical framework for sensory and systems neuroscience. More recently, a theory known as the Bayesian Brain hypothesis has focused on the brain's ability to integrate sensory and prior sources of information in order to perform Bayesian inference. Although pieces of a connection between these two hypotheses have appeared in prior work, a general formulation that treats the optimality criterion as an arbitrary functional of the posterior distribution - and thereby admits both information-based and other objectives within a single framework - has remained largely implicit. Here we make this formulation explicit, developing a Bayesian theory of efficient coding that defines Bayesian efficient codes in terms of four basic ingredients: (1) a stimulus prior distribution; (2) an encoding model; (3) a capacity constraint, specifying a neural resource limit; and (4) a loss functional, quantifying the desirability or undesirability of various posterior distributions. Classic efficient codes arise as the special case in which the loss functional is the posterior entropy, leading to a code that maximizes mutual information, but alternate loss functionals give solutions that differ dramatically from information-maximizing codes. Within this framework we introduce covtropy, a novel family of losses defined on posterior distributions and parameterized by a single exponent, and use it to show that decorrelation of sensory inputs - optimal under classic efficient codes in low-noise settings - can be disadvantageous for objectives that penalize large errors. We then reanalyze Laughlin's seminal data on contrast coding in the blowfly large monopolar cell, and find that the measured response nonlinearity is better explained by minimizing Lp reconstruction error with p = 1/2 than by information maximization, overturning a forty-year-old interpretation. Bayesian efficient coding thus enlarges the family of codes that are optimal under different objectives and provides a more general framework for understanding the design principles of sensory systems.

works.title: Shapley fields reveal mosaic chemotopic organization in the mouse Olfactory bulb across diverse chemical feature sets
works.abstract: Neural representations in the olfactory bulb (OB) remain poorly understood compared to well-established coding principles in other sensory systems. This difficulty arises because a natural coordinate system for olfactory stimulus space has not yet been identified, complicating the characterization of neural receptive fields analogous to those in other sensory modalities. Moreover, the extent to which these tuning properties are spatially organized within the OB remains unclear. To advance our understanding of the olfactory coding, we introduce an interpretable method of Shapley fields, as an olfactory analog of retinotopic receptive fields. Shapley fields are spatial distributions of chemical feature importance for the tuning of OB glomeruli. We used this tool to investigate chemotopy in the OB with diverse sets of chemical features using widefield epifluorescence recordings of the mouse dorsal OB in response to stimuli across a wide range of the chemical space. We found that Shapley fields reveal a weak chemotopic organization of the chemical feature sensitivity of dorsal OB glomeruli. This organization was consistent across animals and mostly agreed across very different chemical feature sets: (i) the expert-curated PubChem database features and (ii) features derived from a Graph Neural Network trained on human olfactory perceptual tasks. This chemotopy involved at least three chemical feature dimensions, rather than one or two dominant properties. Moreover, we found that the principal components of the Shapley fields corresponded to single commonly accepted chemical classification groups. This implies that these chemical groups could have been identified purely from the mouse olfactory responses. Our findings suggest that Shapley fields may serve as a chemical feature-agnostic method for investigating olfactory perception.

works.title: MoleMap: fast alignment-free molecule mapping for long-read and linked-read sequencing data
works.abstract: Abstract Background With sequencing costs continuing to decline, the computational expenses of read alignment in genome analysis are becoming an increasingly important consideration.
