When only portions of the genome are of interest – as in most clinical genome analyses – or base-pair precise alignment is not required, performing full read alignment on whole-genome sequencing (WGS) data imposes unnecessary computational costs. Alignment provides the base-by-base precision necessar​y to identify variants relative to a reference sequence. To improve efficiency, sequence reads can first be rapidly mapped to approximate chromosomal locations, allowing expensive alignment to be restricted to specified target regions subsequently. This mapping-first approach avoids performing base-pair precise alignment across the entire genome. Results We introduce MoleMap , a “molecule mapping” method for long reads and linked-read molecules that pre-filters WGS data for downstream targeted analyses. MoleMap uses a minimized open-addressing k -mer index of the reference genome and a fast k -mer clustering procedure to assign reads or molecules to genomic regions. In our evaluation, MoleMap identifies the correct mapping location for a comparable number of reads as other mapping and standard alignment tools on simulated data and achieves high agreement with other tools on real data while running 3 − 8 × faster than other mappers and 10 − 60 × faster than full aligners on 32 threads. In addition, its low memory footprint allows whole-genome processing on a standard laptop computer. As proofs of concept, we use MoleMap to filter reads for local assembly of a known variant region that involves non-reference sequence and showcase its use in diagnosing a patient with a rare disease. Conclusions MoleMap is a practical mapping tool for whole-genome data that accelerates targeted analyses by selecting reads from loci of interest before costly alignment. By identifying locus-specific reads, it decreases the volume of data passed to downstream processing steps. In a clinical sequencing setting, this can substantially reduce computational costs and diagnostic turnaround times.

works.title: ToxiFusion: Integrating Contextual and Compositional Sequence Representations for Toxic Peptide Prediction
works.abstract: Abstract Motivation Accurate prediction of toxic peptides from sequence information is important for peptide safety assessment and therapeutic development. However, reported performance of computational predictors can be affected by representation limitations and evaluation bias. Results We present ToxiFusion, a leakage-controlled framework integrating protein language model-derived contextual representations with interpretable sequence descriptors for toxic peptide prediction. ToxiFusion combines ProtBERT embeddings with amino acid composition and dipeptide composition features using an XGBoost classifier. Preprocessing, model selection, and threshold optimization used training-derived information only. On the locked ToxTeller independent test set, ToxiFusion achieved a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.718. External evaluation on an overlap-audited ToxIBTL cohort achieved a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.835 after removing exact training-sequence overlaps. Ablation analyses supported incremental contributions from the representation blocks, while feature-attribution analyses showed broadly consistent patterns for contextual and compositional features across evaluation cohorts. ToxiFusion provides a reproducible framework for toxic peptide prediction and highlights the importance of leakage-controlled validation. Availability and implementation Source code, frozen model artifacts, processed data, and analysis outputs are available at https://github.com/ameneayyoubi-hub/ToxFusion.

works.title: Maftools-MCP: A Model Context Protocol–enabled Framework for LLM–driven Somatic Mutation Analysis
works.abstract: Abstract Motivation Somatic mutation analysis is routine in cancer genomics, but the scale and complexity of next-generation sequencing data can make analysis challenging. Maftools is widely used for somatic variant analysis and visualization, yet its R-based workflow can be difficult for non-programmers, while graphical interfaces may provide access to only predefined analytical options. Results We developed Maftools-MCP, a framework based on the Model Context Protocol that translates natural-language requests into structured tool calls for Maftools analysis. Maftools-MCP demonstrates how this protocol can enable natural-language interaction with an R-based analytical package while allowing flexible control of exposed functions and parameters. We also developed an agent skill to support upstream variant annotation before downstream Maftools analysis. Evaluation included per-tool validation, repeated execution of three representative use cases across five language models, including commercial and locally deployed models, and comparison of an integrated annotation workflow with a directly executed reference workflow. Availability and implementation Maftools-MCP is publicly available at http://tardis.cgu.edu.tw/maftools-mcp.

works.title: BiGGViz: A MATLAB App for Visualization of Genome-Scale BiGG-Based Metabolic Networks
works.abstract: Abstract Motivation Genome-scale metabolic reconstructions have become essential tools in systems biology for studying cellular metabolism and supporting in silico experimentation. The Biochemical, Genetic, and Genomic (BiGG) knowledge base provides standardized, open-source metabolic models in multiple formats, including Systems Biology Markup Language (SBML) and MATLAB MAT files, facilitating model reuse and integration with computational frameworks such as the COBRA Toolbox. However, visualizing and exploring large-scale metabolic networks remains challenging, particularly for users without extensive programming expertise. Accessible and interactive visualization tools are needed to improve the interpretation, communication, and exploration of dense reaction and metabolite networks. Results We developed BiGGViz, a MATLAB-based application for interactive visualization and exploration of COBRA-compatible BiGG metabolic models. BiGGViz automatically constructs reaction-reaction and metabolite-metabolite graphs and provides an interactive graphical interface for network exploration. Users can switch between reaction- and metabolite-centric views, customize node appearance, apply topology-based filtering, inspect local neighborhoods, highlight pathways with configurable hop-based expansion, and export visualizations or network structures for downstream analyses. Optional annotation tables support overlay of user-defined attributes and COBRA-derived analyses, including flux balance analysis (FBA) results, enabling flux-aware exploration of genome-scale metabolic networks. BiGGViz supports exploratory systems biology analyses, result communication, educational applications, and integration with downstream Cytoscape-based workflows. A scriptable wrapper, exportBiGGViz, is also provided to support reproducible, code-driven analysis pipelines. Availability and Implementation BiGGViz is implemented in MATLAB and is freely available at https://github.com/mogystats/BiGGViz. Browser-based documentation and a detailed Getting Started tutorial are available at https://mogystats.github.io/BiGGViz/GettingStarted.html.

works.title: Longitudinal single-cell profiling of breast tumors highlights immune and epigenetic mechanisms associated with sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors
works.abstract: Estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer treatment is based primarily on endocrine therapy. To dissect mechanisms of sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors in ER-positive breast cancer, we profiled tumor biopsies from 25 patients during neoadjuvant therapy using single-cell RNA sequencing, immune receptor sequencing and enhancer activity mapping. Malignant cells with high ER signaling and elevated activity of enhancers with ER binding sites were sensitive to treatment. Resistance was associated with androgen receptor signaling, dedifferentiation and epithelial–mesenchymal transition. Poor responders preferentially used the androgen receptor cis-regulome under treatment pressure. The baseline tumor microenvironment was associated with tumor downstaging. Poor responders exhibited a ‘hot’, yet ineffective immune landscape enriched for naive lymphoid and undifferentiated myeloid cells. Good responders showed an active immune microenvironment with sustained clonal expansion of T cells. Our longitudinal single-cell analyses elucidate the genetic, cellular and epigenetic mechanisms driving sensitivity and resistance to neoadjuvant aromatase inhibition in ER-positive breast cancer. This longitudinal single-cell study of estrogen receptor (ER)-positive breast cancer suggests that strong estrogen signaling, ER-linked enhancers and active T cell responses could predict sensitivity to aromatase inhibitors, whereas resistance involves androgen signaling though hormone-sensing enhancer activity.

works.title: The Participant Engagement and Cancer Genome Sequencing Network to accelerate research in rare and understudied cancers
authors: On behalf of the Participant Engagement and Cancer Genome Sequencing (PE-CGS) Network

works.title: LIGOR: A Geospatial Multi-omic Atlas of Intra-tumor Spatial Heterogeneity in Hepatocellular Carcinoma
works.abstract: Intra-tumor heterogeneity is one of the central hallmarks of hepatocellular carcinoma, yet its spatial and multi-modal organization remains poorly resolved. Here we present the Liver Cancer Geospatial Omics Resource called LIGOR, a platform that captures spatial intra-tumor heterogeneity through multi-regional, multi-omic profiling. LIGOR integrates 719 spatially resolved tumor sectors from 136 patients together with 43 inter-patient cohorts comprising 6068 patients, forming one of the most comprehensive databases for hepatocellular carcinoma. LIGOR is organized into genomic, transcriptomic, immunologic, and biomarker layers, capturing key dimensions of intra and inter tumor heterogeneity. These modules support analyses of driver landscapes, clonal evolution, transcriptomic subtypes, tumor microenvironment states, and spatially resolved biomarkers, while a multi-modal integration framework links genotypic alterations to phenotypic variation. Together, LIGOR provides a comprehensive, spatially informed framework to resolve the geospatial and molecular architecture of hepatocellular carcinoma and has the potential to translate these insights into clinically relevant biomarker evaluation and therapeutic strategies. LIGOR is freely available at http://ligor.especies.cn/home.

works.title: XGBoost-SHAP analysis prioritizes lower-frequency variants predicted to affect HNF4A binding motifs in pancreatic progenitors
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: Noncoding genetic variants underlie many complex traits, yet predicting their regulatory impact in cell type-specific contexts remains a major challenge. Transcription factor binding is a primary mechanism through which noncoding variants influence gene regulation, but the relationships among chromatin accessibility, variant frequency, and transcription factor binding are complex and nonlinear, limiting the performance of traditional linear models. METHODS: We generated single-nucleus ATAC sequencing data from seven induced pluripotent stem cell-derived pancreatic progenitor cell samples and identified 93,803 heterozygous single nucleotide polymorphisms overlapping accessible chromatin regions. Allele-specific effects (ASE) were quantified for each variant via binomial tests. We trained XGBoost, logistic regression, and regularized logistic regression models to predict allele-specific effects via chromatin read depth, peak score, variant minor allele frequency (MAF), and transcription factor binding prediction for five pancreatic transcription factors: HNF4A, HNF1A, NEUROD1, NKX6-1, and PDX1. Model performance was assessed by the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) via fivefold cross-validation as well as using test and validation SNP sets. Shapley (SHAP) value analysis was used to interpret model predictions and to cluster variants on the basis of their regulatory feature contributions. RESULTS: XGBoost significantly outperformed linear models, particularly at stringent allele-specific effect thresholds, consistent with its ability to capture nonlinear interactions among features. Chromatin read depth, peak score, and minor allele frequency were the strongest predictors. Stratification by read-depth and MAF deciles showed that XGBoost retained better overall predictive performance across deciles than the linear models, indicating that its advantage was not explained by these variables alone. Dimensionality reduction of variants on the basis of Shapley value profiles revealed seven clusters with distinct chromatin states and variant allele frequencies. These findings were supported by highly significant pairwise differences in allele frequency distributions across the seven clusters. One cluster was enriched for lower-MAF SNPs showing strong predicted interactions with HNF4A binding motifs. Because MAF and its SHAP contribution were inputs to the embedding, the lower-MAF identity of this cluster was expected; its high ASE enrichment and distinctive HNF4A interaction structure were the biologically informative findings. Combined Annotation Dependent Depletion (CADD) analyses further supported a stronger relationship between HNF4A-related predictions and predicted deleteriousness in this cluster. CONCLUSIONS: Integration of single-nucleus chromatin accessibility data with an interpretable XGBoost-SHAP framework provides a method for prioritizing noncoding variants and identifying nonlinear regulatory relationships in a specific developmental context. Within this framework, the stronger relationship between HNF4A-related predictions and CADD-predicted deleteriousness in the lower-MAF cluster is consistent with selective constraint on HNF4A-bound regulatory elements and suggests a hypothesis for how lower-frequency noncoding variation may contribute to intrafamilial phenotypic variability in HNF4A-related Maturity-Onset Diabetes of the Young (MODY1).

works.title: Limitations of de novo peptide sequencing in resolving sequence ambiguity
works.abstract: De novo peptide sequencing enables peptide identification from fragmentation spectra without relying on sequence databases. However, incomplete spectra create ambiguity, making unambiguous identification challenging. Recent deep learning advances have produced numerous de novo models that predict sequences and refine peptide-spectrum matches under such conditions. Yet, their relative strengths, weaknesses and ability to handle spectrum ambiguity remain unclear. Here we benchmark eight state-of-the-art models on three publicly available proteomics datasets, comparing performance using established metrics and quantifying inter-model agreement. We assess post-processing approaches, including iterative refinement, rescoring and reranking, for their ability to improve identification accuracy, and perform an error analysis to identify common mispredictions and their causes. Model performance varied, with considerable overlap of correct identifications. Post-processing yielded no or only modest improvements. Most sequencing errors were model-independent and driven by limited fragment ion coverage, a limitation also observed in database searches with large search spaces.

works.title: Head-mounted camera for reconstructing outdoor behavior in freely flying birds
works.abstract: Capturing the fine details of behavior when animals perform complex tasks, such as prey pursuit and capture, in natural environments is a challenging endeavor. For birds of prey, commonly used tracking approaches, such as lightweight GPS and inertial measurement units, cannot simultaneously track the bird's position and the fine details of body part motion or moving external objects. Here we designed a head-mounted, tetherless, 4π camera system which, combined with a high-resolution environmental scan, enabled detailed three-dimensional measurement of both head position and orientation in freely flying Harris's hawks (Parabuteo unicinctus) performing aerial pursuit in the wild. This stable head-mounted imaging approach enabled reconstruction of flight trajectories in natural environments, detailed quantification of head motion, optic flow and target position, while the bird tracked and captured airborne targets.

works.title: Reconstructing a predatory bird’s aerial pursuit behavior in the wild
EnzyREx: deep learning enables reaction-based comprehensive enzyme screening
works.abstract: Orphan enzymes for which the corresponding genes remain unidentified represent a major gap in functional annotation in genomic analysis. We present EnzyREx, an AI-based framework for comprehensive enzyme screening, to explore novel enzyme candidates. EnzyREx consists of two deep learning models to classify proteins as enzymes and non-enzymes and predict catalytic capability for enzyme‒reaction pairs. Both models achieved performance comparable to or better than that of existing software. When applied to 1,255 microbiome-related orphan reactions, EnzyREx identified candidate proteins for 897 reactions. EnzyREx provides a scalable approach for linking unannotated proteins to orphan reactions and extending functional annotation.

works.title: UniqSketch: sensitive and resource-efficient strain-level detection in metagenomes
works.abstract: Microbial communities contain diverse organisms, including multiple coexisting strains of the same species that display phenotypic differences influencing pathogenicity and host interactions. Detecting strains is challenging because of computational demands and their low abundance in metagenomes. We present UniqSketch, an open-source toolkit for identifying target strains across species within a single metagenome. It tracks specific microbial signatures or contaminants even in complex, multi-species samples. UniqSketch uses unique genomic fingerprints and a compact Bloom filter for efficient computation and accurate abundance estimation. Results show improved precision and accuracy over existing tools, with reliable performance at sequencing coverage as low as 0.1×.

works.title: PhenX Toolkit: a knowledgebase that enables consistent data collection and facilitates cross-study analysis and data reuse
works.abstract: The PhenX (consensus measures for Phenotypes and eXposures) Toolkit (https://www.phenxtoolkit.org/) is a publicly available knowledgebase of well-established, broadly validated measurement protocols recommended for use in genomic, clinical, translational, and epidemiological research involving human participants. Consistent use of PhenX protocols, including questionnaires, bioassays, and physical assessments, improves the rigor, transparency, reproducibility, and comparability of research data. The Toolkit was recently highlighted in the National Institutes of Health (NIH) implementation plan, "Leading in Gold Standard Science," as an example of efforts to advance reproducible biomedical research. The Toolkit currently includes 1010 protocols spanning a wide range of diseases, exposures, and study designs. Content development is guided by the scientific community through a consensus-based process involving expert Working Groups, community input, and strategic oversight from the PhenX Steering Committee. Collaborations with NIH Institutes have expanded Toolkit content in priority areas, including substance use and cardiovascular disease. The PhenX Toolkit enhances study design and supports implementation of selected protocols. PhenX also collaborates with resources that facilitate data collection (REDCap), data standards (LOINC), and data repositories to promote interoperability and cross-study analyses. To date, the Toolkit has been recommended in 711 NIH funding opportunities and cited in >1300 publications. Future directions are discussed.

works.title: Correction to ‘DFF-ChIP: a method to detect and quantify complex interactions between RNA polymerase II, transcription factors, and chromatin’
works.abstract: In the originally published paper, the x axis scale in panel D of Figure 4 was labeled incorrectly as -500 to + 500, the correct scale is -250 to + 250.

works.title: The influence of ensemble size and composition on the performance of combined real-time COVID-19 forecasts
works.abstract: During infectious disease outbreaks, short-term forecasts can play an important role for both decision makers and the general public. While previous research has shown that combining individual forecasts into an ensemble improves accuracy and consistency, practical guidance for organisers of multi-model prediction platforms on how to construct an ensemble has been scarce. In particular, it is not entirely clear how ensemble performance relates to the size of the underlying model pool, a relevant question when relying on voluntary contributions from modelling teams that face competing priorities. Furthermore, the exact composition of an ensemble forecast may influence its performance. Ensembles can either include all models equally or, alternatively, discriminate based on past performance or other characteristics. Using data from the European COVID-19 Forecast Hub we investigated these questions, with the aim of offering practical guidance to organisers of multi-model prediction platforms during infectious disease outbreaks. We found that including more models both improved and stabilised aggregate ensemble performance, while selecting for better component models did not yield any particular advantage. Diversity among models, whether measured numerically or qualitatively, did not have a clear impact on ensemble performance. These results suggest that for those soliciting contributions to collaborative ensembles there are more obvious gains to be made from increasing participation to moderate levels than from optimising component models.

works.title: Global sensitivity analysis for stochastic models of infectious diseases: Re-emergence of yellow fever virus in the Americas as a case study
works.abstract: Emerging infectious diseases are a persistent public health threat that challenge deterministic, mechanistic modeling approaches. Because outbreaks initially start with a low number of infected hosts, their dynamics are highly stochastic, making traditional deterministic methods, e.g., ordinary differential equations, unable to qualitatively or quantitatively capture the transmission dynamics. In place, stochastic models are used, such as Markov chain models, but these models present their own challenges. Often, to infer a quantity of interest with stochastic models, we need to sample the model’s distribution many times over, introducing an additional source of noise to our analysis. This additional noise makes the inference of our quantity of interest more difficult and computationally expensive. Here, we show how novel tools from the field of uncertainty quantification can be used to efficiently separate these two channels of noise, allowing us to make rigorous statistical inferences about processes important for disease emergence. We illustrate these techniques with a model of yellow fever virus spillover in the Americas, a virus that has seen rapid re-emergence amongst multiple hosts and vectors in South America over the last decade. We show that only a handful of parameters’ uncertainties greatly affect variation in cumulative disease incidence. In particular, uncertainty in patch connectivity and non-human primate latency has the greatest impact on the variation of cumulative disease incidence of yellow fever virus across patches.

works.title: Folding without glutamine: Proteome-scale removal of a canonical amino acid
works.abstract: All known life uses a canonical alphabet of 20 amino acids, yet which residues are structurally essential remains untested at proteome scale. Isoleucine was recently eliminated from ribosomal proteins in Escherichia coli, establishing that amino acid alphabet reduction is feasible. Here we ask whether an entire amino acid can be eliminated from a proteome, and develop a computational framework to identify the best target. Using two independent approaches - ProteinMPNN structure-based probabilities and multiple sequence alignment conservation - we define "keep-score" as the fraction of positions where the native residue is optimal. Both methods converge on an unexpected candidate: glutamine has the lowest keep-score, with proline and glycine the highest - counter to substitution-matrix intuition. Glutamine's low keep-score is not explained by a single obvious substitute; glutamate is preferred in only 14% of replacements. Removing this target proteome-wide, we replaced every glutamine across 4,148 proteins with ProteinMPNN-optimal alternatives and modeled the resulting sequences with AlphaFold2. The recoded proteome maintained native-like structures: 85.5% of models exceeded a TMscore of 0.8, indistinguishable from the 85.9% baseline for rebuilt native sequences. Orthogonal validation - ESMFold predictions, Rosetta energy calculations, and conformational ensemble comparisons - revealed no evidence of systematic misfolding attributable to glutamine removal. As a consistency check, a glutamine-free TEM-1 β-lactamase designed with ProteinMPNN conferred ampicillin resistance in E. coli, indicating fold preservation can extend to biological function. Evolutionary evidence further supports these findings: 24% of E. coli proteins have glutamine-free orthologs in prokaryotic genomes, and glutamine ranks lowest in keep-score in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. These results show that an entire amino acid can be removed from a proteome with folds broadly preserved, establishing keep-score as a general framework and glutamine as the primary candidate for recoding. Crucially, this reflects a computational analysis of structural replaceability, not a demonstration of biological dispensability.

works.title: Predicting protein-RNA binding signals with a hybrid deep neural network
works.abstract: RNA-binding proteins play critical roles in post-transcriptional regulation by interacting with RNA to regulate various cellular processes. Inferring the binding signals and sequence patterns of these interactions is essential for elucidating the mechanisms underlying gene expression regulation. In this study, we present RBPSignal, a deep learning-based computational tool designed to predict RBP binding signals on RNAs and identify potential sequence motifs associated with these interactions. RBPSignal leverages the deep learning framework and trains on comprehensive eCLIP datasets, demonstrating an enhanced predictive accuracy. Furthermore, the integration of model interpretability through Integrated Gradients enables the detailed analysis of binding motif syntax. We validate the efficacy of RBPSignal on chromosome data and compare the discovered motifs with existing motif database, showcasing its ability not only to predict binding signals but also to uncover sequence patterns correlated with binding signals. Our findings provide insights into the sequence specificity of RBPs and explore the protein-protein motif-sharing network. RBPSignal serves as a valuable tool for exploring RBP-RNA interaction landscapes, facilitating further investigations into the regulatory networks underlying gene expression. The web server is freely available at http://www.csbio.sjtu.edu.cn/bioinf/RBPSignal/ .

works.title: LEEN: local equivariant energy networks with evolution-guided structural reasoning for protein stability prediction
works.abstract: Accurate prediction of changes in protein thermodynamic stability ( Δ Δ G ) caused by single amino acid substitutions is important for protein engineering, therapeutic design, and interpretation of disease-associated variants. Recent approaches combine protein language models with structural neural networks via feature fusion, often yielding large, computationally expensive models that do not explicitly enforce thermodynamic consistency. We present LEEN (Local Equivariant Energy Network), a lightweight architecture that combines energy-based prediction with evolution-guided structural reasoning for protein stability prediction. LEEN is based on three complementary principles. First, mutation effects are predicted as the difference between mutant and wild-type energies evaluated in a shared local context, which guarantees fixed-context anti-symmetry algebraically; a symmetrized-context variant extends this to exact anti-symmetry when the same symmetrized context is applied to both mutation directions. Second, local protein geometry surrounding the mutation site is encoded using an E(n)-equivariant graph neural network, enabling rotation- and translation-equivariant structural representation learning. Third, evolutionary information extracted from a protein language model is incorporated via message gating, allowing sequence-derived context to modulate the flow of structural information rather than being concatenated with structural features. Despite using only approximately 2–3 million trainable parameters, LEEN achieves competitive performance on multiple low-sequence-similarity protein stability benchmarks. The full model obtains Spearman correlations of 0.657 on S461 and 0.470 on S669, while the best-performing variants reach 0.658 and 0.482, respectively. Ablation studies further show that incorporating evolutionary information contributes substantially more to predictive performance than the choice or complexity of the geometric encoder, while gating provides an additional, benchmark-dependent benefit. LEEN provides a compact framework for protein stability prediction that combines local equivariant structural reasoning with evolutionary information from frozen protein language model representations. The energy-difference formulation guarantees fixed-context anti-symmetry, and a symmetrized-context variant extends this to exact anti-symmetry for independently constructed mutation inputs when a shared symmetrized context is used, at a measurable accuracy cost. Across eleven benchmarks, LEEN achieves competitive predictive performance with a substantially smaller task-specific trainable component than larger multimodal predictors. These results highlight the importance of integrating evolutionary and structural information while making the trade-offs between predictive accuracy and thermodynamic consistency explicit.

works.title: SHAKIRA: Scaled hierarchical ancestry K-population inference from RNA-seq alignments
works.abstract: Abstract Background Genetic ancestry estimation is an underutilized analytical approach that provides valuable biological context for studies investigating population-associated variation in gene expression, disease biology, and treatment response. Admixture-based ancestry estimates have historically relied on DNA microarray data, whole-genome sequencing, and whole-exome sequencing. However, RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data contains informative markers suitable for broad ancestry estimates. Given the widespread availability of RNA-seq datasets, a standardized and accessible RNA-seq-based ancestry estimation pipeline would expand opportunities to incorporate genetic ancestry into transcriptomic analyses. Results Herein, we describe Superpopulation-level Haplotype Ancestry from K-population Inference of RNA Assays (SHAKIRA), a bioinformatic pipeline for estimating global genetic ancestry from cancer-derived RNA-seq data and evaluate its performance using both experimental tumor RNA-seq samples and an external reference dataset. First, we applied the pipeline to RNA-seq data from 86 pancreatic neuroendocrine tumor samples and compared predominant ancestry coefficients to self-reported race. Using a 60% admixture proportion threshold to assign predominant ancestral superpopulation, 38 of 39 patients who self-reported as Black were assigned predominant African ancestry, and all 47 patients who self-reported as White were assigned predominant European ancestry. We then externally validated the pipeline using 144 Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia (CCLE) samples with published DNA microarray–based ancestry estimates. Ancestry estimates derived from RNA-seq data from CCLE samples demonstrated strong concordance with DNA-based estimates for African, American, and European ancestry components, with Pearson correlations of 0.995, 0.979, and 0.994, respectively. Conclusions These findings support the feasibility of using RNA-seq-derived variants to estimate broad genetic ancestry, particularly for African and European superpopulation components. SHAKIRA provides a practical approach for incorporating genetic ancestry into RNA-seq-based studies when matched DNA sequencing or genotyping data are unavailable.

works.title: Modality-aware external attention with explicit cross-omics interaction modelling for breast cancer subtype classification
works.abstract: Breast cancer is molecularly heterogeneous, and multi-omics measurements provide complementary information for molecular subtype classification. Their high dimensionality and modality-specific characteristics, however, make effective integration challenging. We developed a modality-aware external attention (MAEA) framework for classifying five breast cancer subtypes using mRNA expression, DNA methylation, and miRNA expression data. Boruta feature selection is performed separately for each modality within each training fold. Modality-specific encoders generate latent representations, while pairwise Hadamard interaction tokens explicitly represent cross-omics relationships. These structured tokens query shared external key and value memories and are combined through a learned token gate. In stratified 10-fold cross-validation on TCGA-BRCA, MAEA achieved 86.78 ± 2.46% accuracy, 83.47 ± 4.38% macro-recall, 81.36 ± 3.48% macro-F1, and 0.9694 ± 0.0115 macro-AUC. A matched modality-aware self-attention model achieved 85.65 ± 3.76% accuracy and 81.26 ± 3.61% macro-F1, with no statistically significant fold-wise difference. MAEA improved accuracy by 3.40 percentage points and macro-F1 by 3.54 percentage points compared with a concatenation-based external-attention baseline. Ablation experiments further supported the contribution of feature selection, interaction modelling, and external-memory attention. MAEA provides a structured multi-omics fusion strategy that preserves modality identity while explicitly modelling pairwise cross-omics interactions. Independent external validation remains necessary before clinical application.

works.title: AMR GeoMapper: client-side geospatial and temporal visualization of user-provided antimicrobial resistance data
works.abstract: Abstract Background Geographic visualization is a key method for monitoring the profile of global antimicrobial resistance (AMR). While current mapping tools are capable, they lack the ability to visualize or compare to user-provided data. To address this gap, we have developed and deployed AMR GeoMapper (AMR-GM) to https://camra.acegid.org/amr-geomapper/ . AMR-GM is a web-based tool that allows for client-side geographic and temporal analysis of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) metadata. Results AMR-GM is a tool that enables users to produce interactive charts and maps of AMR genotypic/phenotypic and bacterial abundance data. Data can be easily formatted for AMR-GM by following the standards specified in the documentation. Additionally, AMR-GM natively loads data downloaded from amr.watch, allowing users to compare their data with publicly available datasets. The source code and documentation for AMR-GM is freely available at https://github.com/JCVenterInstitute/AMR-GeoMapper-Public . Conclusions AMR-GM allows for private analysis of AMR data without reliance on public databases, giving researchers quicker access to high-quality visualizations. Because analysis of unpublished data is possible with AMR-GM, public health officials and researchers will have better software tools for analysis and surveillance of AMR and AMR pathogen spread in a geospatial framework.

works.title: Dingent: a configurable agent framework for biological database retrieval and integration
works.abstract: Abstract AI-driven data search and integration represent an emerging research direction. Although several LLM-based backend frameworks and agentic frameworks have emerged, significant gap remains in developing a one-stop, configurable agent framework that supports various data sources and provides a web interface for efficient data retrieval using natural language. To address this, we present Dingent, a novel and configurable agent framework that facilitates data access from various resources and enables the flexible constructions of agent applications. We demonstrate its capabilities across three distinct application scenarios, achieving promising results. The Dingent framework can be readily applied to other fields, such as earth sciences and ecology, to facilitate data discovery.

works.title: Multi-omics characterization of COVID-19 severity in a Korean cohort informs drug-repurposing candidates
Enumerating and Exploring the Space of Clonal Trees
works.abstract: Abstract Motivation Tumors are the result of a complex evolutionary process. Researchers use a structure called a clonal tree, which depicts ancestral relationships between mutated cell populations, to represent a tumor’s evolutionary history. A better understanding of the complete space of all clonal trees under certain assumptions has important implications for understanding and interpreting output from clonal tree inference algorithms. It is also an interesting mathematical problem. Results We designed several algorithms for enumerating different categories of clonal trees with a specified number of mutations. We then provide theoretical analysis of four different categories of clonal trees that utilize two models of mutation acquisition (Infinite Sites Assumption and k-Dollo). We used our algorithms to generate several datasets and analyzed the generated trees, uncovering some expected and some unexpected patterns. Our analysis includes comparison of our enumerated datasets to two common sampling procedures used to create simulated data, and shows that they sample from the space differently. Finally, for one dataset we found that for small numbers of mutations, linear trees were much more prevalent than branching trees. Availability and Implementation Code associated with the project is available at: https://bitbucket.org/oesperlab/tree-space/src/main/.

works.title: Progress and disparities in fungal genomics in the long-read era
A framework for genome-wide characterization of DNA methylation and variant effect prediction
works.abstract: DNA methylation plays a critical role in many essential biological processes, including transcriptional regulation, genomic imprinting, chromosomal maintenance, genomic stability and development, and has phenotypic and disease impacts. However, genome-wide characterization of methylation patterns across cell types and tissues remains a major challenge. Here, to address this, we present a framework that enables systematic genome-wide analysis of methylation and sequence-based prediction of context-specific methylation effects of variants. Our data-driven discovery of methylation classes reveals context-dependent roles for methylation across tissues, cell types and regions of the genome. The framework also includes Wreath, a deep learning-based sequence model specifically designed to accurately predict the context-dependent impact of any genetic variant on methylation. These developments leverage a compendium that harmonizes disparate methylation profiles from disparate studies including over 90 tissues and cell types. Using Wreath, we systematically characterized the impact of noncoding pathogenic variants on tissue-specific methylation, generating mechanistic hypotheses for individual regulatory variants. We make the full framework, including the compendium, the methylation classes and the model, available for use by the community. This study introduces a framework for integrating DNA methylation data across more than 90 tissues and cell types, characterizing genome-wide methylation patterns and predicting context-specific effects of genetic variants on DNA methylation and regulatory function using a deep learning model, Wreath.

works.title: Hematotoxicity: the hidden legacy of CAR T cell therapy
AI-based precision prognostics and therapy personalization for childhood brain tumors
works.abstract: Accurate prediction of patient outcomes remains a critical challenge in oncology, in particular for childhood brain tumors, in which treatment decisions need to carefully balance risk of tumor recurrence and death against severe therapy-induced sequelae. Here, we developed MANTIS (methylation profiling and artificial neural networks for time-dependent individualized survival predictions), a precision artificial intelligence (AI) tool for medulloblastoma and ependymoma outcome prediction built on genome-wide DNA methylation array data from 2,786 patients. MANTIS generates individualized survival probabilities over a 10-year period and achieves concordance indices as high as 0.80 ± 0.07, significantly exceeding the predictive accuracy of current clinical indicators. Extending MANTIS to estimate individualized treatment effects identifies ~60% of patients with average-risk medulloblastoma without a significant survival disadvantage (P = 0.683) when treated with less intensive craniospinal irradiation doses, which is associated with improved neurocognitive outcomes. In conclusion, our study establishes a foundation for AI-based precision prognostics and therapy personalization in childhood brain tumors and offers a blueprint for similar initiatives in other cancer types.

works.title: Cryptic spread of SARS-CoV-2 undermined targeted travel restrictions
works.abstract: The effectiveness of travel restrictions in mitigating the spread of novel viral variants remains understudied, particularly in regions with sparse genomic surveillance. We evaluated the efficacy of these restrictions in Western Asia, where countries sequenced less than one percent of SARS-CoV-2 cases in 2021, focusing on Iraq’s travel ban on India and the tourist travel restriction. We generated 535 SARS-CoV-2 whole-genome sequences from clinical samples collected in Duhok, Iraq, between June 2021 and February 2022, encompassing the Delta and Omicron variant waves. Using discrete Bayesian phylogeographic modeling, we reconstructed spatiotemporal viral spread patterns to determine whether travel restrictions delayed the introduction of the variants into the country, postponed community transmission onset, or altered the geographic sources of viral introductions over time. We found that the Delta variant was introduced into Iraq three months before the targeted travel ban was enacted, predominantly from Western and Southern Asia, whereas the Omicron variant was introduced despite the tourist travel restriction already being in place. We also show that both variants had established community transmission within the country despite travel restrictions, rendering these measures ineffective. Analysis of travel restrictions on a global scale reveals similar patterns of limited efficacy in mitigating the introductions of novel SARS-CoV-2 variants, challenging the usefulness of such measures. In this study, we demonstrate that border controls are largely ineffective, since VOCs typically spread internationally before detection, and potentially discourage countries from transparent reporting. Hence, rapid genomic sequencing and real-time international data sharing are our most effective tools against emerging VOCs. Public health responses should prioritize vaccination alongside proven non-pharmaceutical measures, including stay-at-home orders, mask mandates, restrictions on gatherings to fewer than 10 people, and the closure of high-exposure businesses, schools, and universities.

works.title: Cellular and spatial continuum of TAM functional states governs immune exclusion and dictates immune checkpoint resistance in melanoma
works.abstract: Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy has transformed melanoma treatment, yet many patients either fail to respond or develop resistance after an initial response. The cellular and spatial determinants within the tumor microenvironment (TME) that underlie these divergent ICI therapy outcomes remain poorly defined. Here, we aimed to characterize the immune composition and spatial organization of the TME associated with ICI response and resistance. We integrated public scRNA-seq data ( N = 32) with in-house spatial transcriptomics and imaging mass cytometry from an independent melanoma cohort ( N = 6) to achieve high-resolution spatial profiling of the TME. This multimodal approach allowed us to map cellular heterogeneity within discrete spatial neighborhoods. To validate our findings, we constructed a scRNA-seq derived signature-matrix and deconvoluted a bulk RNA-seq cohort ( N = 334). Clinical associations were assessed using Kaplan–Meier survival analysis, Cox hazard models, and a machine-learning classifier. We identified a distinct tumor-associated macrophage (TAM) state, termed lipid-associated TAMs (LA-TAMs), characterized by conserved lipid metabolic programs and tumor-specific adaptations in glycolysis under hypoxic conditions. Deep spatial multi-omics profiling revealed divergent immune architectures associated with treatment outcomes. In non-responder patients, LA-TAMs colocalized with sparsely distributed TIM3⁺ exhausted CD8⁺ T cells within an immune-excluded TME. In contrast, responder patients harbored interferon-primed CCL4 + TAMs (IFN-TAMs) spatially associated with Granzyme B⁺ activated CD8⁺ T cells, reflecting an immune-active microenvironment. These findings define contrasting macrophage-centered immune neighborhoods linked to ICI response. Interestingly, patients with LA-TAM–enriched neighborhoods were consistently non-responders or progressed during follow-up, irrespective of the presence of IFN-TAM neighborhoods. Lastly, we constructed a single-cell–derived signature matrix that estimates TAM fractions from bulk RNA-seq data and revealed LA-TAM abundance as a robust, independent predictor of poor ICI response and survival in a validation cohort. Our study defines the spatial landscapes of TAM-heterogeneity in melanoma and identifies LA-TAM neighborhoods as an important feature of ICI resistance. Although patients span a continuum of TAM-centered immune states, the presence of LA-TAM is likely to diminish the beneficial effects of IFN-TAM–associated immune activation. Finally, our proposed Melanoma-TME–derived signature-matrix provides a translatable framework to robustly predict ICI response and resistance.

works.title: Integrated single-nucleus and spatial transcriptomics define tumour cell metaprograms and tumour microenvironment organisation in choroid plexus tumours
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: Choroid plexus tumours (CPTs) are rare intraventricular brain neoplasms derived from choroid plexus epithelium, predominantly affecting young children. They include benign choroid plexus papilloma (CPP), atypical CPP (aCPP), and malignant choroid plexus carcinoma (CPC) and segregate into three DNA-methylation subgroups: paediatric A (pedA), paediatric B (pedB), and adult. METHODS: To resolve subtype-specific biology, we performed single-nucleus RNA sequencing on 43 CPTs and integrated 12 non-neoplastic foetal, paediatric, and adult choroid plexus references, complemented by spatial transcriptomics in a subset of 16 tumour sections and 2 normal choroid plexus samples. RESULTS: Tumour embeddings and correlation analyses demonstrated that CPTs cluster by methylation subtype rather than WHO grade, revealing epigenetically driven relationships despite divergent histology. We identified 10 tumour metaprograms spanning epithelial differentiation, ciliogenesis, proliferation, extra cellular matrix remodelling, and stress responses. PedA and adult tumours showed relatively homogeneous program distribution dominated by differentiation or ciliation states, whereas pedB tumours exhibited marked heterogeneity with selective enrichment of hypoxia, interferon signalling, early stress response, and TGF-β signalling. Spatial mapping revealed consistent anticorrelation of these programs with ciliogenesis and differentiation programs, suggesting stress-associated dedifferentiation. Elevated stress and hypoxia scores correlated with poorer survival. PedB tumours showed enrichment of interferon- and lipid-associated myeloid populations, that carried pro-angiogenic signatures. They were spatially co-localised with hypoxic and interferon I expressing tumour areas, that were predicted to interact with myeloid cells via immunosuppressive cues, shaping a pro-angiogenic, pro-tumour environment. CONCLUSIONS: This study identifies stress- and hypoxia-associated dedifferentiation programs that are selectively enriched in pedB tumours, correlate with poor clinical outcome, and antagonise multiciliogenesis and epithelial differentiation. Their spatial co-localisation with immunosuppressive, pro-angiogenic macrophage populations links developmental arrest to microenvironmental remodelling and aggressive behaviour. These findings provide a biologically grounded framework for risk stratification and highlight hypoxia, angiogenesis and macrophage polarisation as candidate therapeutic targets in high-risk CPTs.

works.title: Genomic epidemiology and potential dissemination of carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa clones among One Health sectors in China
works.abstract: The dissemination of carbapenem-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa (CRPA) across human, environmental, and agricultural interfaces represents an increasing One Health challenge. We analyzed 716 P. aeruginosa isolates collected over four seasons from hospitals, farms, and wastewater treatment plants in five provinces of China using whole-genome sequencing, clonal network analysis, and comparative genomics. Among the collected isolates, 477 (66.62%) isolates were identified as CRPA, comprising 63 carbapenemase-producing CRPA (CP-CRPA) and 414 non-carbapenemase-producing CRPA isolates. Despite substantial population diversity, comprising 189 known and 9 novel sequence types (STs), clonal dissemination was highly concentrated within specific epidemic lineages. Four major putative clonal clusters, dominated by ST381, ST360, ST463, and ST244, persisted across seasons in multiple hospitals. Clonal dissemination occurred predominantly within and between hospitals, with ST463 contributing prominently to possible inter-provincial dissemination, whereas potential cross-sector clonal links were limited to a small number of clusters connecting hospitals with farms or wastewater treatment plants. ST463 was strongly associated with CP-CRPA (26/31, 83.87%) and mainly carried bla KPC-2 on IncU plasmids with a conserved NTE-KPC structure (IS 26 -IS Kpn6 - bla KPC-2 -IS Kpn27 -IS 26 ). Analysis of publicly available genomes suggested that NTE-KPC elements facilitated the expansion of bla KPC-2 across diverse P. aeruginosa lineages in China. Multiple clones were frequently detected in hospital wastewater before or concurrently with detection of the same clones in clinical samples, supporting wastewater as a complementary matrix for genomic surveillance. We further developed a multidimensional framework for assessing hospital-level CRPA risk. Our findings identify hospitals as the predominant settings for CRPA clonal dissemination and highlight the potential of integrating wastewater surveillance and genomic risk assessment to support earlier detection and targeted infection-control interventions.

works.title: Whole-proteome structure/function prediction in uropathogenic E. coli reveals previously missed host-microbe and microbe-phage interaction pathways
works.abstract: The rapid advancement of high-throughput sequencing technologies has vastly increased the number of known protein sequences, but the experimental characterization of their structures and functions lags behind. This gap in knowledge impedes our understanding of biological mechanisms of these proteins, hinders the interpretation of high-throughput experiments, and exposes a significant challenge in modern biology: deducing the structural and functional information of proteins based on their sequences. Most computational approaches rely on homology with well-annotated proteins, yet many proteins lack identifiable homologues, reducing the power of this approach. Here, we integrated cutting-edge protein structure and function prediction methods to develop a complete sequence-structure-function pipeline that predicts structures and functions based on primary sequences. We applied this pipeline to predict the structure and function of all proteins in Escherichia coli UTI89, a model strain of uropathogenic E. coli. Based on the predicted functions, we performed enrichment analysis on the whole genome and revealed the possible roles and related biological mechanisms of poorly annotated proteins in this organism. Moreover, the performance of our pipeline was further validated through detailed case studies of the UTI89_C0931 and ybtS genes. Finally, we compiled the UTI89 structure and function database (https://seq2fun.dcmb.med.umich.edu/UTI89), offering it as a crucial resource to aid researchers in elucidating the roles of unannotated proteins. This database aims to bridge critical knowledge gaps in microbial pathogenicity and resistance, enhancing our capacity to tackle emerging health threats.
