works.title: Selective profiling of translationally active tRNAs and their dynamics under stress
works.abstract: During translation, transfer RNAs (tRNAs) deliver specific amino acids to the ribosome in a coordinated manner with the sequence encoded by the messenger RNA. Despite their central role in protein synthesis, their precise contribution to the modulation of translation remains poorly understood, primarily due to lack of methods to characterize tRNA abundances and their modifications from actively translating ribosomes. Here we develop tRIBO-seq, a simple and robust nanopore-based method to selectively capture ribosome-associated native tRNA populations (ribo-tRNAs) from actively translating ribosomes, providing tRNA abundance, modification and fragmentation information from a single experiment. Using tRIBO-seq, we find that ribo-tRNAs, but often not total tRNAs, are significantly altered on stress. Notably, we find that tRNAome alterations strongly vary depending on the stress type; while viral infection and leucine deprivation leads to changes in ribo-tRNA abundances, methionine starvation causes a dramatic loss of methyl-based tRNA modifications. By contrast, we find that arsenite exposure does not alter tRNA abundances nor modification patterns, but rather causes major fragmentation events in selected subsets of ribo-tRNAs. Altogether, tRIBO-seq offers a robust and reproducible approach to map the full tRNA landscape-capturing tRNA abundance, modification and fragmentation patterns-across both total and actively translating tRNA populations, revealing the dynamics of the tRNAome with unprecedented resolution, in a single experiment.

works.title: THEOBROMA: an aggregated open database of 1.13 million natural products with per-compound license auditing, three-tier classification, and stereochemistry-aware deduplication
works.abstract: Abstract Natural products remain one of the most productive sources of pharmacologically active compounds for drug discovery. Open aggregators attribute licenses at database granularity, and the consequences of that choice have become tangible as the field grows. A recent relicensing event in one constituent source (the September 2024 transition of the Natural Products Atlas to CC BY-NC 4.0) demonstrates how database-level licensing propagates across an aggregate and motivates the per-compound audit framework presented here. The same peer cohort separately leaves classification provenance and stereoisomer-family relations coarser than either layer warrants. THEOBROMA, accessible at https://theobroma.l3s.uni-hannover.de, integrates 1 132 805 natural products from 29 open sources under a per-compound license audit that resolves each compound’s license tier across all attesting sources under a most-restrictive-wins rule. 896 242 compounds (79.12%) are identified under open-use licenses, and the per-source attestation chain, together with the resolved tier, is exposed through a dedicated audit endpoint and a query-time license filter. A three-tier classification labels all but 21 compounds by the provenance of the assignment (55.3% curated source labels, 18.2% NPClassifier tool assignments, 26.5% model-inferred). Deduplication at the full 27-character InChIKey retains 1 132 805 entries across 486 032 connectivity families, exposed via a dedicated /api/stereoisomers/<comp_id> endpoint and a radial-family display. Any result set renders directly onto a taxonomic cladogram of its source organisms, so compositional queries are answered in the interface rather than downstream. Per-compound license provenance is the primary differentiator, while classification stratification and stereoisomer-family exposure add finer-grained access to two related axes. Together, they support license-compatible virtual screening and isomer-specific bioactivity analysis at corpus scale. As an evolving open resource, THEOBROMA pairs continuous pipeline maintenance with interactive geographic, taxonomic, and chemical-space exploration.

works.title: RNAactDrug 2.0: an updated resource for systematically exploring molecular features associated with drug sensitivity across multi-omics datasets
works.abstract: RNAactDrug 2.0 (available at https://bio-bigdata.hrbmu.edu.cn/RNAactDrug or https://bio-datamining.hrbmu.edu.cn/RNAactDrug) is an updated resource for systematically exploring molecular features associated with drug sensitivity across multi-omics datasets. We have updated the RNAactDrug 2.0 database with significantly expanded data and improved features, including (i) ∼30 000 drugs, 38 908 RNA molecules, and 22 800 375 drug-RNA associations from large-scale pharmacogenomic databases, covering four molecular layers: expression, copy number variation (CNV), mutation, and methylation; (ii) 11 099 cases from The Cancer Genome Atlas across 33 cancer types are integrated to support clinical and pan-cancer analyses of drug sensitivity-associated RNA features; (iii) ∼3.8 million cells from >200 single-cell RNA sequencing datasets, spanning 34 cancer types and 38 tissues, enable analysis of cell type-specific patterns and intratumoral heterogeneity; (iv) 26 440 enhancers and 788 444 drug-enhancer associations, combined with potential target prediction, provide an exploratory epigenetic regulatory dimension; (v) enhanced search and browsing functionalities, together with seven tools for functional annotation, pan-cancer analysis, tumor microenvironment profiling, single-cell trajectory and CNV analysis, and enhancer-related analyses. In summary, RNAactDrug 2.0 is a crucial resource for the multi-omics dissection of drug sensitivity-associated molecules, providing important support for the discovery of drug resistance biomarkers and the advancement of personalized therapeutic strategies.

works.title: InterPro: the protein sequence classification resource in 2027
works.abstract: InterPro (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/interpro) is a freely accessible resource for the classification of protein sequences. It integrates predictive models, known as signatures, from multiple member databases to classify sequences into families and to predict the presence of domains and functionally important sites. The InterPro database provides annotations for hundreds of millions of sequences, ensuring extensive coverage of UniProtKB, the standard repository of protein sequences, and includes mapping to several other major resources, such as Gene Ontology, the Protein Data Bank in Europe (PDBe), and the AlphaFold Protein Structure Database. In this publication we report on the status of InterPro (version 110.0), detailing new developments in the database, its associated web interface, and software. Notable updates include InterPro-N, a deep-learning method that increases sequence coverage of UniProtKB to over 90%; the transition from InterProScan 5 to the completely re-engineered InterProScan 6; the integration of structure-based domain classifications and predicted structures from AlphaFold; a redesigned protein viewer offering a concise summary view; and a new Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that allows AI assistants to query InterPro programmatically. Over the past two years, 9484 new InterPro entries have been created, bringing the total to 54 922. InterPro data, software and tools are freely available.

works.title: The TCR Motif Atlas: a database of specificities for TCRs recognizing viral, cancer, and autoimmune epitopes
works.abstract: T-cell recognition is elicited by the binding between T-cell receptors (TCRs) and epitopes. Many machine learning approaches have been proposed to model TCR-epitope recognition specificity, but most of them act as black boxes. To visualize TCR-epitope recognition specificity, we developed the TCR Motif Atlas (https://tcrmotifatlas.unil.ch). This database builds upon the probabilistic framework of TCR specificity profiles (TSPs) to visualize V and J genes as well as complementarity-determining Region 3 (CDR3) lengths and amino acids enriched in epitope-specific TCRs with respect to baseline TCR repertoires for hundreds of epitopes. An interactive interface enables users to build TSPs based on their own set of TCR sequences to investigate epitope recognition specificity or to explore potential biases in TCR repertoires of known or undetermined specificity. The TCR Motif Atlas further provides links to curated compilations of epitope-specific TCRs and crystal structures of TCR-epitope complexes.

works.title: CircaVal: a gene-centric multi-omics platform for exploring circadian regulatory features
works.abstract: The circadian clock orchestrates daily physiological processes through coordinated regulation of clock-controlled gene expression across multiple molecular layers. However, systematic characterization of this multilayered rhythmic regulation remains challenging because relevant information is distributed across independent datasets and rhythmicity is evaluated using diverse analytical approaches. Here, we developed CircaVal, a gene-centric multi-omics platform for the integrated exploration and interpretation of circadian regulatory features in humans, mice, and baboons. To support this framework, CircaVal processes public datasets using standardized, data-type-specific pipelines, and gene rhythmicity is integrated with tissue-specific expression, cross-species orthology, functional annotations, and multi-omics regulatory features. CircaVal further introduces an integrated rhythmicity score (IRS), which combines concordance across multiple rhythm-detection methods with reproducibility across independent datasets to provide a quantitative basis for prioritizing candidate rhythmic genes. The platform enables users to examine gene rhythmicity across datasets, identify tissue-enriched rhythmic genes, compare rhythmicity across species, and explore associated regulatory features. Additional functions include interactive gene-centric exploration, genome-browser visualization, rhythmicity analysis of user-uploaded time-series data, and programmatic data access. Together, these capabilities provide an integrated framework for rhythmic gene prioritization and gene-level interpretation of circadian regulatory features across tissues, species, datasets, and omics data types. CircaVal is freely available at https://CircaVal.com.

works.title: tModBase v2.0: an expanded database of tRNA modifications with an AI-powered assistant
works.abstract: Chemical modifications of transfer RNAs (tRNAs) are crucial for tRNA stability, codon decoding, translational fidelity, and tRNA-derived small RNA (tsRNA) biogenesis. Changes in these modifications are associated with stress responses, physiological regulation, and human disease, underscoring the need to integrate modification information with experimental evidence and biological context. We previously established tModBase, a web resource to organize and explore tRNA modification-related data. Its first release integrated modification sites, high-throughput sequencing-derived signals, and condition-dependent changes. Since then, tRNA profiling has expanded through modification-specific and direct RNA sequencing strategies, with rapidly growing datasets across species and conditions. Here, we present tModBase v2.0 (http://www.tmodbase2.com/), containing 528 datasets across 23 species, 40 sequencing and library-preparation methods, and 42 modification types. It includes 68 third-generation and 210 modification-specific sequencing datasets, extending coverage of direct-RNA and modification-specific approaches. tModBase v2.0 further integrates sequencing-derived signals, condition-dependent information, and biological annotations linking modifications with enzymes, genetic variants, tsRNAs, diseases, and expression profiles. The LLM- and retrieval-augmented generation-powered assistant tModBot enables natural-language exploration across database modules while grounding responses in retrieved tModBase evidence. tModBase v2.0 therefore provides an expanded resource for investigating the diversity, dynamics, and biological context of tRNA modifications.

works.title: The European Nucleotide Archive in 2026
works.abstract: The European Nucleotide Archive (ENA, https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena), hosted at EMBL's European Bioinformatics Institute, is an open resource that supports the global life sciences community by enabling submission, archiving, dissemination, and reuse of the world's nucleotide sequencing data. In 2026, the ENA continues to explore and address challenges related to a rapidly evolving landscape. This includes sustaining the growth of the data volume, increasing diversity in data types, the need for more standardized metadata, and the connection of sequence data with data from other disciplines. To address these challenges, the ENA has enhanced its services to adopt the INSDC minimum specification for data requirements, introduce new sample checklists and collaborate on an experiment checklist, and progress on the implementation of GFF3 for annotations. The ENA continues to support global science through its global engagement that includes understanding its Access and Benefit Sharing (ABS) requirements to the wider community. Sustainability is a major aspect of the archive, which has seen updates to incremental indexing and SRA read removal. Additionally, the broker community continues to be supported and expanded. In this paper, we discuss these challenges and opportunities as we continue to keep pace with the evolving life science data resource ecosystem and requirements.

works.title: Direction-selective retinal ganglion cells encode motion direction uniformly, despite having discretely distributed cardinal preferences
works.abstract: On-Off direction-selective retinal ganglion cells (DS RGCs) exhibit broad tuning curves, responding robustly to motion aligned with or near their preferred direction. These cells comprise four major subtypes, each tuned to motion along one of the four cardinal axes: nasal, superior, temporal, or inferior. However, natural stimuli can move in any direction, and it remains unclear whether intermediate directions are encoded less effectively, or whether this cardinal organization nevertheless supports uniform direction encoding. Here, we combined previous electrophysiological recordings of DS cells presented with a moving light bar stimulus with an information-theoretic measure, the Stimulus Specific Information, to estimate the directional sensitivity of small populations of recorded neurons. This analysis revealed that DS RGC populations are uniformly sensitive across all directions of motion. We then asked whether the observed homogeneous sensitivity was a consequence of DS RGCs maximizing the average stimulus information. Simulations with artificially modified tuning curve widths revealed that DS cells prioritize avoiding pronounced drops in sensitivity over maximizing the average transmitted information. This property reduces large deficits in sensitivity for certain directions, thereby limiting potential "blind spots" in the encoding of motion. More generally, our results raise the possibility that maintaining a high minimum sensitivity could be one factor influencing the organization of sensory representations.

works.title: SpatioCAD: Context-aware graph diffusion model for pinpointing spatially variable genes in heterogeneous tissues
works.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables comprehensive characterization of tissue architecture, and the identification of spatially variable genes (SVGs) is a critical step for defining region-specific molecular markers and uncovering spatially regulated mechanisms across diverse biological contexts. However, most existing methods for SVG detection overlook cell density variations, a major confounding factor in complex tissues such as tumors, where heterogeneous cellularity frequently introduces false-positive calls. Here we present SpatioCAD, a computational framework that explicitly decouples genuine spatial expression patterns from confounding effects driven by cellularity. SpatioCAD introduces a graph diffusion model that inherently incorporates cell-density-aware conditions to simulate expression propagation, supporting the identification of SVGs across a broad range of expression levels. Systematic evaluations on simulated datasets demonstrate its superior statistical power and specificity. Applied to breast cancer, lung cancer, and glioma datasets, SpatioCAD identifies functionally diverse SVGs, including low‑abundance transcripts with established roles in tumor progression, while also recapitulates biologically meaningful tissue architecture features. Importantly, SpatioCAD is fast and scalable to large tissues.

works.title: Traction force microscopy using temporal information
works.abstract: Traction force microscopy is a simple, non-invasive method that can quantify cellular contact forces at the cell-substrate interface. It solves an inverse problem of determining the force field from measured substrate deformation. Because this problem is ill-posed with a large condition number, it is necessary to suppress the amplification of measurement noise during inversion. Previous studies have employed algorithms such as regularization or filtering that utilize spatial information to discriminate noise and true signals. Here, we propose an alternative approach that utilizes temporal information of the system. This method employs Kalman filter, a simple data assimilation algorithm in time series analysis, to recover the force field. Using numerically generated data, we show that the method is more accurate than standard algorithms including L2-regularization and is effective at filtering out temporal noise. Using experimental data on locomoting cells, we demonstrate that the method can reliably infer time-varying cellular traction forces. We also demonstrate two extensions of the proposed method: incorporation of additional knowledge and direct inference of low-dimensional force characteristics. These practical advantages will motivate the use of proposed framework for analyzing dynamic cell mechanics.

works.title: The promiscuity and degeneracy of ten unique RNA base-pairing rules can determine the success of adaptive RNA evolution
works.abstract: The topography of fitness landscapes strongly influences the outcome of Darwinian evolution. This topography in turn is determined by the effects of genotypic changes on phenotypes, such as the structure and function of biomolecules like proteins and RNA. Thus, understanding the evolution of biomolecules requires an understanding of the relationship between genotype and phenotype. Here, we study how this relationship is influenced by the fundamental biochemical rules that determine which RNA bases can form base-pairs in RNA secondary structure. To this end, we computationally study the secondary structure genotype-phenotype maps of RNA molecules using all ten possible different such RNA base-pairing rules. We simulate adaptive evolution on fitness landscapes in which an RNA's fitness is defined by its secondary structure. We find that the base-pairing rules strongly affect how likely an evolving population is to find the global peak of a fitness landscape. The base-pairing rule of most biological RNA molecules (A-U, G-C, G-U) is among the top three most favorable rules for adaptive evolution, in which over 80% of evolving populations find a landscape's highest fitness peak. Simple characteristics of the genotype-phenotype map, such as the fraction of genotypes that constitute local peaks can help to predict how likely evolving populations are to find a landscape's global fitness peak. These characteristics can in turn be explained by two elementary properties of base-pairing rules that we call promiscuity and degeneracy.

works.title: EIHR-PROT: explicit modelling of homology reliability for protein function prediction
works.abstract: Sequence-derived predictions and homology evidence provide complementary inputs for protein function annotation, but how their contributions should vary across proteins remains an open question. We investigated EIHR-PROT (Explicitly Incorporated Homology Reliability Signals for PROTein Function Prediction), which combines frozen ESM-2 embeddings, trainable attention pooling, and a neural prediction branch with DIAMOND-derived homology priors. A learned gate assigns protein-specific fusion weights using maximum bitscore, maximum query coverage, log-transformed retained-hit count, and hit availability. On Protein Data Bank (PDB) and low-homology AlphaFold (AF) test sets, EIHR-PROT achieved Fmax values of 0.604, 0.731, and 0.676 on PDB and 0.425, 0.507, and 0.564 on AF for biological process (BP), molecular function (MF), and cellular component (CC), respectively. These exceeded the evaluated naïve, DIAMOND Score, DeepGOPlus, and TALE+ baselines. Relative to sequence-conditioned gating, EIHR-PROT improved Fmax and area under the precision–recall curve and reduced minimum semantic distance for BP and MF on both datasets, with paired 95% bootstrap intervals excluding zero. It also improved PDB Fmax across all aspects relative to learned fixed fusion. However, advantages over fixed and identity-conditioned fusion varied by dataset and metric, with both alternatives remaining competitive on AF. Mean homology weights varied little across retained-hit identity bins, with the largest change occurring when no hits were retained. EIHR-PROT supports reliability-conditioned sequence–homology fusion, with benefits clearest for BP and MF relative to sequence-conditioned gating. Its practical advantage over alternative fusion strategies depends on the dataset and evaluation objective. The implementation is available at github.com/uwidia/EIHR-PROT.

works.title: Soft-voting for robust common line assessment in cryo-EM angular reconstruction
works.abstract: Single-particle cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) reconstructs three-dimensional (3D) macromolecular structures from two-dimensional (2D) projection images acquired at unknown orientations. Common line-based angular reconstruction estimates projection orientations from pairwise common lines, but reliable common line detection remains challenging at the low signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) typical of cryo-EM experiments. Existing voting-based approaches either assign equal weight to all votes or apply hard binary thresholds, thereby discarding valuable confidence information and limiting orientation estimation accuracy. We present Soft-Voting, a common line assessment framework that replaces binary vote weighting with continuous confidence weighting. For each projection pair, Soft-Voting constructs a consensus histogram of candidate dihedral angles using information from all remaining projections, with each vote weighted according to the reliability of its supporting common lines. The resulting common-line reliability scores are used to construct pairwise weights for spherical embedding, enabling globally consistent orientation recovery. Experiments on a synthetic dataset (EMD-33026) with SNRs ranging from 1 to 1/16 show that Soft-Voting generally achieves lower orientation errors than existing common line-based methods, especially under low-SNR conditions. Experiments on three real cryo-EM datasets (EMPIAR-10028, EMPIAR-10328, and EMPIAR-10455) further show that Soft-Voting produces competitive ab initio reconstructions based on Fourier shell correlation against reference maps. The results indicate that Soft-Voting can improve common-line assessment and the robustness of cryo-EM angular reconstruction, particularly under challenging low-SNR conditions.

works.title: Subgenome-resolved assembly of the mahseer Tor tambra reveals allotetraploid subgenomes shared with Tor sinensis
oddSNP: a predictive framework for optimizing multiplexed single-cell RNA-seq experiments
works.abstract: Abstract Motivation Donor multiplexing is a powerful strategy to increase scale, lower the costs, and reduce batch effects in single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNAseq), but clear guidelines for experimental design are lacking, forcing researchers to risk costly demultiplexing failures. Results We introduce SNP-Information Content (SNP-IC), a quantitative metric computable from simple unpooled pilot data that accurately predicts the success of genotype-based demultiplexing. Across multiple large-scale datasets using stem cell and organoid models, we establish a robust SNP-IC threshold of approximately 50, above which cells can be reliably assigned to their donor of origin. For more challenging genotype-free approaches, we define a pairwise metric, cpSNP-IC, and demonstrate a much higher requirement of approximately 3,000. Availability and Implementation Our open-source framework, oddSNP, implements this predictive model to enable in-silico titration of sequencing depth and donor complexity, allowing researchers to optimize study design before large-scale deployment, while managing costs and minimizing the risk of catastrophic data loss. oddSNP can be installed directly from PyPI and Bioconda. Source code is also freely available from GitHub at https://www.github.com/nemoto-lab/oddSNP (with release versions also available in Zenodo at DOI 10.5281/zenodo.19378022). Novel scRNAseq data used as part of this study is available at the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) website under accession GSE334633.

works.title: PTGCDA: a PU-learning-driven Transformer and GraphSAGE framework for circRNA-disease association prediction
works.abstract: Abstract Motivation Circular RNAs play key regulatory roles in many human diseases, making accurate prediction of circRNA-disease associations essential for understanding diseases and discovering biomarkers. Existing methods are limited by insufficient sequence utilization, network sparsity, and noisy negative samples from unlabeled data. Results We propose PTGCDA, a computational framework that integrates sequence representation learning, graph representation learning, Transformer, and positive-unlabeled learning for circRNA-disease association prediction. PTGCDA extracts circRNA sequence features using k-mer embeddings, Word2Vec, and TextCNN; GraphSAGE learns node representations of circRNAs and diseases by aggregating neighborhood information from the heterogeneous network; and multi-head attention in Transformer further captures interactions between circRNA and disease representations. Meanwhile, a two-step positive-unlabeled learning strategy identifies reliable negative samples to reduce label noise during training. Five-fold cross-validation on four benchmark datasets and one integrated dataset demonstrated that PTGCDA outperformed existing methods, achieving an AUROC of 0.9202 on Dataset4. De novo prediction on the same dataset achieved an AUROC of 0.8646 and an AUPR of 0.1874, while ablation and case studies further supported the effectiveness of PTGCDA and its ability to identify potential circRNA-disease associations. Availability and implementation The PTGCDA code is freely available at https://github.com/WANGSicong1113/PTGCDA.

works.title: Clonal hematopoiesis and cytopenias following CAR19 therapy
works.abstract: CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor T cell therapy (CAR19) improves survival in relapsed/refractory large B cell lymphoma compared with immunochemotherapy with intent for autologous hematopoietic cell transplantation (autoHCT). However, major toxicities include prolonged cytopenias, infection and secondary hematologic malignancies. Here, to investigate these complications, we studied patients with lymphoma receiving CAR19 and compared clinical outcomes to propensity-matched autoHCT-treated controls. CAR19-treated patients exhibited impaired immune reconstitution and increased infection. Bone marrow analysis showed that prolonged post-CAR cytopenias are associated with clonal cytopenias of undetermined significance and interferon-mediated inflammation. Clonal hematopoiesis (CH) commonly expanded following CAR19 infusion and was associated with impaired immune reconstitution and treatment-related myeloid malignancy (tMN). Post-CAR tMN was molecularly and clinically comparable to post-autoHCT tMN. Single-cell DNA analysis revealed mostly independent CH clones, while CAR integration into CH-mutant T cells occurred frequently and may drive expansion and persistence. Together, these findings implicate CH expansion and marrow inflammation in key CAR19-associated toxicities. This study shows that clonal hematopoiesis expands after chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T cell therapy and contributes to secondary myeloid cancers. In addition, the CAR vector frequently integrates into pre-existing clonal hematopoiesis.

works.title: A catalog of transcriptome genetic regulation in a consanguineous Middle Eastern biobank
works.abstract: Ancestry-specific genetic mapping of transcriptome regulation is pivotal for understanding genome function, especially in underrepresented consanguineous populations. Here we characterized 1,882 Qatar Biobank participants, integrating blood RNA sequencing, whole-genome sequencing and phenotypic data across 45 clinically relevant traits. We cataloged ~7 million significant quantitative trait loci (QTLs), both short and structural variants, impacting gene expression, isoform usage, splicing and allele-specific expression, uncovering 1,379 novel eGenes. Fine-mapping resolved 29,953 high-confidence, independent causal loci including 24% previously unreported as well as those with effect alleles showing significant divergence across global populations, while 1,371 were absent from public databases. Leveraging elevated autozygosity, we found that causal variants are depleted from runs of homozygosity, consistent with purifying selection, while recent autozygosity increased the burden of homozygous regulatory variants. We identified QTLs with recessive deleterious effects on 10 Mendelian disease genes and homozygous QTLs causing extreme outlier expression in 66 genes including dosage-sensitive ones. Colocalization analysis revealed 58 causal variants acting on 20 clinically relevant phenotypes, implicating novel genes including ATP6V0B and RQCD1 in metabolic and blood disorders. These findings establish this QTL catalog as a valuable Middle Eastern resource for genome interpretation and genomic medicine.

works.title: Genomics for chronic overlapping pain conditions
Sequencing and analysis of the human adaptive immune receptor repertoire
Single-cell Sequencing Reveals Multi-omics Dynamics During Lymph Node Metastasis in Breast Cancer
works.abstract: Single-cell sequencing and analysis have advanced our understanding of intra-tumoral heterogeneity for breast cancer lymph node metastasis. However, how alterations at multi-omics levels coordinate together in a single tumor cell to drive metastasis remains unclear. Here we performed single-cell multi-omics sequencing of paired primary tumors and metastatic lymph nodes from breast cancer patients. This enabled a comprehensive reconstruction of dynamic molecular landscapes by simultaneously profiling genome, epigenome and transcriptome in the same single tumor cell. During metastasis of patients with higher heterogeneity, clonal evolution analysis based on copy number variations at single-cell resolution showed a specific clone possessing metastatic advantages. Meanwhile, the genome-wide DNA methylation underwent stageable changes. In contrast, gene expression was specifically reprogrammed concentrated at tumor cell transition, suggesting a remodelling by organ microenvironment. By integrative multi-omics analysis, we identified genes that were dysregulated at more than one omics, and showed the importance of SLC39A6, ELP2 and RPL13 genes in breast cancer metastasis or prognosis. Our study traces the genomic, epigenomic and transcriptomic dynamics simultaneously from primary tumors to metastatic lymph nodes in the same single cell, providing new insights into breast cancer metastasis.

works.title: Adjusting for medication status in genome-wide association studies
works.abstract: When conducting genome-wide association studies, addressing medication status that is relevant to the trait of interest can prevent biases that could distort estimates of the true genetic effect. Here, we introduce the genetic empirical medication reduction adjustment (GEMRA) method which uses a heuristic search for an empirical adjustment to be applied to phenotypic values of participants reporting medication use. Through simulations we show that the direct genetic effect estimates in the GEMRA approach exhibited less bias and greater statistical power than common strategies such as including medication as a covariate, restricting the sample to unmedicated users or including all samples without adjustment. We then applied the GEMRA approach to estimate statin medication adjustment for analysis of low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels and antihypertensive medication adjustment for analyses of systolic (SBP) and diastolic (DBP) blood pressure using multi-population data from UK Biobank and the Uganda Genome Resource. We found that a relative rather than an absolute adjustment better modelled the effect of medication on LDL cholesterol, SBP and DBP, with an effect of 40%, 10% and 10% reduction appearing to be consistent across populations, respectively. We also show that spurious differences in medication effects across populations can arise when the effect scale is misspecified.

works.title: A common pathogenic founder variant in Rwandan breast cancer cases
works.abstract: Germline data from African populations remain sparse, limiting characterization of population-specific BRCA1/2 pathogenic variants (PV). In a study of 175 Rwandan women with breast cancer, 7 unrelated carriers (4% of cases; 22% of PV carriers) harbored the same BRCA1 frameshift PVs, c.4065_4068del (p.Asn1355Lysfs*10), which is extremely rare in gnomAD yet recurrent in European, Asian, and Middle Eastern cohorts. Whole-exome sequencing and haplotype analysis of all 7 carriers revealed a shared ancestral block of approximately 581 kb surrounding the variant, and extended haplotype homozygosity and network analyses confirmed a common founder origin. Coalescent-based age estimation placed the founder event approximately 4,000--10,000 years ago. Comparison with 1000 Genomes Project data showed the founder haplotype is absent or exceedingly rare outside African and South Asian populations. These findings strongly suggest the c.4065_4068del variant as a pre-historical BRCA1 founder variant in Rwanda, with implications for targeted genetic testing, cascade screening, and cancer prevention in the region.

works.title: Genetic architecture of the murine serum metabolome reveals carboxyl esterases as master regulators of circulating fatty acid metabolism
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: The systemic biochemical diversity of circulating metabolites and lipids reflects the integrated effects of genetic variation and environmental exposure. Metabolite quantitative trait locus (mQTL) studies in humans have established gene-metabolite associations, but genetic contributions can be obscured by sex, diet, age, medication use, and environmental exposures. Genetically diverse model systems offer a powerful complementary strategy to isolate genetic contributions to the biochemical diversity of the circulating metabolome. METHODOLOGY/PRINCIPAL FINDINGS: We applied mass spectrometry profiling to serum samples in 541 mice from the Diversity Outbred (DO) population and identified 1,933 mQTL across 240 metabolites, 561 lipids, 43 oxylipins, and 4,465 MS/MS features. QTL hotspots on chromosomes 8, 9, 10, and 17 implicated distinct loci in the regulation of serum lipids, metabolites, and peptide-like features. The chromosome 8 Ces1 and Ces2 gene clusters were associated with lipids, acylcarnitines, and acyl-CoAs, while chromosomes 9 and 10 loci included additional lipid and metabolite QTL. On chromosome 17, MHC and C3 regions were associated with untargeted peptide-like MS/MS features. Comparisons with matched red blood cell mQTL revealed widespread compartment-specific genetic control. CONCLUSIONS/SIGNIFICANCE: Collectively, these findings provide a high-resolution map of the genetic regulation of the circulating metabolome, offering mechanistic insights that complement and extend human metabolic genetics.

works.title: Enhancing cell type deconvolution in spatial transcriptomics through incorporating multiple reference panels
works.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) captures gene expression with spatial context but often at resolutions where each spatial location contains multiple cells. Deconvolution of cell-type proportions is therefore essential, yet existing methods typically rely on a single scRNA-seq reference, limiting accuracy when references are incomplete or mismatched especially in complex tissues. These limitations highlight the need for a framework that can integrate multiple references while leveraging spatial information. We introduce SWIMR (Spatially Weighted Integration for Multi-Reference deconvolution), a statistical framework that integrates multiple scRNA-seq references while accounting for spatial correlations. SWIMR models each spatial location as a weighted combination of references, with both cell-type proportions and reference weights varying across tissue locations. Across comprehensive simulations and diverse ST datasets, SWIMR consistently outperformed single-reference approaches. In developing human heart tissue, it recovered ground-truth cell-type compositions with the highest accuracy. In human lung and breast cancer, SWIMR delineated tumor, stromal, and immune compartments, uncovered tumor-adjacent populations, and detected cell type-specific spatially variable genes missed by other methods. In mouse embryo and liver cancer, it leveraged context-specific references to resolve organ-specific cell types and increase sensitivity for biologically relevant pathways. Together, these results establish SWIMR as a robust framework for multi-reference deconvolution in spatial transcriptomics.

works.title: CalDyn: an advanced high-throughput automated algorithm for monitoring intracellular calcium dynamics and electrophysiological signals in patient-derived cells
works.abstract: BACKGROUND: Quantitative analysis of intracellular calcium and electrophysiological signals is challenging when signals exhibit baseline drift, low-amplitude events, irregular waveforms, or multicomponent transients. We developed CalDyn, a MATLAB-based graphical application for automated peak detection, waveform characterization, event classification, batch processing, quality control and data export. METHODS: CalDyn combines Savitzky-Golay filtering, LOESS-assisted derivative detection, optional baseline correction, waveform-boundary fitting and rule-based peak classification. It was evaluated on calcium recordings (healthy and disease-associated hiPSC-derived cardiomyocytes, hiPSC-derived neurons, primary skeletal myotubes), current-clamp action potentials and cardiac optical-mapping signals. Outputs were compared with PeakInspector, Clampfit and BV Workbench using paired and Bland-Altman analyses. Detection was assessed against 142 expert-annotated events and synthetic signals of known timing and amplitude. RESULTS: CalDyn achieved 94.4% sensitivity, 89.9% precision and an F1 score of 0.92. Performance peaked for healthy cardiomyocytes, paced myotubes and action potentials, with lower recall in arrhythmic cardiomyocytes and variable precision in neurons. CalDyn detected candidate low-amplitude diastolic and multicomponent Ca2+ events in arrhythmic cardiomyocytes, although the biological identity of CalDyn-only events was not independently confirmed. Comparisons with software revealed parameter-specific systematic differences, notably for rise rates and classifications. Action-potential measurements showed limited mean bias but non-negligible limits of agreement. In synthetic signals, amplitude error increased with noise and uncorrected drift, and timing error with low sampling rates. Detection remained stable across moderate parameter variation. CONCLUSIONS: CalDyn provides an accessible, reproducible and versatile workflow for automated analysis of heterogeneous calcium and electrophysiological signals. With appropriate quality control, it offers a robust alternative to modality-specific tools.

works.title: HiCP2GAN: a plug and play foundation model-based GAN for Hi-C enhancement
works.abstract: The 3D organization of chromatin shapes gene regulation and cellular function, and Hi-C has become the primary technique for mapping chromatin interactions genome-wide. However, high-resolution data remain costly and scarce, leaving many studies with sparse contact maps that limit downstream analysis. Deep learning methods, especially generative adversarial networks (GANs), have shown promise for enhancing low-resolution Hi-C data, but most existing GAN-based approaches rely on custom discriminators trained from scratch, which can yield unstable training and limited generalization. Hi-C foundation models pretrained on large-scale data capture rich, transferable representations of chromatin structure, yet their use as discriminators within adversarial enhancement frameworks had not been explored. We introduce HiCP2GAN, a plug-and-play GAN that employs a pretrained Vision Transformer-based Hi-C foundation model as its discriminator. The discriminator was pretrained on 118 million Hi-C patches across diverse species and cell types, providing biologically meaningful gradients for adversarial supervision. The framework is generator-agnostic: any compatible Hi-C resolution enhancement architecture can serve as the generator, enabling fair comparison across methods. The encoder phase of the foundation model was adapted as a discriminator backbone, finetuning the first few layers from the input while freezing the deeper transformer layers to preserve pretrained knowledge while allowing task-specific adaptation. Experiments across various cell lines show that HiCP2GAN outperforms traditional GAN-based methods in most settings and improves the reconstruction quality and biological reproducibility of existing Hi-C enhancement models in most evaluated cases. HiCP2GAN is publicly available at https://github.com/OluwadareLab/HiCP2GAN.

works.title: Multi-omics survival prediction under modality incompleteness via dynamic modality graphs and product-of-experts fusion
works.abstract: Multi-omics data integration provides rich complementary information for cancer survival prediction, yet modality incompleteness is pervasive in real-world medical data and undermines the stability and applicability of existing models. To address this challenge, we propose DMG-PoE, a robust learning framework for multi-omics survival prediction. The framework introduces a dynamic modality graph (DMG) that propagates complementary information across modality nodes to compensate for missing inputs, combined with an uncertainty-aware product-of-experts (PoE) fusion mechanism that adaptively weights each modality by its estimated precision, and a consistency-constrained training strategy that stabilizes predictions across varying modality subsets. Systematic evaluation on the SurvBoard benchmark across 10 TCGA cancer types and seven omics modalities demonstrates that DMG-PoE achieves the highest average C-index under both the standard setting (complete-modality training/testing) and the missing-augmented setting (training additionally includes real incomplete samples and nonclinical modality dropout, with complete-only testing); controlled per-modality masking experiments validate effective test-time recovery in 22/24 cancer-modality combinations, and cross-cohort transfer with only two of seven modalities available further confirms generalization under severe input restriction.

works.title: Comments on “SpatialDG: a novel spatial domain identification method for spatially resolved transcriptomics data based on dual-graph neural network”
works.abstract: Dear Editor, In a recent article in Briefings in Bioinformatics, a new spatial domain identification method, namely, SpatialDG, has been proposed [1]. The clustering performance of the model has been reported to be significantly better than existing methods in the literature. However, upon closer inspection of the implementation, we noticed that the clustering performance metrics reported were not accurate, but inflated due to label leakage. We have discussed this concern in the following sections with relevant details. Spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies have advanced rapidly in recent years, enabling researchers to gain a better understanding of tissue biology by providing both gene expression and location information of measured spots on the tissue slice. One principal goal in this field is spatial domain identification, clustering ST spots into continuous areas on biological tissue with similar gene expression patterns. Over 50 methods have been developed for this purpose [2]. SpatialDG [1] is a recently published method that utilizes a dual-graph self-supervised contrastive learning framework to delineate spatial domains in ST data. The method was evaluated on four ST datasets, but the Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) scores were reported for only two of them. The first dataset is the widely used benchmark dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) dataset [3] acquired with the 10x Visium platform. DLPFC dataset includes 12 slices of postmortem human DLPFC tissue from three donors, labeled by white matter and cortical layers 1 to 6. The second dataset contains one slice of human breast cancer tissue, also acquired with 10x Visium [4]. This dataset was annotated by [5] into 20 regions representing areas with different levels of malignancy. When we examined the code of SpatialDG (https://github.com/Izzilab/SpatialDG), we found that while calculating the ARI scores for the two datasets, the model chooses the highest ARI among different epochs. This is clearly seen between lines 131 and 136 in dlpfctest.py and between lines 129 and 134 in HBC_test.py (accessed 11 September 2026). We reproduced the results and calculated the ARI scores for every epoch for the DLPFC dataset (Fig. 1). For each slice, the maximum ARI achieved corresponded to a different epoch. We compared the reported ARI scores with those obtained at the final epoch, which SpatialDG sets to 80 (Table 1). The mean difference between reported and last-epoch ARI scores among 12 slices was 0.15. The median final-epoch ARI across slices was 0.41, and the reported median ARI was 0.60. For the breast cancer dataset, the reported ARI score was 0.66. When we reproduced the results using the authors' chosen setting of 200 epochs for this dataset, the maximum ARI score across epochs was 0.66, obtained on epoch number 126. The final-epoch ARI was 0.58. Comparison of the reported ARI scores with the ARI obtained at the final training epoch for the 12 DLPFC slices. Variability of ARI scores across epochs in SpatialDG for the 12 DLPFC slices. The maximum ARI score and the corresponding epoch are marked for each slice. The authors also claim that SpatialDG maintains a more consistent performance across slices in the DLPFC dataset than other methods. Since the reported ARI scores are chosen among different epochs based on the ground truth, a lower variance is expected because lower-performing epochs are replaced with the best-performing ones. The article reports ARIs of three representative slices 151671, 151673, and 151676 with five different seeds. We calculated the final-epoch ARI scores for these slices across the same seeds (Table 2). The mean final-epoch ARI across five seeds was lower than the reported mean and standard deviations were higher. Comparison of reported ARI (selected based on ground truth) and final-epoch ARI across five random seeds for three DLPFC slices. The values in the final rows are mean and standard deviation across seeds. Our analysis showed that the ARI scores reported in this article are inflated. The reported performance is based on ground-truth-informed model selection and does not constitute a fully label-independent evaluation of the method. The clustering accuracy does not surpass comparison methods when the epoch number is fixed. Selecting the model based on ground truth is impossible with datasets that do not include annotations and scientifically invalid. We suggest that the authors revise the reported clustering results, choose a more appropriate stopping strategy, and document this issue explicitly. This revision is very important and urgent to avoid misleading researchers who may adopt SpatialDG as a top-performing method. SpatialDG’s reported accuracy is inflated due to ground-truth label leakage during evaluation. SpatialDG picked peak accuracy scores across training epochs by checking against known ground-truth labels. Evaluating fairly at the final epoch drops the median score significantly, failing to beat existing methods. Ground-truth selection also reduced performance variance across tissue samples and random seeds. The dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC) dataset used in this paper is available at http://spatial.libd.org/spatialLIBD/.

works.title: AxialTAD: an axial contrast architecture for TAD boundary prediction from Hi-C
works.abstract: Topologically associating domains (TADs) are fundamental units of 3D chromatin organization, and accurate identification of TAD boundaries from Hi-C contact matrices remains an active challenge. Recent deep learning approaches have advanced substantially, but these rely on increasingly large architectures, raising the question of how much of this capacity boundary-centric analysis requires. Here we propose AxialTAD, a compact deep learning model centered on an Axial Contrast Module (ACM) that explicitly encodes directional contrast in contact intensity along the row and column axes of local Hi-C patches, an operator aligned with the geometric signature of TAD boundaries. Evaluated on four human cell lines (GM12878, HeLa-S3, IMR-90, K562) within cell lines and under leave-one-cell-out generalization, AxialTAD performed comparably with a recent convolutional neural network (CNN)+Transformer baseline (deepTAD) while using 76%-80% fewer trainable parameters (113K-137K versus 571K). A parameter-matched conventional CNN achieved similar F1 to AxialTAD in the human 25 kb experiments. When trained and evaluated within each of two mouse datasets, AxialTAD outperformed both this control and deepTAD. Orthogonal validation against CTCF and cohesin ChIP-seq supported the biological plausibility of the predicted boundaries. These results indicate that, within the range of architectures examined, a large architecture is not necessary to reach this level of boundary prediction.

works.title: Inferring causal networks for genomic trios with high-dimensional confounding variables
works.abstract: Causal structure inference under the principle of Mendelian randomization (PMR) enables the study of causal relationships between two molecular phenotypes (e.g. gene expression) by leveraging genetic variants as instrumental variables to impose constraints on edge direction. In practice, inference is often affected by numerous confounding variables, such as other genes, other processes and demographic variables, making it essential to robustly account for confounders. However, existing methods have limited ability to accommodate high-dimensional confounding. Here, we introduce Mendelian randomization for genomic networks (MRGN), a regression-based method under the PMR for inferring causal models in genomic trios from individual-level data while accounting for many confounders. MRGN extends beyond the canonical mediation model to distinguish among multiple causal relationships. By prioritizing conditional independence tests given the genetic variant and confounders, MRGN can detect causal relationships between phenotypes even when their marginal association is weak. Through extensive simulations, we demonstrate improved inference accuracy, robustness, and computational efficiency over existing approaches. We further apply MRGN to data from the Genotype-Tissue Expression Consortium to investigate how genetic variants may regulate gene expression in cis and trans.

works.title: Identifying multi-omics spatial domains via masked autoencoder and diffusion-based latent regularization with SpaMEDM
works.abstract: Spatial multi-omics data provide complementary molecular views of tissue organization. However, their integration remains challenging due to data sparsity, technical noise, and modality-specific distributions. Here, we present Spatial Masked autoEncoder and Diffusion-based Model (SpaMEDM), an end-to-end graph representation learning framework that augments a dual-attention graph-integration backbone with masked reconstruction and diffusion-based latent noise-prediction regularization. In the masked track, randomly masked spot features are recovered by leveraging modality- and graph-specific neighborhood information. In parallel, Gaussian perturbations are applied to modality-specific latent representations at randomly sampled noise levels, and a spatial-graph-informed network is trained to predict the injected noise. This diffusion-based objective is used exclusively during training to encourage robustness to latent perturbations, rather than to perform iterative reverse diffusion or sampling during inference. Furthermore, cosine-based paired-spot directional alignment and adjacency reconstruction encourage compatible cross-modality representations and preservation of the selected graph structure. SpaMEDM flexibly supports purely spatial, dual feature-spatial, and modality-specific feature-pruned spatial graph configurations. Evaluations across diverse spatial multi-omics datasets demonstrate competitive spatial-domain identification performance and produce integrated embeddings that facilitate downstream exploratory analyses.

works.title: MultiMHC: a multiscale learning framework integrating sequence and residue contact topology for peptide–MHC binding prediction
works.abstract: Accurate prediction of peptide-major histocompatibility complex (pMHC) binding is central to understanding antigen presentation and identifying T-cell epitopes in cancer immunotherapy. Although recent methods have achieved notable progress, most approaches rely predominantly on sequence-based features and only partially capture structural determinants of pMHC recognition. In this study, we present MultiMHC, a multiscale deep learning framework that integrates complementary sequential and biologically-informed residue contact topology for pMHC binding prediction. MultiMHC combines a recurrent neural network to model global sequence context with a graph-based representation to encode residue contact patterns derived from known pMHC binding interfaces. Features from these two pathways are subsequently fused to generate binding predictions across peptides of varying lengths. Benchmark evaluations show that MultiMHC achieves performance comparable to existing state-of-the-art methods, with particularly strong performance in ranking-based assessments. Moreover, evaluation on the Tumor Neoantigen Selection Alliance dataset showed that MultiMHC binding scores can enrich experimentally validated T-cell epitopes among top-ranked candidates, supporting its potential utility as an upstream binding-based filtering step in neoantigen discovery workflows. Together, these results highlight the value of incorporating residue interaction patterns and lightweight structural information into pMHC modeling and establish MultiMHC as a robust and extensive framework for antigen presentation analysis.

works.title: Metapath-guided topology and domain knowledge fusion for predicting miRNA–drug–disease triplet resistance and sensitivity associations
works.abstract: Accurately predicting drug resistance and sensitivity is critical for understanding disease treatment mechanisms and improving therapeutic strategies. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) play essential roles in regulating drug response. However, existing computational methods mainly focus on miRNA-drug pairwise associations and overlook the disease-specific context. In this study, we propose a metapath-guided topology and domain knowledge fusion framework (MTDKF) for predicting miRNA-drug-disease triplet resistance (MRDR) and sensitivity (MRDS) associations. Specifically, we construct a triplet heterogeneous graph to model the interactions among miRNAs, drugs, and diseases. A metapath topology view encoder is designed to capture regulatory patterns between nodes. Additionally, a domain knowledge view encoder is introduced to incorporate sequence, structural, and semantic features of biological entities. These two views are further integrated to learn robust and discriminative representation. We manually curate two benchmark datasets from experimentally validated associations. Extensive experimental results demonstrate that MTDKF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches across multiple evaluation metrics. Furthermore, case studies on two breast cancer drugs doxorubicin and tamoxifen demonstrate its potential in discovering novel miRNAs related to drug resistance and sensitivity under disease-specific contexts.

works.title: Nondisruptive 3D profiling of combinations of epigenetic marks in single cells
works.abstract: Advances in single-cell sequencing and spatial omics technologies have enhanced our understanding of diverse cellular identities, compositions, architectures and functions. However, the single-cell three-dimensional (3D) organization of the epigenome is still not well understood, due to an absence of spatial single-cell methods that allow high-resolution, locus-specific detection of combinations of epigenetic marks while maintaining 3D genome organization. Here we develop epigenetic proximity hybridization reaction (Epi-PHR), a nondisruptive image-based single-cell spatial epigenetic profiling technology. Epi-PHR detects combinations of epigenetic marks in situ at hundreds of gene targets within single cells while preserving 3D genome organization. Phased Epi-PHR combined with chromatin tracing reveals unexpected associations between epigenetic mark enrichment and chromatin folding of an imprinted gene cluster at the single-chromatin-copy level for the distinct alleles from different parental origins. We expect Epi-PHR will be broadly applicable in research requiring single-cell spatial epigenetic information, advancing our understanding of the combinatorial epigenetic code and its relationship with chromatin organization. Epi-PHR is an imaging method that maps combinations of epigenetic marks at single genes while preserving 3D genome structure, revealing how chromatin folding and histone modifications are linked among single-chromatin copies.

works.title: Biological foundation models
Making AI approachable, one byte at a time
Corrigendum: Transcriptional programs mediating neuronal toxicity and altered glial–neuronal signaling in a Drosophila knock-in tauopathy model
IsoAPA: a multi-species long-read RNA-seq atlas of isoform-resolved alternative polyadenylation
works.abstract: Genes are often treated as the primary unit of regulation, yet it is transcript isoforms that ultimately execute regulatory output, shaping mRNA stability, localization, and protein production. Alternative polyadenylation (APA) diversifies these outcomes by generating alternative 3' ends. However, existing resources catalogue polyadenylation sites (PASs) primarily as genomic events, obscuring the transcript isoforms on which individual sites are used. Here, we present IsoAPA (https://isoapa.sls.cuhk.edu.hk), a systematically curated database that leverages PacBio and Oxford Nanopore long-read RNA-seq to resolve PASs while preserving their native isoform context. The current release contains over 2.3 million transcript-resolved PAS records from 816 sample groups across 99 species. IsoAPA reveals widespread PAS multiplicity within fixed transcript backbones, with a mean of 2.52 distinct retained PASs per observed transcript in the union across 286 human sample groups. Transcript-level analysis further uncovers PAS usage patterns that are masked by gene-level aggregation, both in PAS diversity and in context-dependent dominant-site usage. By anchoring each terminal site within its assigned transcript model, IsoAPA reframes APA analysis from a gene-centred description of terminal-site usage to an isoform-resolved view of transcript-end regulation.

works.title: UC Irvine’s BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) Brain Procurement Program for the Center for Multiomic Human Brain Cell Atlas Project
works.abstract: SUMMARY High-quality neurotypical postmortem human brain tissue is essential but difficult to obtain for constructing comprehensive human brain cell atlases. Here we describe the establishment of UC Irvine’s Brain Procurement Program, a coordinated initiative to collect and process neurotypical donor brains for multiomic mapping studies within the NIH BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network (BICAN) consortium. Through partnerships with the Orange County Coroner’s Office, the UC Irvine Willed Body Program, UCI Medical Center, and the Children’s Hospital of Orange County, we have developed standardized workflows encompassing donor identification, postmortem brain recovery and processing, region-of-interest dissection, neurotypical donor selection, and data management. Our experience demonstrates the feasibility of a community-based, multi-institutional procurement framework while highlighting challenges in recruiting neurotypical donors and ensuring demographic representation reflective of Southern California. We further identify opportunities to strengthen outreach and donation pathways. This program provides a scalable model for advancing population-reflective, high-quality human brain cell atlas efforts. Highlights Establish a multi-site pipeline for procuring high-quality neurotypical human brains. Demonstrate feasibility of donor collection across childhood to adulthood. Identify barriers and propose strategies to improve broad donor recruitment.

works.title: Uncertainty-aware localization microscopy by variational diffusion
works.abstract: Fast extraction of physically relevant information from images using deep neural networks has led to significant advances in fluorescence microscopy and its application to the study of biological systems. For example, the application of deep networks for kernel density (KD) estimation in single-molecule localization microscopy (SMLM) has accelerated super-resolution imaging of densely labeled structures in the cell. However, localization of fluorescent molecules in dense images is a difficult inverse problem with potentially multiple solutions. To model a probability distribution of solutions to this problem, we propose a generative modeling framework for KD estimation in SMLM based on a conditional variational diffusion model (CVDM). In this framework, CVDM is trained to perform localization tasks on low-resolution measurements by modeling a distribution of high-resolution KD estimates. This approach allows us to probe the structure of the distribution on KD estimates and express uncertainty, which is not currently offered by existing deep models for localization microscopy. We demonstrate that this model permits high-fidelity super-resolution, enables the uncertainty estimation of regressed KD estimates, and has important implications for image restoration in single-molecule and super resolution microscopy.

works.title: MurineCyto-Det: A High-Resolution Murine BALF Cytology Dataset for Leukocyte Segmentation and Detection During Acute Respiratory Viral Infection
works.abstract: Automated analysis of murine bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) cytology is important for preclinical respiratory research, yet progress has been limited by the lack of publicly available, well-annotated mouse BALF image datasets. We present MurineCyto-Det, a high-resolution murine BALF cytology dataset comprising 333 image tiles of size 1024 × 1024 pixels, annotated across five cytological categories with both pixel-level segmentation masks and one-to-one matched bounding boxes. The dataset contains 14,551 annotated cell instances and supports two complementary analysis tasks: morphology-oriented cell segmentation and object-level cell detection. To establish reproducible benchmark baselines, we evaluated representative segmentation and detection models. The results demonstrate the practical utility of MurineCyto-Det while highlighting realistic challenges arising from class imbalance, small object size, irregular cell morphology, and ambiguous debris-like structures. MurineCyto-Det provides a standardized resource for developing, evaluating, and comparing automated methods for murine BALF cytology analysis. The dataset is publicly available at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.17608677.

works.title: Modeling molecular dose-response in toxicology: from omics features to mechanistic insight
Dietary Composition Is Associated With Tissue Metal Concentrations in Two Sympatric Bats
Population-scale integration of spatial omics networks for clinical prediction and biological discovery by SPIN
works.abstract: Spatial omics enables the integration of high-dimensional molecular organization with clinical outcomes, yet incorporating spatial single-cell information into predictive models at the population scale remains challenging. Here, we adapted BSNMani, Bayesian scalar-on-network regression with manifold learning, to integrate subject-specific, spatially informed co-expression networks into clinical prediction. The benchmark comparison showed that the feature selection by BSNMani significantly outperformed Elastic Net and Lasso methods for prediction performance. On SEA-AD MERFISH transcriptomics cohort, BSNMani framework achieved an accuracy of 0.74 for Alzheimer's disease (AD) prediction and revealed four distinct gene-gene co-expression subnetworks with clear biological relevance, such as glutamatergic synapses and neurogenesis. Furthermore, BSNMani achieved a good survival prediction of another breast cancer cohort measured by Imaging Mass Cytometry (IMC) (C-index=0.74) with 2 subnetworks being identified. Furthermore, BSNMani can also use cell-type-specific spatial omics data to enhance the granularity and better pinpoint biological patterns. In summary, BSNMani is a powerful tool that uses high-dimensional spatial omics data for clinical outcome prediction at the population scale across diverse disease settings, revealing deep biological insights while maintaining easy interpretation.

works.title: Multi-platform framework for mapping somatic retrotransposition in human tissues
works.abstract: Mobile element insertions (MEIs) shape the human genome in both germline and somatic tissues. While inherited MEIs are well characterized, identifying somatic MEIs (sMEIs) in non-cancer tissues remains challenging due to their low allelic fraction and repetitive nature. Here, we present an integrative framework for sMEI mapping that leverages modern sequencing technologies and analytical innovations. We first benchmarked sMEI detection methods, demonstrating advantages of long-read and MEI-targeted sequencing for ultra-rare events, and established an effective cross-platform integrative approach using a mixture of well-established cell lines. Haplotype phasing and donor-specific genome assemblies further refined sMEI calls by distinguishing germline and false signals in in silico tumor-normal mixtures. We also developed a source-tracing approach based on sequence variation within MEIs, expanding the catalog of active source elements beyond traditional transduction-based inference. Applying this framework to benchmark donor tissues, we detected rare somatic L1 insertions in all four tissue types examined, revealing structural and source diversity. Our work provides a foundational framework and biological insight into somatic retrotransposition in the human body.

works.title: Leveraging human pangenome for improved somatic variant detection
works.abstract: Somatic variant detection is technically challenging due to low variant allele fractions, the confounding presence of germline variation, and reference bias. Linear references, such as GRCh38, miss sample-specific variation, leading to misalignments and incorrect variant calls. Although telomere-to-telomere donor-specific assemblies (DSAs) accurately represent individual genomes, their application is limited by cost and technical barriers. Alternatively, the graph-based human pangenome provides a scalable framework to improve read alignment and perform genome inference. Here, we benchmarked somatic variant detection using GRCh38, graph-based pangenomes, and pangenome-inferred DSAs with a HapMap mixture dataset and the COLO829 melanoma cell line. Pangenome-guided alignment improves read mapping and somatic variant calling accuracy. Furthermore, personalized pangenomes partially reconstruct donor-specific genomic content, improving accuracy, reducing germline contamination, and enabling detection of events in loci absent or poorly represented in GRCh38. These findings demonstrate that graph-based and personalized pangenomes are effective strategies for enhancing somatic variant detection compared with GRCh38.

works.title: Genome-wide association study meta-analysis identifies susceptibility loci informing Ewing sarcoma etiology and potential mechanisms of risk
works.abstract: Ewing sarcoma (EwS) is a rare, aggressive pediatric malignancy driven by FET::ETS family fusions (EWSR1::FLI1 in >85% of cases) with no established environmental risk factors. We analyzed 2,014 EwS cases and 10,525 cancer-free controls in a two-stage analysis that combined an international genome-wide association study and a case-parent trio study. The combined meta-analysis identified 18 variants at 14 susceptibility loci (9 novel and 5 replicated) with moderate effect sizes (odds ratios ≥ 1.25). Integrative analyses of the EwS loci revealed enrichment of enhancer-like GGAA microsatellites, with evidence for binding of the EWSR1::FLI1 fusion at most loci. EWSR1::ETS knockdown in EwS cell lines resulted in dysregulated genes at susceptibility loci related to skeletal/muscle development, RNA binding/processing, and chromatin regulation. Our findings provide insights into the inherited component of EwS, highlighting a genetic architecture in which common germline variation with moderate effects interacts with somatic EWSR1::FLI1 fusions to promote sarcomagenesis by dysregulating local genes.

works.title: Toward comprehensive maps of somatic mosaic mutations
works.abstract: The Somatic Mosaicism across Human Tissues Network has established complementary benchmarks for somatic mutation detection, extended mutation analysis into underexplored genomic regions, and highlighted chromatin states as potential records of cellular history. These studies show that detection performance depends on reference representation, benchmark quality, and experimental design, requiring careful calibration when integrating technologies.

works.title: Tracing the evolutionary history of human neocortical regulation
works.abstract: Anderson et al. extend comparative brain multi-omics across nine mammals and zebrafish, combining sequence conservation and predicted enhancer-gene relationships with functional assays to examine how regulatory elements with different evolutionary histories contribute to brain function and disease risk.

works.title: Q&A with Dr. Philip Awadalla
works.abstract: Editor-in-Chief Laura Zahn asked Dr. Philip Awadalla from the University of Oxford to tell us about his research and his recent Cell Genomics paper, "Pre-diagnosis plasma cell-free DNA reveals early signatures of prostate and breast cancer risk up to eight years prior to clinical detection."

works.title: Leveraging evolutionary conservation to define cell identity
works.abstract: Wölbert et al. established a strategy that integrated conserved cell-type-specificity with conservation of transcriptional levels to identify robust signature genes. By leveraging evolutionary conservation as an additional dimension of cell identity, this strategy would facilitate cell identity annotation across species, particularly in non-model organisms and rare cell populations.

works.title: Amyloid and tau display distinct patterns across Alzheimer’s in anterior caudate
Tissue-to-bytes: A digital twin for single-cell omics data integration across BRAIN Initiative Cell Atlas Network
Recurrent de novo ABI2 p.Tyr491Cys variants define a neurodevelopmental syndrome with corpus callosum hypoplasia and white matter abnormalities
works.journal: The American Journal of Human Genetics
works.abstract: ABI2 (MIM: 606442) encodes a cytoskeletal adaptor protein that regulates Rac-WAVE signaling and actin remodeling through interactions with ABL-family kinases and the WAVE regulatory complex. These pathways are essential for neurite extension, axon guidance, and synapse formation.1 Experimental studies support a role for ABI2 in corticogenesis, with Abi2 deficiency causing impaired neuronal migration, abnormal dendritic spine morphology, and corpus callosum abnormalities in mice.2 However, evidence linking ABI2 to human disease remains limited, with only two reported de novo missense variants in individuals with autism spectrum disorder, with no additional clinical information available, precluding establishment of gene-disease association.

works.title: Scaling haplospecific antisense oligonucleotides from N-of-1 to broad use in genetic disease populations by diplotyping
works.journal: The American Journal of Human Genetics

works.title: Population-scale genomics reveals divergent pathogenicity of variant classes across paralogous collagen IV genes
works.journal: The American Journal of Human Genetics
works.abstract: Monoallelic pathogenic or likely pathogenic variants in COL4A3 and COL4A4 occur in approximately 1 in 106 individuals, yet whether these paralogous genes confer equivalent pathogenicity for the same variant classes has not been tested at population scale. Using whole-genome sequencing data from the UK Biobank (UKB; n ≈ 500,000), with replication in the All of Us Research Program (n ≈ 414,000), we performed per-variant association testing, gene-based collapsing analyses, and phenome-wide association studies (PheWASs) across hematuria, proteinuria, and chronic kidney disease. We identified 64 COL4A3 and 92 COL4A4 rare variants significantly associated with hematuria or proteinuria, providing population-level quantitative evidence that may support variant interpretation. Glycine substitutions within collagenous domains conferred similar risks in both genes. In contrast, truncating and non-collagenous domain (NC1) missense variants were strongly associated with hematuria and proteinuria in COL4A4 heterozygotes but showed substantially attenuated or absent associations in COL4A3 heterozygotes despite comparable allele frequencies and predicted pathogenicity scores. These findings were independently replicated in All of Us. Genome-wide association analysis identified the COL4A3 and COL4A4 locus as the dominant genetic determinant of hematuria, attributable to the aggregate effects of rare coding variants with no evidence of independent common variant or trans-acting modifier effects. These findings demonstrate marked gene-specific differences in association with hematuria and proteinuria for truncating and NC1 variants between COL4A3 and COL4A4, challenging assumptions of equivalent pathogenicity across paralogous collagen IV genes. Gene identity, not variant class alone, should inform risk stratification, variant interpretation, and genetic counseling in collagen IV heterozygotes.

works.title: Deep CRISPR mutagenesis predicts cancer risk in Li-Fraumeni syndrome
works.journal: The American Journal of Human Genetics
works.abstract: TP53 encodes for the transcription factor TP53, which controls the expression of genes involved in cell cycle, apoptosis, senescence, stem cell differentiation, metabolism, and DNA repair.1 ∼50% of all human cancers harbor somatic TP53 mutations, while germline or postzygotic somatic mosaic TP53 pathogenic variants cause Li-Fraumeni syndrome (LFS [MIM: 151623]), a cancer predisposition syndrome associated with a lifelong increased risk for various solid tumors as well as hematologic neoplasms.2 A cancer surveillance protocol has been shown to statistically significantly improve long-term survival in individuals with LFS.

works.title: This month in The Journal

works.title: DBAASP V4: condition-resolved bioactivity and chemical structures for data-driven peptide and peptidomimetic discovery
works.abstract: The current peptide renaissance-driven by metagenomic and proteomic mining, molecular de-extinction, protein language models, and generative or evolutionary design-is producing millions of candidates, but useful machine learning depends on experimentally anchored, context-rich labels. The Database of Antimicrobial Activity and Structure of Peptides (DBAASP) is a manually curated resource linking peptides and peptidomimetics to quantitative antimicrobial, antibiofilm, anticancer, hemolytic, and mammalian-cell cytotoxicity measurements and their experimental conditions. DBAASP v4 contains >25 000 entries and extends the resource from a sequence-centered database to a structure-aware repository. Major additions include systematic SMILES representations, enhanced annotation of intrachain bonds and ring architectures, dedicated antibiofilm, and synergy records, PubChem links, >9200 molecular-dynamics trajectories, and new prediction services. The condition-resolved data support supervised learning, strain-, and target-specific models, model calibration, and surrogate fitness functions for genetic algorithms. SMILES representations further enable modeling of noncanonical peptides and peptidomimetics that cannot be adequately described by sequence alone. DBAASP therefore complements large peptide catalogues by providing the experimentally curated activity and structure layers, needed to convert sequence information into testable predictions, design, and optimization of biologically active compounds. DBAASP v4 is freely available at https://dbaasp.org.

works.title: MultiTargetDB: a comprehensive database of multitarget ligands for polypharmacology research and drug discovery
works.abstract: Multitarget drug discovery has gained considerable traction in recent years, particularly for the treatment of complex diseases. Despite the growing demand for dedicated, well-curated resources to advance polypharmacology research and rational multitarget drug discovery, such resources remain severely limited. Here, we present MultiTargetDB, a database of multitarget ligands integrated with comprehensive biological annotations and measurement-level provenance. At the small molecule level, MultiTargetDB integrates chemical structures (including molecular scaffolds), their drug development stages, and target information, whereas at the target level, MultiTargetDB incorporates protein domains and families, functional associations, and pathway-disease annotations.
