In this Application Note, we provide a generalized implementation of this approach, which we call EGTool. EGTool compares genomes to each other (multigenome topology) or loci to each other across genomes (multilocus topology), accepts arbitrary positional and orthology inputs, works in base-pair or index coordinates, projects new genomes onto an existing embedding without refitting, and recovers the features that characterize any chosen region of the projection via inverse transform. A 510-genome, 1,274 locus example is included to illustrate these functionalities and can be run on a laptop within 30 minutes. Availability and Implementation EGTool is implemented in Python (≥3.8) with dependencies on NumPy, pandas, umap-learn, matplotlib, NetworkX, and scikit-learn. It is installable via pip after cloning the repository. The optional ancestral linkage group detection step (egtool alg) requires R. A Perl script is provided for converting genome annotation files to the input .chrom format. Source code, example data, and tutorials are available at: https://bitbucket.org/viemet/egtool/src/main/

works.title: A multiscale framework for hypothesis generation from sex-stratified X-linked gene networks
works.abstract: Abstract Stratified gene co-expression network analyses compare molecular organisation across biological groups; however, their interpretation is challenged by cohort imbalance, network instability, correlation-method dependence, and multiplicity. These issues are particularly relevant when comparing network structures across heterogeneous cohorts, where apparent patterns may not be reproducible. This study presents a reproducible framework for stratified gene co-expression network analysis. It integrates cohort balancing, bootstrap-stabilised consensus networks, topology-based statistics, paired label permutations, multiplicity control, and correlation-method benchmarking. Its design distinguishes robust statistical evidence from exploratory signals and their biological interpretation. The framework is illustrated through a multi-cancer case study of sex-associated co-expression network organisation among X-linked genes classified as escape, inactive, or variably escaping from X-chromosome inactivation. The analysis included 15 TCGA cancer cohorts and 90 sex-stratified networks, enabling systematic comparison of network structure across cancer types and X-inactivation gene classes. Across 315 paired permutation tests, none survived Benjamini–Hochberg correction, providing no multiplicity-adjusted evidence. Nevertheless, exploratory graphlet profiles revealed cancer- and gene-class-specific patterns of network organisation, highlighting candidate structures for independent replication. The case study illustrates how the framework can distinguish nominal or visually compelling differences from multiplicity-adjusted evidence while preserving informative exploratory patterns for structured hypothesis generation.

works.title: PlasmidNL: an interactive R/Shiny application for comparative plasmid epidemiology and surveillance-based data exploration
works.abstract: Abstract Summary Plasmids are key drivers of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) dissemination via horizontal gene transfer, yet their epidemiological analysis remains challenging due to fragmented analytical workflows and limited integration of genomic and contextual metadata. We present PlasmidNL, an interactive R/Shiny-based application for comparative plasmid epidemiology. PlasmidNL integrates precomputed plasmid clustering results with plasmid typing outputs (PlasmidFinder and MOB-suite), antimicrobial resistance gene profiles, and epidemiological metadata within a unified analytical environment. The platform enables interactive exploration of plasmid population structure, distribution of resistance determinants, and associated metadata across large datasets. A key feature is the ability to contextualize user-provided datasets against a curated Dutch national surveillance collection comprising 4,596 plasmids from carbapenemase-producing organisms collected between 2012 and 2022. We additionally provide a reproducible preprocessing pipeline that generates standardized input files compatible with the application. PlasmidNL is freely available as both a web-based service and a locally deployable application. Availability and implementation PlasmidNL is implemented in R using the Shiny framework and is accessible online at https://apps.rivm.nl/bsr-ids-ienv/plasmidnl/. Source code is available at https://github.com/gidjes/PlasmidNL under an MIT license.

works.title: Benchmarking High-Dimensional Mediation Methods in Epigenome-Wide Studies
works.abstract: Abstract Motivation High-dimensional mediation analysis is increasingly used in omics studies to investigate molecular mediators of exposure–outcome relationships. In epigenome-wide studies, the number of CpG sites often greatly exceeds the sample size, while strong correlations among sites challenge reliable mediator selection and effect estimation. We systematically benchmarked four high-dimensional mediation methods—HIMA, HIMA2, HDMA, and a strategy combining high-dimensional mediation testing with stepwise regression (HDMTS)—under simulation settings varying signal strength, correlation structure, and the mediator-to-sample ratio (p/N). Results HIMA and HDMA consistently provided stringent false discovery proportion (FDP) control, whereas HIMA2 generally controlled FDP, with some inflation observed when the p/N ratio was high and mediator errors were independent. HDMTS showed greater sensitivity but exhibited reduced FDP control, particularly when mediator–outcome associations were weak and residual correlations among mediators were strong. Application to epigenome-wide DNA methylation data further demonstrated differences in mediator selection across methods and identified biologically plausible candidate mediators. Overall, our results highlight important trade-offs among false discovery control, sensitivity, and estimation accuracy and provide practical guidance for selecting high-dimensional mediation methods in epigenome-wide studies. Availability and implementation The HDMTS code is available at https://github.com/WanYuLin/HDMTS, and the simulation code is available at https://github.com/WanYuLin/HDMTS/tree/main/Simulations.

works.title: The lipid raft marker flotillin FloA drives relocalization of the plasma membrane H+-ATPase PmaA as a protective response to calcium stress
works.abstract: Biological membranes are laterally heterogeneous and contain specialized microdomains called lipid rafts. Lipid rafts serve as organizational platforms that cluster signaling molecules or modulate membrane protein conformation through their unique lipid environment. There are specific lipid raft marker proteins whose functions remain obscure. One of these proteins is flotillin which has been linked to endocytosis. Here, we investigated the regulation and function of FloA, the sole flotillin homolog in the model fungus Aspergillus nidulans . FloA expression is specifically upregulated in response to calcium stress, which is a regulatory pattern also conserved in Aspergillus fumigatus . BioID proximity labeling revealed that A. nidulans FloA physically interacts with proteins in the endocytic pathway as well as another lipid raft marker, the plasma membrane H + -ATPase PmaA. Under calcium stress, PmaA undergoes internalization from the cytoplasmic membrane. However, when floA is deleted, PmaA internalization is prevented, resulting in cell death. This phenotype of the Δ floA strain could be mimicked by treating the cells with an endocytosis inhibitor during calcium stress. Together, we demonstrate that FloA is essential for the internalization of PmaA during calcium stress, a process that prevents intracellular calcium overload and promotes cell viability. Our results also provide further evidence for flotillin-assisted endocytosis.

works.title: Nicotinic receptor in dopamine neurons mediates learned odor choice
works.abstract: Nicotinic acetylcholine signaling modulates dopaminergic output in mammalian midbrain circuits and can thereby influence decision-making. In Drosophila, dopamine neurons (DANs) in the protocerebral anterior medial (PAM) cluster convey sugar reward signals and promote approach toward a rewarded odor after associative learning. Although nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) have been implicated in regulating PAM DAN excitability and transmitter release, how this modulation supports specific cognitive operations during learning and memory remains unclear. Here, we tested the role of nAChRs in PAM DANs in odor-sugar associative learning and memory. Among nine nAChR genes examined, loss of the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor α1 subunit (Dα1) in PAM neurons impaired appetitive memory. Consistent with this requirement, Dα1 was detected in these DANs at both the transcript and protein levels, with Dα1 puncta observed in PAM axon-terminal and putative dendritic regions. Importantly, live imaging showed that Dα1 knockdown in PAM DANs attenuated odor-evoked synaptic Ca2+ signals, whereas sugar-evoked Ca2+ responses were largely preserved. Behaviorally, Dα1 knockdown in PAM DANs reduced performance in a two-odor forced-choice discrimination task, whereas no performance deficit was detected across the single-odor pursuit conditions or innate odor choice. Together, these results identify a nicotinic mechanism in PAM DANs that supports odor-evoked synaptic activity and contributes to learned odor-choice performance when competing odor cues are present.

works.title: rustybam : a composable toolkit for alignment analysis and visualization with SafFire
works.abstract: SUMMARY: We present rustybam, a Rust-based command-line toolkit for CIGAR-aware manipulation of PAF and BAM alignments, and SafFire, a browser-based tool for interactive genome comparison visualization with annotation overlays. rustybam's composable subcommands provide overlap resolution, coordinate liftover, alignment splitting at structural variants, scaffolding, and identity statistics. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Both tools are open source under the MIT license. rustybam is available via Bioconda (https://anaconda.org/bioconda/rustybam), crates.io, and GitHub (https://github.com/vollgerlab/rustybam). SafFire is hosted at https://vollgerlab.com/SafFire/ with source code at https://github.com/vollgerlab/SafFire. Archived versions are available on Zenodo: rustybam (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.4654875) and SafFire (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5765964).

works.title: Thyra: bridging mass spectrometry imaging and SpatialData for unified multimodal analysis
Cellular-resolution three-photon ultra-deep imaging (TrUDI) of neuronal population activity at 2-mm depth in the mammalian brain
Aptamer-mediated multivalent endogenous ADAR1 recruitment for highly efficient RNA editing
works.abstract: Adenosine-to-inosine RNA editing mediated by endogenous ADAR enzymes represents a promising therapeutic strategy because it can correct mutations at the transcript level without inducing permanent changes to the genome. However, existing systems face challenges, particularly the limited editing efficiency, which limits their practical applications. Here we introduce MARRS (multivalent ADAR1-recruiting RNA editing system)—an efficient and specific RNA editing platform that leverages engineered multivalent RNA aptamers to robustly recruit endogenous ADAR1 enzymes. By optimizing aptamers targeting the Zα domain of ADAR1 p150 and embedding them in a circular RNA scaffold, MARRS enables near-complete adenosine-to-inosine editing of RNA targets in cultured cells and mouse models, achieving efficiencies up to 100% in vitro and 84% in vivo. MARRS also exhibits remarkable versatility across a range of transcript targets while maintaining high specificity with minimal off-target effects. Operating without the need for exogenous enzymes, the MARRS system offers a safe, efficient and programmable platform. The multivalent ADAR1-recruiting RNA editing system (MARRS) is an RNA editing platform that efficiently recruits endogenous ADAR1 to achieve precise adenosine-to-inosine editing. MARRS enables up to 100% editing in vitro and 84% in vivo with high specificity across diverse RNA targets.

works.title: CopilotJ: a conversational multi-agent system for intelligent and efficient bioimage analysis
Author Correction: Prediction of protein subcellular localization in single cells
Chemogenomic profiling of diverse Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains using the novel CRISPR-Cas9 markerless barcoded library BarMix
works.abstract: Natural populations are rich reservoirs of genetic variation, and incorporating this diversity into functional genomic screens can reveal the genetic and phylogenetic determinants underlying trait differences. Genetic barcoding is a powerful tool for yeast functional genomics, enabling scalable fitness profiling and high-throughput gene-trait interaction mapping. Nevertheless, few barcoded libraries capture the natural diversity of Saccharomyces cerevisiae . Here, we introduce BarMix, a novel barcoded library of diverse S. cerevisiae strains designed and validated for high-throughput fitness profiling. Using CRISPR-Cas9, we integrate distinct markerless genetic barcodes into the genomes of 262 strains representing multiple phylogenetic clades of wild, domesticated, and admixed origins. To evaluate its utility for genotype–phenotype mapping, we quantitatively profile the pooled library by barcode-sequencing against 33 small-molecule compounds with diverse bioactivities and identify 281 chemogenomic interactions through genome-wide association analysis. Chemical fitness signatures differ between domesticated and wild clades, particularly under stresses affecting ergosterol biosynthesis, DNA alkylation, microtubule depolymerisation, TORC1 inactivation, and membrane permeability. We validate seven associated alleles through allele-swap experiments, including variants in genes that modulate multidrug export (Yrr1), tRNA-specificity (ArgRS), and small-molecule methylation (Crg1). Several alleles display variable penetrance across strains, suggesting a complex genetic basis for trait variation. Importantly, including admixture into the genome-wide association design enhances variant detection in S. cerevisiae . These results establish BarMix as a powerful platform for genotype–phenotype discovery with diverse applications in functional genomics and biotechnology, and highlight the value of incorporating natural variation into model-systems biology.

works.title: On real-time calibrated prediction for complex model-based decision support in pandemics: Part 1
works.abstract: Infectious disease models are used to predict the spread and impact of outbreaks of a disease. Like other complex models, they have parameters that need to be calibrated, and structural discrepancies from the reality that they simulate that should be accounted for in calibration and prediction. Whilst Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) techniques have been applied to infectious disease models before, they were not routinely used to inform policymakers in the UK during the COVID-19 pandemic. In this paper, we will argue that during a fast moving pandemic, models and policy are changing on timescales that make traditional UQ methods impractical, if not impossible to implement. We present an alternative formulation to the calibration problem that embeds model discrepancy within the structure of the model, and appropriately assimilates data within the simulation. We then show how UQ can be used to calibrate the model in real-time to produce disease trajectories accounting for parameter uncertainty and model discrepancy. We apply these ideas to an age-structured COVID-19 model for England and demonstrate the types of information it could have produced to feed into policy support prior to the lockdown of March 2020.

works.title: Individualised electrophysiological neural field models for the assessment of thalamocortical function in disorders of consciousness: A multicentre study
works.abstract: Understanding the neural mechanisms underlying disorders of consciousness (DoC) remains a major challenge, particularly in distinguishing limited awareness in minimally conscious state (MCS) and complete unawareness in unresponsive wakefulness syndrome, also coined vegetative state (UWS/VS). In this multicentre study, we fitted a biophysically informed corticothalamic neural field model to high-density EEG data from two large independent datasets, comprising 203 UWS patients, 270 MCS patients and 74 healthy controls. We then used the fitted parameters to simulate EEG time series on a per-subject basis and compared empirical and simulated complexity metrics. The model reliably captured the spectral features across different states of consciousness and revealed reduced corticothalamic integrity in DoC patients that was more pronounced in UWS than in MCS, supporting the mesocircuit hypothesis. Furthermore, the simulated EEG reproduced the complexity patterns of the empirical recordings, with permutation entropy emerging as a sensitive marker capable of distinguishing between MCS and UWS for both real and simulated time series.

works.title: The evolutionary advantage of replacers in the Moran process
works.abstract: Evolution occurs in populations of reproducing individuals. In stochastic descriptions of evolutionary dynamics, such as the Moran process, individuals are chosen randomly for birth and for death. If the same type is chosen for both steps, then the reproductive event is wasted, because the composition of the population remains unchanged. Here we introduce a new phenotype, which we call a replacer. Replacers are efficient competitors. When a replacer is chosen for reproduction, the offspring will always replace an individual of another type (if available). We determine the selective advantage of replacers in well-mixed populations and on one-dimensional lattices. We find that being a replacer substantially boosts the fixation probability of neutral and deleterious mutants. In particular, fixation probability of a single neutral replacer who invades a well-mixed population of size N is of the order of 1/N rather than the standard 1/N. Even more importantly, replacers are much better protected against invasions once they have reached fixation. Therefore, replacers dominate the mutation selection equilibrium even if the phenotype of being a replacer comes at a substantial cost: curiously, for large population sizes and small mutation rates, the relative reproductive rate of a successful replacer can be as low as 1/e.

works.title: Modeling reaction–diffusion processes in simplified to complex astroglial branchlet geometries using different simulation tools
works.abstract: Computational modeling of spatial biochemical processes in neuroscience is increasingly important as advances in experimental and imaging techniques provide detailed insights into cellular organization. Reaction-diffusion models are commonly used to study the diffusion and interactions of ions and molecules within neuronal cells, and multiple open-access simulation platforms have been developed to support such analysis. However, a comprehensive analysis of commonly used simulation tools, including MCell, STEPS, NeuroRD, and NEURON, remains lacking, particularly for realistic glial cell geometries, as these tools were originally developed for neurons. Here, we present a systematic analysis of these four simulation environments by implementing equivalent calcium diffusion and calcium-calmodulin reaction-diffusion models across a range of spatial domains. These include simplified geometries (cylinders and rectangular cuboids) as well as biologically realistic astroglial morphologies derived from electron microscopy data, including mouse Bergmann glia and mouse and human cortical astrocytes. Using matched kinetic parameters and diffusion constants, we examine simulation outputs and morphological variations across platforms under comparable conditions. We find that all tools produce overall consistent results for the systems considered, indicating that each can reliably capture diffusion and reaction-diffusion dynamics in simplified and complex geometries. At the same time, we show that the structural heterogeneity of branchlets from human astrocytes and mouse Bergmann glia gives rise to distinct calcium signaling, demonstrating that fine-scale morphology critically shapes astroglial dynamics and must be accurately captured by simulation frameworks. In addition, notable differences emerge in geometry representation, implementation strategies, computational aspects, and usability of the tools. By highlighting key trade-offs between geometric fidelity, flexibility, and computational cost in modeling intracellular biochemical processes, these findings provide practical guidance for selecting appropriate simulation tools. More broadly, our results support the use of reaction-diffusion modeling in morphologically realistic astrocytic environments and contribute to enabling mechanistic studies of localized signaling events at synaptic and perisynaptic sites.

works.title: Early vs late fusion of qMIDS with machine learning based classifiers for oral cancer diagnosis from gene expression data
works.abstract: Different fusion architectures of the quantitative Malignancy Index Diagnostic System (qMIDS) method with machine learning classifiers for oral cancer diagnosis from gene expression data are investigated. The proposed fusion architectures are tested on geographically and ethnically diverse datasets and the evaluation results showed performance improvements with late fusion, which significantly outperformed early fusion in more matched model configurations than the reverse in every cohort, although at the best-performing configuration the two architectures were statistically indistinguishable in most cohorts. Inter-dataset analysis showed robustness of the proposed architectures when the training/test samples are from different populations.

works.title: Preference-guided CT projection correction for surface-based feather morphometrics
works.abstract: Traditional imaging pipelines often optimize for human-readable images and generic quality metrics, but algorithm-facing morphometric workflows require preservation of the information used by downstream measurement. Acquisitions that appear overexposed or visually nonstandard may therefore be appropriate when they expose subtle structures to an analysis algorithm. We developed a task-aligned projection-correction framework for reducing morphology-relevant CT motion artifacts without relying on human visual interpretability as the final quality standard. Using CT-based feather morphometry as a motivating example, we treated a previously published feather-growth computer-vision workflow as the downstream task to be protected during correction. A residual denoising autoencoder defined a bounded projection-correction space, and an expert human-preference ranker scored candidate residual corrections for preservation of task-relevant morphology. In a five-scene synthetic proof-of-concept benchmark comprising four development seeds and one fully held-out seed, rank-weighted evolution-strategy updates optimized latent corrections under projection-preservation, latent-bound, and angular-smoothing constraints. The development-inclusive five-scene summary showed 67.9% lower reconstruction RMSE and 72.0% lower density-map RMSE than motion-corrupted data, with the fully held-out seed showing the same direction and similar magnitude of improvement. Preference-guided correction also outperformed a feed-forward residual-autoencoder baseline (reconstruction RMSE 0.00260 ± 0.00013; density-map RMSE 0.0500 ± 0.0021), whereas TomoPy joint reprojection alignment changed the principal morphology-error endpoints by approximately 1% or less under the local non-rigid feather-motion benchmark. Clean-data controls produced only small perturbations when no motion correction was needed. In two illustrative real-data case studies, the same framework reduced visible feather ghosting and improved downstream crest-density mapping and agreement with manual reference masks when inserted upstream of the published morphometric workflow. These results support task-aligned projection correction as a route toward CT imaging workflows optimized for downstream biological measurement rather than generic visual image quality alone. The study provides proof-of-concept evidence that expert preference signals can guide bounded projection-domain correction for surface-based biological morphometrics.

works.title: Cell-type-specific explainable spatial features extracted from digitized H&E slides explain gene expression variability beyond cell-type composition
works.abstract: Cell-type composition and tissue architecture jointly influence gene expression patterns. Although single-cell and spatial transcriptomic technologies can characterize both factors, their cost limits widespread use. Bulk RNA deconvolution estimates cell-type composition but lacks spatial context. In contrast, routine H&E whole-slide images provide a scalable source of explainable cell-type-specific spatial features describing tissue architecture. However, the extent to which the spatial features explain gene expression variability beyond cell-type composition remains largely unknown, and in this study, we aim to address this gap. The study leveraged a dataset of 471 normal prostate tissue samples with bulk RNA gene expression and paired WSIs. The WSIs are processed for nuclei segmentation and cell-type classification to extract cell-type-specific proportions ( n = 7) and spatial features ( n = 38) reflective of local neighborhood and tissue architecture. We model the gene expression as a function of cell-type-specific features to assess their contribution to gene expression variability, and evaluate the incremental explanatory effect of spatial features over the cell type compositions. Likelihood ratio testing comparing the full model (cell-type-specific spatial and proportion features, with the proportions-only model serving as the null model) to the proportions-only model identified 2330 of 24,075 genes with significantly improved model fit after adjustment for multiple testing (FDR-adjusted p-value < 0.05). Among significant genes, the full model shows the highest ability to explain gene expression variability (median adjusted \(\:{R}^{2}\) = 0.195 [IQR 0.122, 0.289]), compared to the spatial features only model (0.176 [0.109, 0.263]), and the proportions only model (0.068 [0.031, 0.128]). Finally, gene expression was modelled using XGBoost with cell-type-specific features. Feature importance analysis identified nine distinct, biologically relevant gene clusters and confirmed the regression-based results, with cell-type-specific spatial features contributing substantially to gene expression variability beyond cell-type composition. These findings demonstrate that explainable cell-type-specific spatial features derived from routine H&E slides capture transcriptionally relevant tissue architecture that is not reflected by cell-type composition alone. Such features provide a scalable and cost-effective approach for explaining gene expression variability in bulk tissue samples.

works.title: WinPopLDdecay: a hardware-adaptive and reproducible reimplementation of PopLDdecay with a graphical interface
MALER: a web server to build, evaluate, and apply machine learning models for numerical biomedical data analysis
works.abstract: ABSTRACT The explosive growth of numerical biomedical data poses a challenge in uncovering meaningful insights within from vast omics and clinical data. In recent years, machine learning has emerged as a powerful tool for processing and dissecting numerical biomedical data, making it a popular choice for addressing analytical challenges in biomedical research. Nevertheless, the intricate algorithms and complex optimization processes of machine learning model frameworks have deterred numerous non-machine learning experts. To address the need for comprehensive signatures exploration in biomedical field, we have developed Maler ( http://www.inbirg.com/maler/home ), a platform designed to facilitate the effortless and efficient application of machine learning models to high-dimensional biomedical data for bioscientists. Maler primarily offers four machine learning modes and a variety of machine learning algorithms to accommodate diverse analysis requirements. Simultaneously, it employs multiple feature selection methods to acquire relevant features and selects the optimal combinations of features based on machine learning models to achieve the best predictive outcomes. Maler is expected to provide a user-friendly and efficient platform for marker discovery, catering to the needs of biologists and clinical experts.

works.title: Sequencing meets repetition coding: quadratic substitution error suppression through homotrimer redundancy
works.abstract: Abstract In cryptography, triple modular redundancy (TMR) is a fault-tolerant error correction technique in which a single data bit is copied and transmitted three times (e.g., 0 is encoded as 000)1. This technique has widely been used to protect data integrity in noisy communication channels across fields, such as aerospace systems2, satellite communications3, and safety-critical embedded devices4. In sequencing, the same principle of redundancy has been echoed and applied in homotrimer unique molecular identifier (UMI) demultiplexing to counteract synthesis errors and then remove PCR artefacts, ensuring accurate molecular quantification5. A homotrimer UMI consists of building blocks in which each nucleotide is tripled (e.g., A turns to AAA). Despite this being a simple modification, it has a positive impact on sequencing accuracy: most synthesis errors are effectively corrected through majority voting. While the empirical benefit of this approach is well established, its theoretical basis has not been formally articulated. Here, we present an interpretation grounded in information theory, specifically through the lens of repetition coding and error correction mechanisms.

works.title: CAN-IMMUNE: a computational platform to facilitate cancer-specific neoantigen identification
Predicting Translation Readthrough from Sequence Features in Saccharomyces cerevisiae
works.abstract: Understanding translation readthrough in eukaryotes is fundamental for elucidating transcript evolution, deciphering gene expression codes, and advancing biotechnological applications.In this study, we present the first comprehensive analysis of the transcript features that determine readthrough efficiency in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.To predict readthrough efficiency, we engineered a set of novel sequence-derived features and trained multiple machine-learning models, achieving a mean Spearman correlation of 0.535 between predicted and experimentally measured values, substantially improving predictive performance compared with models based solely on previously established features.Feature importance analysis identified codon usage-related features, particularly the tRNA Adaptation Index (tAI), Codon Adaptation Index (CAI), and similar-to-stop codon counts, as the strongest contributors to model performance.Lower tAI values near the stop codon were strongly associated with increased readthrough, indicating that reduced translational efficiency promotes termination errors.In contrast, higher similar-to-stop codon counts were positively associated with readthrough, supporting the hypothesis that local tRNA competition increases the likelihood of stop codon misreading.Together, these findings highlight the central role of codon usage and local sequence context in modulating translation termination fidelity.This work provides a predictive framework for readthrough that can facilitate future studies aimed at understanding and modulating translation termination.

works.title: Population-scale single-nucleus multi-omic profiling of skeletal muscle reveals extensive context-specific genetic regulation
Tracing cell fate in space and time with SPACE-seq
Longitudinal single-cell RNA sequencing of a neuroendocrine transdifferentiation model reveals transcriptional reprogramming in treatment-induced neuroendocrine prostate cancer
works.abstract: Neuroendocrine prostate cancer (NEPC), a lethal outcome of androgen deprivation, arises through neuroendocrine transdifferentiation (NEtD) of prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD), yet its initiating drivers and their temporal order remain only partially defined. Clinical single-cell studies primarily capture established PRAD or NEPC at single timepoints, so they cannot directly resolve transitional states or the order and direction of transdifferentiation. We generated longitudinal single-cell RNA sequencing of the LTL331 patient-derived xenograft across eight timepoints spanning pre-castration PRAD to relapsed NEPC (51,726 cells) with matched whole-exome sequencing, integrating inferred single-cell copy-number profiles, trajectory inference, regulon and transcription-factor-activity analysis, and chromatin-accessibility data from a clinical metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer atlas. Lineage states were tested for replication in two clinical single-cell cohorts by embedding-free, label-level comparison. NEtD proceeded by transcriptional reprogramming of a single clone, not clonal outgrowth: PRAD and NEPC shared copy-number architecture and a truncal TMPRSS2 :: ERG rearrangement, with the androgen receptor ( AR ) locus copy-number stable despite loss of AR transcription. Every PRAD-to-NEPC path funneled through one transient, obligate mesenchymal gateway (~0.25% of cells, peaking 12–16 weeks post-castration) that re-engaged the early neural-crest program in developmental order: the neural-plate-border regulator MSX1 peaked with the EMT-delamination program, and border specifier PAX7 persisted into the early neuroendocrine state. From this gateway the lineage bifurcated with strong bias toward a tuft-negative ASCL1− fate (≈0.94 versus ≈0.06; paired p = 4.8 × 10 −23 ; POU2F3 < 1%), diverging from the canonical ASCL1 / PHOX2B route and the ASCL1 -versus-tuft split of other NEPC models. MSX1 is a candidate priming regulator, supported by transcription-factor-activity analysis and AR−/NE+-specific footprints in patient NEPC chromatin. Adenocarcinoma and ASCL1 + neuroendocrine programs replicated in patient cohorts (AUROC 0.82–0.83), and neuroendocrine identity tracked the clinical neuroendocrine-differentiation (odds ratios 134.6 and 31.4). In the LTL331 patient-derived model, NEtD is a directional, stepwise transition rather than a stochastic loss of identity. To our knowledge, this study provides the first time-resolved evidence that prostate NEtD re-engages the early neural-crest program in developmental order before committing to a predominantly ASCL1− fate. The obligate gateway is a potential opportunity for intervention, and its regulators are candidate targets for intercepting NEtD. Not applicable.

works.title: Fast probabilistic whitening transformation for ultra-high dimensional genetic data
works.abstract: Statistical methods often make assumptions about independence between the samples or features of a dataset, yet correlation structure is ubiquitous in real data. In statistical genetics, correlation between regression summary statistics due to linkage disequilibrium (LD) between nearby variants complicates downstream analysis. Many methods use LD reference panels to account for this correlation. Whitening transformations comprise a family of methods to remove correlation structure, and are used implicitly by many common models. Here we propose a probabilistic model for data whitening, and propose parameter estimates and efficient algorithms to improve statistical and computational performance. In an application to impute z-statistics from unobserved genetic variants from a genome-wide association study of schizophrenia, the probabilistic whitening transformation, had the lowest mean square error while being up to an order of magnitude faster than other methods. Using this approach, we also identify tandem repeats that explain genetic regulatory signals for disease-relevant genes. Analyses are implemented in our novel open source R packages decorrelate and imputez .

works.title: Starlng: STability Analysis of coReguLated "Nests" of Genes
works.abstract: MOTIVATION: Single-cell assays (both single and multi-omics) represent the state-of-the-art for detailed characterisation of cell phenotypes, a task frequently initialised with the identification of groups of genes linked to well-defined, stable subpopulations of cells. Gene expression covariation patterns are simplified precursors of Gene Regulatory Networks (GRNs), and play a crucial role in inferring causality and dynamics within GRNs. However, current gene clustering methods struggle to capture spatial organisation and relationship dynamics along developmental trajectories, while remaining vulnerable to noise and algorithmic stochasticity. RESULTS: Expanding on the ClustAssess framework, which shifted the cluster-centric assessment of populations of cells to an element-centric perspective, we propose to assess the covariation induced by gene graph clustering. The Starlng (abbrev) framework provides an optimised, interactive environment for the identification of the filtered modules. The pipeline identifies the stable configuration of clustering parameters and robust gene modules (nests of genes), followed by the removal of the outlier clusters based on the pseudotime variance. We illustrate Starlng on the identification of reliable, reproducible communities of genes, as well as reveal unbiased hierarchical relationships between higher-level cell clusters and more granular subgroups of genes. AVAILABILITY: Starlng is implemented in R and freely available at https://github.com/Core-Bioinformatics/Starlng . SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION: Supplementary data are available at Bioinformatics online.

works.title: CSK-DDI: Compensating Structural Incompleteness with Knowledge Graph World Knowledge for Drug–Drug Interaction Modeling
works.abstract: MOTIVATION: Drug-drug interaction (DDI) prediction is critical for drug safety, yet existing methods suffer from structural incompleteness in drug representation. Motif and molecular graph encodings capture local substructures and global topology but remain confined to the closed structural space of individual molecules, lacking cross-entity and contextual information and leading to limited generalization, especially in cold-start scenarios. To address this issue, we propose CSK-DDI (Compensating Structural Incompleteness with Knowledge Graph World Knowledge for Drug-Drug Interaction Modeling), a multimodal framework that jointly encodes motif-level chemical patterns, molecular graph topology, and biomedical knowledge graph (KG) context as complementary drug representations. The KG encodes drugs' contextual positions and relational semantics through multi-entity and multi-relation connections, providing global cross-entity and cross-semantic information that complements structural representations. The resulting fusion captures local chemical patterns, global topology, and biomedical context in a unified embedding. RESULTS: CSK-DDI employs a cross-attention mechanism to enable multi-view interaction among motif, molecular graph, and KG representations, producing unified structure-aware and context-aware drug embeddings. To improve robustness under sparse conditions, the model further incorporates a cold-start-oriented representation enhancement strategy. Experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate consistent improvements over state-of-the-art methods, with particularly notable gains in cold-start scenarios. AVAILABILITY AND IMPLEMENTATION: Source code and data are available at https://github.com/cgwcbz2/CSK-DDI and on Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.21415769.

works.title: Graphics processing unit-accelerated quantum simulation for molecular biology and drug discovery: algorithms, platforms, and emerging applications
works.abstract: Artificial intelligence has intensified the need for methods that describe molecular systems with quantum-mechanical accuracy. Gate-based quantum computing offers a principled framework for simulating electronic structure, molecular interactions, and biological processes at a fidelity inaccessible to classical force fields or density functional theory alone, yet scarce, noisy hardware limits direct experimentation. Graphics processing unit (GPU)-accelerated quantum simulation has emerged as a practical bridge, allowing quantum algorithms to be developed, validated, and benchmarked on classical infrastructure at 30-40 noiseless qubits, and far beyond where tensor-network methods apply. Unlike recent reviews organized around quantum machine learning (QML) or around hardware, this review is organized around the simulation layer itself and asks, for each domain, what can be established in simulation, what requires a quantum processor, and how the two connect in one hardware-agnostic workflow. We examine how the variational quantum eigensolver, quantum phase estimation, and sample-based hybrid schemes address electronic structure in small-molecule pharmacology; how quantum-enhanced conformational sampling complements AlphaFold; and how QML introduces alternative feature spaces for drug-target, structure-activity, and genomic modeling. We compile published GPU benchmarks, identify the molecular systems for which tensor-network simulation is and is not adequate, explain how GPU platforms accelerate error mitigation, and critically assess 2023-6 developments, including quantum-centric supercomputing, hybrid quantum Monte Carlo on trapped-ion hardware, protein binding-site prediction on utility-scale processors, below-threshold error correction, and a classically verifiable quantum-advantage claim. Framing GPU simulation as a near-term enabler rather than a final objective, the review offers a practical entry point for biological and pharmaceutical scientists.

works.title: Impact of training data on deep learning–based RNA 3D structure quality assessment
works.abstract: Accurate reference-free assessment of predicted RNA 3D structures is essential for large-scale RNA modeling, yet the impact of training data on deep learning-based quality predictors remains poorly understood. Here, we present a systematic cross-training analysis of three deep learning predictors for RNA 3D structure quality assessment, each originally developed on distinct training sets. By retraining each predictor on alternative (nonnative) datasets-including RNA3DQA, a new set created specifically for this project-and evaluating performance on independent RNA-Puzzles benchmarks, we systematically assess the relative contributions of model architecture and training data composition. Our results reveal pronounced differences in cross-dataset generalization, with predictors often performing better when trained on nonnative datasets than on their native ones. Notably, the impact of the training datasets varied across predictors, with RNA3DQA yielding the overall best accuracy and ranking stability results specifically for the ARES model. Native training sets yielded better performance for RNA3DCNN and lociPARSE. These findings demonstrate that the characteristics of the training data play a dominant, model-dependent role in shaping the performance and robustness of reference-free RNA 3D structure quality assessment methods. We conclude with practical recommendations for designing transferable training datasets and for benchmarking deep learning-based quality predictors in RNA structural bioinformatics.

works.title: The glutamine-aspartate metabolic tradeoff between fast growth and metabolic flexibility
works.abstract: Abstract Background Cancer cells develop selective dependencies on nutrients, creating potential opportunities for therapeutic intervention. However, how metabolic rewiring enables cancer cells to sustain proliferation while adapting to nutrient limitation remains incompletely understood. Results We develop a systematic framework to investigate nutrient dependencies and apply it to extracellular glutamine dependence. By measuring metabolite exchange rates across 54 cancer cell lines with different degrees of glutamine dependence, together with metabolic profiling of human stem-cell differentiation, we identify tissue-associated differences in the use of glutamine and aspartate for glutamate biosynthesis. These differences are linked to a trade-off between rapid proliferation and metabolic flexibility. Time-resolved intracellular metabolomics following glutamine withdrawal reveal a common limitation in purine biosynthesis. However, this metabolic limitation alone is insufficient to explain glutamine dependency, suggesting that additional regulatory responses to glutamine deprivation contribute to growth arrest. Conclusions Our study provides a systematic framework for identifying metabolic features associated with nutrient dependence and shows how established functions of glutamine, aspartate and asparagine are coordinated across diverse cancer cell types. This approach may support the mechanistic characterization and pharmacological targeting of metabolic dependencies beyond glutamine addiction.

works.title: Mitigating bias in spatial transcriptomic pipelines via human feedback with CSDE
works.abstract: Abstract Biological discovery from large-scale assays requires extensive preprocessing, during which raw outputs (e.g., images, sequences) are processed into structured forms amenable to analysis. In spatial transcriptomics, differential expression analysis depends on cell segmentation, gene expression quantification, and cell-type annotation, all prone to systematic errors. We introduce corrected spatial differential expression (CSDE), building on prediction-powered inference to leverage a small set of expert-validated cells to correct for preprocessing bias. Across three case studies, CSDE yields more reliable differential expression estimates than the prevalent approach neglecting preprocessing.

works.title: ArthroVerse: mapping protein family diversity across arthropod-associated microbiomes
works.abstract: Metagenomic studies of arthropod-associated microbiomes have generated vast amounts of sequence data, yet the functional and structural organization of these proteins remains largely unexplored. Here, we present ArthroVerse, the first comprehensive database of protein families derived from arthropod-associated metagenomes. Non-redundant protein families were generated after rigorous filtering, deduplication, and clustering. The protein families were further annotated with microbial taxonomy, host associations, protein structural information, and carbohydrate-active enzymes predictions. The resulting dataset integrates both metagenomic and reference genome-derived proteins, enabling systematic exploration of functional diversity, evolutionary relationships, and host-microbe interactions in insect microbiomes. ArthroVerse provides a valuable resource for the study of microbial ecology and arthropod physiology, offering unprecedented insight into the protein landscape of insect-associated microbial communities. ArthroVerse is publicly accessible at https://envofams.org/arthroverse/.

works.title: SynBioFooDB: a comprehensive resource for synthetic biology-driven food biomanufacturing
works.abstract: Enabled by synthetic biology and metabolic engineering, microbial biomanufacturing is reshaping the production of food-related compounds by offering sustainable alternatives to resource-intensive extraction and conventional chemical synthesis. However, information linking food-related compounds to biosynthetic pathways and microbial biomanufacturing evidence remains fragmented across the literature and poorly represented in existing food-oriented resources, hindering cross-study comparison, evidence synthesis, and rational design of microbial production systems. Here, we present SynBioFooDB (https://synbiofoodb.biodesign.ac.cn/), a knowledgebase dedicated to synthetic biology-driven food biomanufacturing. SynBioFooDB integrates 74 237 food-related compounds with standardized chemical identities and annotations covering food occurrence, bioactivity, toxicity, and regulatory information. It further provides expert-curated biomanufacturing evidence for 1054 compounds from 5592 publications, linking microbial hosts, substrates, genetic modifications, and quantitative production metrics through structured and traceable records. The database also contains 2002 literature-reported biosynthetic pathways for 971 compounds, enabling comparison of alternative precursors, enzyme combinations, and pathway architectures. For compounds without literature-reported pathways, SynBioFooDB provides computationally predicted candidate pathways to facilitate pathway prioritization and experimental evaluation. By integrating compound-level context, biomanufacturing evidence, and biosynthetic pathway information, SynBioFooDB supports systematic exploration, comparison, and rational design of microbial production strategies for food-related compounds.

works.title: KEGG for characterizing genomes and pathways in the biosphere
works.abstract: The KEGG database (https://www.kegg.jp) has been developed as a model of the biological systems. By organizing knowledge of cellular and organism-level functions in the form of molecular wiring diagrams, the model enables generating new knowledge and finding practical applications. The KO (KEGG Orthology) dataset plays the basic role of organizing knowledge. KO is an ortholog with functional relevance, generalizing experimental evidence in specific organisms to other organisms. KEGG molecular networks, including pathway maps and modules, are generic networks with KOs as network nodes, and thus KEGG mapping from genomes to pathways can be applied to any organism. As the number of KOs increases and the KO annotation rate improves, KEGG mapping is further expanded. A set of KOs in the genome and a set of modules in the metabolic pathways are now used to characterize various data objects in the biosphere, including organisms, organism groups, microbiomes, viruses, and their combinations, such as endosymbiont-host, microbiome-host, and virus-host relationships. Furthermore, a simple measure of similarity either by KO compositions or module compositions is introduced to compare organism groups. The resulting similarity dendrograms possibly reflect similarity of cellular functions or, more specifically, metabolic functions, which can be compared with phylogenetic trees.

works.title: SureChEMBL in 2026: an open database of chemical and biomedical annotations from the patent literature
works.abstract: The patent literature is a major source of scientific and technical information for drug discovery, often disclosing chemical structures, biological targets, therapeutic indications, and structure-activity relationships before they appear in the scientific literature. However, patent documents are difficult to analyse at scale because of their volume, legal and technical language, heterogeneous formats, and frequent use of nonmachine-readable representations for chemical structures. Since 2015, SureChEMBL has provided open access to chemical information automatically extracted from patent documents. Here, we present a major redesign of the SureChEMBL resource. The updated platform is built on a modern architecture and includes redesigned extraction, chemistry registration, search and data-delivery workflows, together with large-scale reprocessing of the historical corpus through a unified standardization pipeline. SureChEMBL also introduces automatically generated biomedical annotations for genes, proteins, diseases, and mechanisms, linking patent chemistry to biological context. The resource currently contains 122 million patents, 44 million chemically annotated documents, 31 million chemical structures, and 1 million biomedical entity annotations, accessible through https://www.surechembl.org/, an API and the downloadable Bulk Data.

works.title: OmniVira: a knowledgebase of source-linked evidence on viral spillover and cross-species transmission
works.abstract: Zoonotic viral emergence poses persistent challenges to global health, yet evidence relevant to spillover and cross-species transmission is dispersed across surveillance, epidemiological, experimental, mechanistic, and genomic studies. Here, we present OmniVira (https://omnivira.org/), a curated knowledgebase that transforms literature-derived findings into structured, traceable, and reusable OmniVira Evidence (OVE) records. OmniVira implements an auditable article-evidence framework linking individual findings and supporting text to normalized virus, host, and geographic entities, and relevant biological context. A domain-specific ontology organizes 14 evidence types into five categories: Zoonotic Surveillance, Transmission Evidence, Experimental Infection, Functional Mechanism, and Genomic Evolution. The platform integrates ontology-guided curation, large language model-assisted literature screening and candidate extraction, automated consistency checks, and curator review of flagged or ambiguous records, enabling daily updates. As of 4 August 2026, OmniVira contained 8072 publicly retrievable OVE records derived from 2623 source articles, spanning 60 ICTV virus families, 55 host orders, and 121 countries. Its responsive interface supports evidence-centred retrieval, source-text verification, and exploration of linked virus-host-literature relationships across desktop and mobile browsers. OmniVira provides a transparent, context-preserving resource for systematic comparison and synthesis of evidence related to zoonotic viral emergence and cross-species transmission.

works.title: PED in 2027: integrating experimental and predicted protein conformational ensembles at scale
works.abstract: The Protein Ensemble Database (PED; https://proteinensemble.org) is the primary deposition resource for structural ensembles of intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs) and intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). PED 2027 (released in September 2026) substantially expands its scope by integrating ensembles determined or refined using experimental data with clearly identified collections of computational predictions. The release introduces a multi-method collection targeting 3319 DisProt proteins and 2452 manually curated disordered regions, together with AlphaFlex ensembles for 10 022 human proteins containing IDRs. Alternative predictions for the same sequence are retained as independent records with method-specific provenance, enabling comparison across ensemble-generation approaches. A scalable deposition workflow accommodates individual experimental studies and proteome-scale collections while preserving quality control and curator oversight. The PED controlled vocabulary standardizes experimental data acquisition, computational generation, selection, and refinement. Precomputed IDPEnsembleTools and CIDER analyses provide structural and sequence-derived descriptors directly on ensemble pages. A redesigned interface and extended REST API support discovery, visualization, download and programmatic access. Interoperability with UniProt, DisProt, MobiDB, and experimental-data repositories connects ensembles with sequences, annotations, and supporting measurements. PED 2027 therefore provides an interoperable, analysis-ready platform for studying IDP/IDR conformational behaviour.

works.title: Omni-ARMD: an integrated genomic and clinical knowledgebase bridging clinical phenotypes and molecular determinants of antimicrobial resistance
works.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat, yet its molecular determinants remain difficult to characterize in real-world settings, as genomic and clinical data are fragmented across resources. Existing databases typically separate gene-level mechanisms, curated genotype-phenotype associations, and large-scale clinical antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) data, limiting cross-scale interpretation. Here, we present Omni-ARMD, an open-access knowledgebase that integrates multi-source genomic and clinical data to systematically infer genotype-phenotype relationships in AMR. Omni-ARMD bridges large-scale clinical AST records and gene-level resistance evidence through a confidence-weighted log-odds enrichment framework, which quantifies genotype-phenotype associations at the organism-antimicrobial level and integrates these associations into aggregated cross-domain evidence representations. The current release includes over 12 million de-identified microbiology records from more than 1 million patients, harmonized to generate over 7.83 million standardized AST records. It also integrates over 0.36 million gene-phenotype associations, spanning 38 organisms, 52 antimicrobials, and 375 resistance genes. Omni-ARMD links over 5.16 million clinical records to genomic evidence, achieving a 65.86% match rate and a 2.61% coverage of organism-antimicrobial pairs. Omni-ARMD provides interactive modules for clinical investigation, genomic evidence analysis, mechanistic interpretation, and artificial intelligence-assisted exploration, enabling integrative and data-driven discovery in AMR. Omni-ARMD is freely available at www.omniarmd.cn.

works.title: In silico prediction of metabolic trait robustness in microbial cells
works.abstract: Microbial strains undergo notable biomass expansion in industrial applications subjecting populations to Darwinian selection. The consequent adaptive evolution may threaten the often tediously developed desired metabolic traits of the strains, such as flavor or platform chemical production. Yet, it remains unresolved how to predict the evolutionary trait robustness. Here, we propose TRAEV (Trait Robustness Against EVolution), a computational framework for in silico prediction of evolutionary robustness of metabolic traits and trajectories of desired traits in application environments. TRAEV uses constraint-based metabolic models for predicting environment-dependent trait-fitness dependencies and accounts for the stochasticity of adaptive evolution by using Monte Carlo-based perturbation analysis. First, TRAEV predicts the immediate metabolic phenotype in the new environment, and then, the subsequent evolutionary trajectories of fitness and desired trait. Metabolic trait robustness is quantified from the evolutionary trajectories as two scores: Robustness Score (RS) and Trade-off Score (TS). RS represents trait robustness and the overall trait level during evolutionary adaptation, whereas TS captures trait–fitness trade-offs. We validated TRAEV by predicting relative evolutionary robustness of heterologous pigmentation of two engineered Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains and two desired aroma generation traits by multiple wine strains of S. cerevisiae if they were developed via a laboratory selection process. Thus, we showed how TRAEV predictions could guide strain development. TRAEV can be integrated into computational strain design workflows across microbial strains, desired metabolic traits, and application environments. Ultimately, model-predicted evolutionary robustness of desired metabolic traits can guide both strain and process development and help enhancing the economic attractiveness of industrial applications using microbial cells.

works.title: KmerSignificance score: A discriminative and biologically informed framework for viral k-mer prioritization
works.abstract: Distinguishing closely related viral strains requires identifying genomic regions where subtle sequence differences carry biological significance. While k -mer-based approaches offer computational efficiency for genome analysis, existing methods lack standardized frameworks for evaluating which k -mers are most informative. Current selection strategies focus primarily on statistical discriminative power without integrating biological context. We introduce KmerSignificance Score (KSS), a k -mer prioritization framework combining three components: an information-theoretic method measuring strain-distinguishing capacity, an optimized amino acid substitution matrix (MIYATA_EVO) for mutation impact assessment, and a protein characterization score derived from annotations and database cross-references retrieved through UniProt. All three component scores and the integrated KSS are bounded in [0,1] by construction, providing a common numerical scale for ranking positions within a dataset. The discriminative component achieved a mean F1 of 0.881, not significantly different from chi-squared (0.876), the strongest of eight baselines. Top-ranked selections from the discriminative component nonetheless differed from those produced by chi-squared, especially for SARS-CoV-2 and HIV-1. The MIYATA_EVO matrix, optimized using a genetic algorithm, increased the composite agreement score across eight amino acid characteristics by 28.4% over the original MIYATA matrix. Across 17,471 viral proteins, the protein characterization score tracked UniProt’s five-level annotation score closely (Kendall’s τ = 0.775 ), as expected for measures drawing on overlapping annotation content. Within each level, the continuous score provided finer numerical resolution among proteins. Literature cross-referencing on SARS-CoV-2 (278,738 sequences, 19 Pango-derived lineage labels), HIV-1 (12,223 sequences, 15 subtype labels), and human cytomegalovirus (HCMV; 399–646 sequences, 4–8 locus-specific genotypes) found that the top-ranked k -mers reported here map to established variant-defining mutations, subtype-specific polymorphisms, and genotype markers. KSS provides a standardized framework for viral k -mer prioritization with potential applications in variant surveillance, molecular epidemiology, and functional annotation. The tool is available at https://github.com/bioinfoUQAM/KmerSignificanceScore .

works.title: Evolutionary and dynamic constraints converge on a conserved coupling sector in thermally adapted GH1 β-glucosidases
works.abstract: How protein sequences evolve to maintain functional conformational dynamics under thermal stress remains an important question in molecular evolution. Thermophilic enzymes are often considered to achieve stability primarily through enhanced structural rigidity, yet thermal adaptation may also involve the preservation or reorganization of correlated motions across the protein scaffold. Here, we compared three glycoside hydrolase family 1 β-glucosidases-BsBgl1A, 9UPT, and LQBG8-that share a conserved (β/α)8 TIM-barrel fold but display distinct optimal temperatures of approximately 45, 65, and 70 °C, respectively. By integrating comparative structural analysis, three independent 1 μs molecular dynamics simulations at 300, 325, and 350 K, neural relational inference of residue-level dynamic coupling, and family-level coevolutionary analysis, we identified distinct dynamic strategies associated with their thermal phenotypes. All three enzymes retained their global compactness and principal secondary-structure framework across the simulated temperatures, indicating that differences in RMSD and residue flexibility did not reflect large-scale unfolding. BsBgl1A showed the strongest temperature sensitivity, with increased structural deviation and residue mobility at 350 K. Its inferred interaction network exhibited a non-monotonic response, characterized by pronounced overcoupling at 325 K followed by reduced connectivity at 350 K. In contrast, 9UPT maintained relatively restrained residue dynamics and a highly reproducible coupling topology across temperatures. LQBG8 combined substantial local conformational flexibility with persistent long-range coupling and retained the highest directed network density at 350 K. Across the three enzymes, the βα5-βα7 region repeatedly emerged as a shared structural and dynamic center. Coevolutionary couplings were also enriched in TIM-barrel-associated regions that spatially converged on this sector. These findings indicate that thermal adaptation in GH1 β-glucosidases is not adequately explained by uniform structural rigidification. Instead, enzymes with the same conserved fold may adopt distinct organizations of correlated motion, while greater thermal adaptation is associated with the persistence or reorganization of a βα5-βα7-centered dynamic coupling pattern under elevated temperature. The correspondence between dynamic coupling and coevolutionary enrichment is consistent with long-term evolutionary constraint on this structural sector, although it does not establish direct selection on the network as an independent functional unit. Our results therefore provide a testable framework in which thermostability reflects a balance among local stabilization, regional flexibility, and the resilience of higher-order dynamic organization.

works.title: An extensible deep learning framework for multi-type chromatin interaction prediction through hierarchical adaptation strategies
works.abstract: Three-dimensional chromatin interactions play essential roles in gene regulation, yet computational prediction of diverse interaction types remains largely dependent on specialized, single-task models. Here, we present UniLoopNet, a multi-task deep learning framework that predicts multiple types of chromatin interactions including enhancer-promoter interactions, enhancer-enhancer interactions, CTCF-mediated loops, and stripe-associated interactions from DNA sequences. UniLoopNet employs a shared encoder-decoder architecture with hierarchical adaptation strategies, integrating multi-task, transfer, and continual learning based on task semantic similarity. Comprehensive benchmarking across multiple cell lines demonstrates that UniLoopNet outperforms existing specialized and multi-task approaches, with AUROCs exceeding 0.90 in most tasks. Under stringent evaluation settings, including chromosome-matched, distance-matched, realistic imbalanced, and locus-disjoint tests, AUROCs range from 0.8934 to 0.9366. In the realistic 1:5 class-imbalance setting, the AUPRCs for enhancer-promoter and enhancer-enhancer interaction prediction are 0.7956 and 0.6935, respectively. Cross-cell-line transfer experiments further show that applying UniLoopNet to another cell line requires adaptation by supervised fine-tuning on target-cell-line data, after which performance is comparable to that of within-cell-line training. Notably, the framework exhibits data efficiency in experiments with substantially reduced training data. Interpretability analyses reveal that the learned sequence features are associated with known transcription factor binding sites and uncover differential regulatory effects of disease-associated variants. UniLoopNet provides a versatile and data-efficient framework for sequence-based prediction and interpretation of diverse 3D genome interactions, complementing existing sequence-to-map approaches while improving the understanding of sequence-encoded regulatory potential.

works.title: Ten simple rules for preparing a job application for an academic position
Eight quick tips for using the reactome knowledgebase
Ten simple rules for designing your career pivot
Attentive interpretable tabular learning (TabNet) for miRNA expression classification in cervical cancer and Alzheimer's disease
works.abstract: The classification of RNA sequencing (RNA-seq) data presents a fundamental challenge in computational biomedicine: raw read counts are high-dimensional, over-dispersed, and heteroscedastic, requiring careful preprocessing before machine learning models can be applied. Existing deep learning approaches for RNA-seq classification have largely overlooked the tabular nature of genomic expression data and have offered limited embedded interpretability. This study proposes TabNet, an attentive interpretable tabular learning architecture, as a framework for miRNA-based disease classification and evaluates its performance and interpretability against three established baseline models. Two publicly available miRNA expression datasets were examined: a cervical cancer cohort (58 samples, 714 miRNAs) and an Alzheimer's disease cohort (70 samples, 503 miRNAs). Raw count data were preprocessed following the MLSeq framework, encompassing DESeq median-ratio normalisation, near-zero variance filtering, supervised gene ranking based on DESeq differential expression analysis, and the DESeq variance-stabilising transformation (vst). Gene subsets corresponding to 5%, 10%, and 30% of the post-filtering feature space were evaluated. TabNet was benchmarked against eight baselines spanning four learning paradigms: a 1D Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), a Long Short-Term Memory network (LSTM), Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest, ElasticNet-regularised logistic regression, a Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), the prior-fitted transformer TabPFN, and the inherently interpretable Explainable Boosting Machine (EBM). Each configuration was assessed over 50 independent random train/test splits (70%/30%) under a strict leakage-free protocol in which all preprocessing, hyperparameter selection, and early stopping relied exclusively on inner validation subsets of the training partitions; all metrics are reported as mean $$\pm $$ SD. Under the leakage-free protocol, a group of four methods reached a statistically indistinguishable accuracy ceiling: on the cervical cancer dataset, ElasticNet (95.06% $$\pm $$ 4.66), EBM (94.94% $$\pm $$ 4.60), TabPFN (94.71% $$\pm $$ 4.64), and Random Forest (94.35% $$\pm $$ 5.82); on the Alzheimer's disease dataset, TabPFN (70.86% $$\pm $$ 10.26), EBM (70.67% $$\pm $$ 12.67), and ElasticNet (70.48% $$\pm $$ 9.76) led. TabNet reached 85.18% $$\pm $$ 11.10 (cervical) and 64.38% $$\pm $$ 11.23 (Alzheimer's) at its respective best levels -- below the top tier, but with the distinctive property of producing sparse, instance-level attention explanations as part of its forward computation. Supplementary analyses showed that self-supervised pre-training conferred no significant benefit at these cohort sizes, that results were robust to the choice between supervised differential-expression and unsupervised variance feature ranking, and that instance-level attention patterns varied substantially across splits, supporting their use as illustrative rather than confirmatory evidence. In rigorously leakage-controlled small-cohort miRNA classification, strongly regularised classical models, glass-box additive models, and prior-fitted transformers converge to the same accuracy ceiling, and no evaluated method -- including attention-based deep learning -- surpasses it. Within this landscape, TabNet remains distinctive as the only evaluated deep architecture whose sequential attention mechanism produces sparse instance-level miRNA attributions as an inherent part of prediction, offering a trade-off between embedded interpretability and a moderate accuracy cost that we quantify precisely. These results argue for protocol-first evaluation and calibrated claims when deep tabular models are applied to small transcriptomic cohorts.

works.title: Experimentally Defined Tm-Guided Exon–Exon Junction Primer Design Enables Specific Discrimination of Transcript Variants with High Structural Overlap
works.abstract: Accurate detection of RNA splice variants is often hindered when transcripts lack large distinguishable exonic regions, making conventional PCR strategies challenging. We developed a simple melting temperature (Tm)-guided exon-exon junction (EEJ) RT-PCR method to enable variant-specific detection under these conditions. Uni-directional primers spanning exon-exon junctions were designed so that approximately each half anneals to adjacent exons. The Tm of each half-site was set >7°C below the annealing temperature, preventing stable binding to individual exons and enforcing junction-dependent amplification. The method was evaluated using HTRA1-AS1 long noncoding RNA variants that share overlapping exon sequences but differ in splice connectivity. HTRA1-AS1 comprises five variants, only one with a large distinguishable exon. Tm-guided EEJ primers robustly discriminated the remaining four variants. After optimization, amplification yielded sharp, single bands with minimal cross-reactivity. Compared with conventional designs, this approach reduced heteroduplex and heteroquadruplex formation, improving band clarity. Sanger sequencing confirmed junction specificity, and the method performed well in multiplex settings. Overall, Tm-guided EEJ RT-PCR is a cost-effective, high-resolution approach for detecting RNA variants lacking easily distinguishable exonic regions, readily compatible with standard RT-PCR and qPCR workflows.

works.title: Candidate Predictors for WJ-MSC ATMP Characterization: An Integrative Machine-Learning Framework
Modeling Antibody Interactions with Hemagglutinin and Neuraminidase Proteins of Influenza A Virus: Insights into Applicability of Docking and AlphaFold3
New biomaterial strategies for ocular repair and regeneration – hydrogels, 3D printing, novel tissue-engineering approaches and breakthrough technologies
works.abstract: In ophthalmology, biomaterials and 3D printing have many applications, including fabricating preoperative eye models, personalized lenses and glasses, orbital implants, and drug delivery systems.This review, however, focuses on new biomaterial strategies for ocular tissue regeneration, taking into account the latest developments in hydrogels, 3D-printing, bioprinting and novel tissue-engineering approaches.Studies on the eye mainly focus on the cornea and retina, with only a few on the sclera and crystalline lenses.Regarding the cornea, 3D printing offers promising advances in creating a complete artificial cornea, and significant progress has been made in developing its three different layers.However, printing its multilayers remains challenging.Concerning the retina, most studies remain in the in vitro stage due to its high complexity and the many cell types that compose it.Ophthalmic biomaterials and bioinks must support cell viability and, in the case of the cornea, preserve transparency and provide high mechanical strength.Both cell-laden and acellular bioinks are being developed.Cell-laden bioinks enable direct tissue regeneration but pose challenges related to cell survival.Consequently, many studies have focused on acellular biomaterials, which offer an extended shelf life, enhanced sterility, and a more straightforward regulatory process.Nowadays, significant progress has been made in cell therapy, reprogramming, biomaterials, and 3D printing for ophthalmology.These advances may help millions of patients regain their vision and significantly improve their quality of life.Iris

works.title: Cross-country comparative genomics of Campylobacter jejuni in East Africa: A harmonized One Health comparative genomic re-analysis
works.abstract: Abstract Motivation Campylobacter jejuni is a major foodborne zoonotic pathogen associated with antimicrobial resistance (AMR), particularly in low- and middle-income countries with limited genomic surveillance. We analysed 225 publicly available C.jejuni genomes from Ethiopia, Kenya, and Tanzania using a harmonized whole-genome sequencing workflow within a One Health framework. Analyses included genome assembly, annotation, AMR and virulence gene screening, plasmid replicon and mobile genetic element detection, multilocus sequence typing (MLST), phylogenetic reconstruction, principal component analysis (PCA), and minimum spanning tree (MST) analysis. Results Using thresholds of ≥ 90% nucleotide identity and ≥60% gene coverage, blaOXA-193 was detected in 66.67% (150/225) of genomes, tet(O) in 18.22% (41/225), tet(O/32/O) in 4.00% (9/225), and blaOXA-61 in 1.33% (3/225). The gyrA T86I substitution occurred in 24.9% (56/225) of isolates. The applied screening approach detected no acquired macrolide resistance determinants. Virulence-associated gene profiles were broadly conserved, with variation in selected genes. Three known plasmid replicon types and prophage-associated intA hits were identified. Phylogenomic analysis revealed 65 sequence types and substantial genetic overlap between poultry- and human-associated isolates, indicating relatedness but not proving direct transmission. These findings highlight the importance of integrated One Health genomic surveillance for monitoring AMR and genomic diversity of C. jejuni in East Africa. Availability and implementation data underlying this article will be shared on reasonable request to the corresponding author

works.title: BRAID: Batch-effect Reconciliation and Anomaly-aware Imputation for Data
works.abstract: Abstract Motivation High-throughput biomedical data often contain missing values, which, if mismanaged, can distort downstream analysis. While various imputation methods exist, few account for systematic bias from batch effects. Moreover, many batch effect correction algorithms require complete data, making imputation a prerequisite. This sequence inadvertently creates confounding issues, as batch effects can hinder imputation performance. Despite this, standard imputation evaluation practices rarely consider imputation-batch interactions. Results To address this, we propose BRAID (Batch-effect Reconciliation and Anomaly-aware Imputation for Data), an evaluation framework that systematically assesses imputation techniques under assumed batch-free and batch-affected conditions, using ComBat as the primary correction algorithm and limma to assess generalization. Via controlled batch and missing value simulations applied to diverse real-world datasets, we find that many popular imputation methods exhibit non-negligible performance degradation or instability when batch effects are present, and that by incrementing batch effect intensities, some degrade with greater sensitivity than others. A case study involving K-Nearest Neighbours applied to samples further highlights how parameter choice can induce batch bias, underscoring the need for batch-conscious imputation. BRAID equips researchers with an evaluation framework to assess and compare imputation methods under controlled or simulated conditions of interest, informing reliability and reproducibility. Availability and implementation BRAID is available at https://github.com/HarvardHui/BRAID.

works.title: The Gujarat Tribal Genome Project (2kTGP)
Decoupling cis and trans transcriptional influences
Using SpliceAI to triage splice-altering variants in 7,220 individuals with rare conditions highlights limitations of the precomputed scores
works.abstract: Abstract Background SpliceAI is a deep learning algorithm that predicts whether genetic variants are likely to affect splicing. Precomputed SpliceAI predictions for all theoretical SNVs and small indels were released in 2019, and are used by variant annotation tools such as VEP and dbNSFP to batch annotate large numbers of variants quickly.
